    - **Name:** Optional DIY hinged pyramidal horn for 1420 MHz (flat-pack panels of 35 cm or less)
    - **Category:** Radio-astronomy antenna (DIY, foldable)
    - **Purpose in lab:** A higher-gain, low-sidelobe 21 cm antenna for rotation-curve work and better Sun-noise contrast, still with no dish.
    - **Key specs:** - Rigid reference (arXiv 2512.19262): 75 x 60 cm aperture, 18.5 dBi simulated, FWHM 18.1 by 21.3 degrees, waveguide can 16.8 x 10.2 x 24.1 cm, SAWbird+ H1. 'Successfully detected the Galactic 21 cm HI line.'
  - A hinged flat-pack copy (each wall split into 2-3 hinged panels of 35 cm or less) is my untested adaptation.
    - **Size weight power:** - Flat-packed: about 35 x 35 x 3 cm plus the waveguide can (estimate).
  - Weight: about 0.6-1 kg in foam board with aluminium tape (estimate).
  - Power: none.
    - **Interface and linux:** SMA probe in the can, then the SAWbird+ H1 and the SDR. Same software as the helicone.
    - **Price:** About $15-30 in materials (estimate).
    - **Tier:** optional
    - **Integration notes:** The horn breaks the size rule unless every wall is hinged. The aperture is at the edge of what a backpack carries. Only build it if helicone results show you need more gain.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://arxiv.org/html/2512.19262v1
    - **Availability:** DIY.
    - **Cheaper alternative:** The reused helicone (previous item).
    - **Safety notes:** Passive. Large wind area: do not leave it unattended on a tripod.
  11.
    - **Name:** CANADUINO 60 kHz (WWVB/MSF/JJY60) or 77.5 kHz (DCF77) atomic-clock receiver module
    - **Category:** LF time-signal receiver (GPIO)
    - **Purpose in lab:** Receive and decode LF time signals, and compare the decoded minute and second marks with GNSS PPS. This is a time-transfer and propagation exercise and independent backup time.
    - **Key specs:** - VERIFIED (Universal-Solder): Micro Analog Systems ICs, 2-5.5 V supply, 10 mA output, antenna Q above 100.
  - Kit form: the crystal and antenna must be soldered on.
  - The 60 kHz loopstick is 60 mm long with a 10 mm core.
  - A comparison page notes that WWVB also uses PSK, which needs ES100-style receivers. This module uses the AM envelope.
    - **Size weight power:** Small PCB plus a 60 mm ferrite rod. A few mA at 3.3 V (estimate).
    - **Interface and linux:** Digital pulse output to one 40-pin GPIO (3.3 V).
  - DCF77: dcf77pi (DCF77 only; 'FreeBSD, Linux: full support'; GPIO pin set in config).
  - MSF/WWVB: write a small libgpiod pulse-width decoder (my own suggestion, untested on the Q6A).
    - **Price:** 60 kHz: CAD 17.90 list (CAD 14.32 sale ended) or USD 10.88 at Universal-Solder. The 77.5 kHz version is listed on Universal-Solder (price not captured). Loopstick C$2.49. The Tindie listing is closed.
    - **Tier:** optional
    - **Integration notes:** - Mount the ferrite at least 15-20 cm from the Q6A bucks, the HDMI cable and the display, ideally in a lid pocket. Turn it broadside to the transmitter.
  - A full decode needs 2 minutes or more without errors.
  - Pick the version for your region: DCF77 for Europe, MSF for the UK and western Europe, WWVB for North America, JJY for Japan.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://universal-solder.ca/60khz-wwvb-atomic-clock-receiver/
      - https://universal-solder.ca/?p=246
      - https://www.universal-solder.ca/comparison-wwvb-msf-jjy-dcf77/
      - https://www.universal-solder.ca/product/loopstick-antenna-60khz-for-atomic-clock-receiver/
      - https://github.com/rene0/dcf77pi
    - **Availability:** Universal-Solder website, eBay, Amazon and DigiKey (per the closed Tindie page).
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Use the HF+ Discovery with the YouLoop to see the carrier and AM keying in SDR++. It needs no extra hardware but gives no automatic decoding.
    - **Safety notes:** 3.3 V logic only. Never feed it 5 V on a GPIO line.
  12.
    - **Name:** SparkFun Lightning Detector - AS3935 (SEN-15441)
    - **Category:** Lightning/sferics sensor (SPI)
    - **Purpose in lab:** Real-time detection of nearby lightning with distance estimates. This is a storm-safety interlock for outdoor antenna work and adds a geophysics data log.
    - **Key specs:** VERIFIED (SparkFun): AMS OSRAM AS3935, detection up to 40 km, distance to the storm front within 1 km in 14 steps, 500 kHz tuned antenna. SPI is supported; I2C hardware is present 'but SparkFun does not support it'. 2.4-5.5 V.
    - **Size weight power:** Small breakout (size and current not listed). mW-class (estimate).
    - **Interface and linux:** SPI plus an IRQ GPIO on the 40-pin header at 3.3 V. Only an Arduino library is listed. On Linux, use spidev with a community Python AS3935 library or your own driver (unverified on the Q6A).
    - **Price:** $34.95 (SparkFun, in stock)
    - **Tier:** optional
    - **Integration notes:** - Its 500 kHz antenna will hear the handheld's switching noise, so mount it at least 10 cm from the bucks and display.
  - Use the indoor/outdoor AFE setting, mask disturbers, and log events with GNSS time.
  - Wire it as an alert: 'storm under 15 km: lower the loop and wire antennas'.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.sparkfun.com/products/15441
    - **Availability:** In stock at SparkFun and its distributors.
    - **Cheaper alternative:** A sferics waterfall from the HF+ Discovery (no distance), or live lightning maps when online.
    - **Safety notes:** An early-warning aid only, not a safety device. Stop outdoor antenna work when it reports storms within about 15 km.
  13.
    - **Name:** Existing RTL-SDR Blog multipurpose dipole kit, re-set per band (FM, DAB, AIS/NOAA WX, radiosondes, ADS-B)
    - **Category:** VHF/UHF antenna (telescopic, reuse)
    - **Purpose in lab:** One 23 cm-collapsed kit covers every new VHF/UHF monitoring band. No new antenna is needed.
    - **Key specs:** VERIFIED (antenna digest): 2 telescopic elements of 23 cm to 1 m, 2 of 5-13 cm, M5 thread, 60 cm + 3 m RG174, tripod and suction mount.
  
  Arm length per band (my calculation, about 0.95 x quarter wave; trim with the VNA):
  - FM at 98 MHz: 73 cm, horizontal
  - AIS / NOAA WX at 162 MHz: 44 cm, vertical
  - DAB Band III at 174-240 MHz: about 33-34 cm, vertical
  - Radiosondes at 403 MHz: 17.7 cm, vertical
  - ADS-B at 1090 MHz: 6.5 cm (short elements), vertical
    - **Size weight power:** Packed 23 x 8 x 5 cm, 150-250 g (estimates from the antenna digest). Passive.
    - **Interface and linux:** SMA to either V4L.
    - **Price:** $17.95 (already in the BOM)
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** - Use it vertical for AIS, ADS-B, sondes and DAB.
  - Remove the FM band-stop for FM-RDS work.
  - Keep the band-stop in for AIS, NOAA WX and DAB. It passes them (under 0.5 dB loss below 1 GHz).
  - The auto_rx wiki says a quarter-wave monopole or a 70 cm antenna is usually enough for sondes.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/buy-rtl-sdr-dvb-t-dongles/
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/DIPOLE
      - https://github.com/projecthorus/radiosonde_auto_rx/wiki
    - **Availability:** Already in the kit. Carry a spare telescopic pair.
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Copper wire quarter-wave ground planes on an SMA bulkhead (DIY, under $5, estimate).
    - **Safety notes:** Passive.
  14.
    - **Name:** Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
    - **Category:** Software (no hardware)
    - **Purpose in lab:** Decoders and loggers for every new capability, all running locally with no network.
    - **Key specs:** VERIFIED packages and repos:
  - wsjtx 2.7.0~rc3 (noble universe, arm64)
  - fldigi 4.2.03 (arm64): WEFAX, 'NAVTEX and SITOR-B', RTTY, SYNOP decoding, frequency measurement
  - multimon-ng 1.3.0 (arm64): use only its EAS mode
  - readsb (Debian package via dpkg-buildpackage, --device-type rtlsdr, works with tar1090)
  - dump978-fa (SoapySDR, rtlsdr)
  - AIS-catcher (RTL-SDR incl. V4, Airspy incl. HF+, SoapySDR; Debian/Fedora install script or source; built-in web viewer)
  - radiosonde_auto_rx (Debian native or ghcr.io Docker; local web UI on port 5000; RS41/RS92/DFM/M10/M20/iMet/LMS6-400/1680 and more)
  - chasemapper (offline tiles via tile_server_enabled; gpsd or serial GPS input)
  - welle.io / welle-cli -w (Debian/Ubuntu packages, Flatpak for arm64)
  - redsea (meson build with liquid-dsp; JSON per RDS group)
  - nrsc5 (US HD Radio, RTL-SDR)
  - Virgo (pip astro-virgo)
  - dcf77pi
  
  SDR++ and GNU Radio are already in the stack.
    - **Size weight power:** Software only. CPU: all are light except welle.io and Virgo FFT averaging (estimate: well under 2 A76 cores).
    - **Interface and linux:** Everything must link the patched V4L librtlsdr2.
  - Docker images and installers that bundle an older librtlsdr will be 'deaf' on the V4L (narrowband digest). Build auto_rx natively, or rebuild its image on the patched package.
  - Check every binary with ldd for the patched librtlsdr.
  - Route SDR++ audio to WSJT-X and fldigi through a PipeWire null sink (pactl load-module module-null-sink).
  - chrony with the LC76G PPS gives WSJT-X far better than 1 s timing.
    - **Price:** Free and open source.
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** - Disable all uploaders by default (auto_rx SondeHub upload is ON by default in station.cfg). Store spots and frames locally and upload later only if wanted.
  - tar1090 and chasemapper need pre-downloaded map tiles for standalone use. Chasemapper supports this; tar1090 offline tiles are unverified.
  - Download the readsb aircraft database while online.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/wsjtx
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/fldigi
      - https://www.w1hkj.org/FldigiHelp/index_of_contents_page.html
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/multimon-ng
      - https://github.com/EliasOenal/multimon-ng
      - https://github.com/wiedehopf/readsb
      - https://github.com/flightaware/dump978
      - https://github.com/jvde-github/AIS-catcher
      - https://jvde-github.github.io/AIS-catcher-docs/installation/overview
      - https://github.com/projecthorus/radiosonde_auto_rx/wiki
      - https://github.com/projecthorus/radiosonde_auto_rx/wiki/Docker
      - https://github.com/projecthorus/chasemapper
      - https://github.com/AlbrechtL/welle.io
      - https://github.com/windytan/redsea
      - https://github.com/theori-io/nrsc5
      - https://github.com/0xCoto/Virgo
      - https://github.com/rene0/dcf77pi
    - **Availability:** apt (noble universe), GitHub and pip.
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Not applicable (free).
    - **Safety notes:** multimon-ng also contains pager and other private-traffic decoders. Do not enable them; use only EAS.
- **Capabilities added:**
  - HF reception from 0.5 to 28.8 MHz on the existing V4L through its built-in 28.8 MHz upconverter (no extra radio): shortwave broadcast, ham-band monitoring and utility broadcasts
  - FT8 and WSPR propagation monitoring (receive-only spotting, logged locally with GNSS-disciplined time)
  - NCDXF/IARU beacon propagation matrix (10 s slots, 3 min cycle, 100 W/10 W/1 W/100 mW power steps)
  - HF weather fax: DWD 3855/7880/13882.5 kHz, NOAA NMF/NMG/NMC, JMH. Also DWD RTTY with fldigi SYNOP decoding and NAVTEX on 518 kHz
  - HF time stations (WWV/WWVH/CHU) for listening and frequency calibration of the SDRs
  - With the HF+ Discovery: VLF/LF from 0.5 kHz, covering lightning sferics, LF time-station carriers, NDBs at 190-535 kHz, NAVTEX on 490 kHz and longwave broadcast
  - LF time-code decoding (DCF77, MSF, WWVB or JJY60, by region) compared against GNSS PPS
  - Local lightning detection with distance estimate up to 40 km, used as a storm interlock for outdoor antennas
  - ADS-B on 1090 MHz with a local map. Where public (US), UAT on 978 MHz with dump978-fa
  - AIS ship tracking on 161.975/162.025 MHz near coasts or large rivers
  - Radiosonde auto-detection, decoding, tracking and chase with offline maps, own GNSS position and IMU bearing. Includes 1680 MHz LMS6 sondes (US) through the existing L-band chain
  - FM broadcast RDS logging and DAB/DAB+ reception, plus US HD Radio (nrsc5) where present
  - NOAA Weather Radio with SAME/EAS header decoding (US and Canada)
  - 21 cm hydrogen-line spectroscopy of the Milky Way with a foldable helix or horn (no dish)
  - Sun-noise Y-factor and G/T checks at 1.4/1.7 GHz (helicone) and 10.5 GHz (QO-100 horn + LNB)
  - Location-tagged RF surveys (FM/DAB coverage, ADS-B range rings, HF noise floor vs site), using the device's own GNSS
- **Procedures:**
  1.
    - **Name:** HF bring-up and self-noise survey (do first)
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Boot on battery only. Unplug the charger, because the IP2368 switcher is an HF noise source.
      - 2. V4L with a 50-ohm terminator: in SDR++, record the noise floor at 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14 and 21 MHz in a 500 Hz RBW, at the chosen gain.
      - 3. Connect the MLA-30+ on 5-10 m of RG174 with ferrites at both ends, loop 2-3 m up and at least 5 m from the case. Turn on the bias tee (rtl_biast -b 1) and confirm with a multimeter at the loop end that it receives about 4.5 V.
      - 4. Repeat the noise readings. A 10-20 dB rise over the terminator on 7-10 MHz means external noise dominates, which is the goal (estimate).
      - 5. A/B each source with the antenna connected: display dimmed vs full, HDMI unplugged, LimeSDR idle vs streaming, Wi-Fi off, 12 V buck load step. Note any spur or line that moves.
      - 6. Fit ferrites, move the loop or change the display mode until the device's own spurs sit at least 6 dB below band noise.
      - 7. Optional bench MDS check: drive a low-level generator into the V4L through at least 60 dB of fixed attenuation. Conducted only; never connect a generator to an antenna.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - MLA-30+ active receive loop (generic; eBay/AliExpress)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  2.
    - **Name:** FT8/WSPR propagation monitor (receive-only)
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Check GNSS time: chronyc sources shows PPS locked, with offset under 1 ms.
      - 2. Set up audio: pactl load-module module-null-sink sink_name=sdr. In SDR++, select USB with a 3 kHz filter and send audio to 'sdr'. In WSJT-X, take input from 'sdr.monitor'.
      - 3. Tune the WSJT-X built-in dial frequency for the band (FT8 or WSPR), with SDR++ in USB on the same dial.
      - 4. Put in the AM high-pass filter if MW overload shows (spurious decodes, raised floor).
      - 5. Log ALL.TXT and wsjtx_log, and tag each session with the GNSS position.
      - 6. Plot distance and SNR against time of day; compare the MLA-30+ and the YouLoop+HF+.
      - 7. Uploading to WSPRnet or PSK Reporter is optional, later, when online.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - MLA-30+ active receive loop (generic; eBay/AliExpress)
      - RTL-SDR Blog Broadcast AM High-Pass Filter
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  3.
    - **Name:** NCDXF beacon propagation matrix
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Each beacon sends once on each band every 3 minutes, in 10 s slots: callsign plus four 1 s dashes at 100 W, 10 W, 1 W and 100 mW (ncdxf.org).
      - 2. Write a small SoapySDR Python script, timed from the GNSS-disciplined clock, that steps 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz each slot. These frequencies are the standard IBP set, not machine-verified here because the NCDXF table is JavaScript.
      - 3. For each slot, measure CW SNR in a 50-100 Hz bin for each dash. The weakest dash still heard gives the path margin in 10 dB steps.
      - 4. Map the slot to the beacon callsign from the NCDXF schedule. Use fldigi CW to spot-check IDs.
      - 5. Store a CSV of time, band, beacon and the highest decodable power step, and draw a beacon x band heat-map.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - MLA-30+ active receive loop (generic; eBay/AliExpress)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  4.
    - **Name:** HF weather fax, RTTY and NAVTEX
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Pick a station from NOAA's worldwide radiofax schedule (dated 7 Mar 2025):
  - DWD DDH3/DDK3/DDK6: 3855, 7880, 13882.5 kHz, 10 kW, F1C, white +425 Hz / black -425 Hz, 120 rpm, IOC 576
  - NMF Boston: 4235, 6340.5, 9110, 12750 kHz
  - NMG New Orleans: 4317.9, 8503.9, 12789.9, 17146.4 kHz
  - NMC Pt. Reyes: 4346, 8682, 12786, 17151.2, 22527 kHz
  - JMH: 3622.5, 7795, 13988.5 kHz
      - 2. In SDR++, select USB with a 3 kHz filter and the dial 1.9 kHz below the assigned frequency (usual practice). Send audio to the PipeWire sink.
      - 3. In fldigi WEFAX: centre 1900 Hz, auto-start on APT, IOC 576. Save the PNGs and tag each with time and GNSS position.
      - 4. DWD RTTY: switch to fldigi RTTY at 50 baud and 450 Hz shift (check DWD's current schedule; not verified here). Enable SYNOP decoding to turn coded weather reports into text.
      - 5. NAVTEX: 518 kHz is just above the V4L's 500 kHz limit. Use fldigi 'NAVTEX and SITOR-B'. Use the HF+ Discovery for 490 kHz or weak 518 kHz reception. Remove the AM high-pass filter for both.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - MLA-30+ active receive loop (generic; eBay/AliExpress)
      - Airspy HF+ Discovery
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  5.
    - **Name:** Time signals and SDR frequency calibration
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. HF: tune WWV/WWVH (2.5, 5, 10, 15 MHz) or CHU (3.33, 7.85, 14.67 MHz), whichever propagates. These frequencies are general knowledge, not fetched in this run.
      - 2. Run fldigi 'Frequency Measurement & Analysis' on the carrier. The offset in Hz divided by the carrier frequency in MHz is the V4L ppm error, give or take ionospheric Doppler of about 0.1-1 Hz. Write the correction into SDR++, SatDump and auto_rx.
      - 3. LF: solder the CANADUINO module for your region and wire it to 3.3 V, GND and one GPIO. Run dcf77pi (DCF77), or a libgpiod pulse-width script for MSF/WWVB.
      - 4. Log the decoded minute frames next to the GNSS time and PPS edge. The module's filter delay dominates the measured offset, so calibrate it once and then watch day/night changes.
      - 5. With the HF+ Discovery and YouLoop, also capture the LF carrier IQ in SDR++ for later phase and amplitude analysis.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - MLA-30+ active receive loop (generic; eBay/AliExpress)
      - CANADUINO 60 kHz (WWVB/MSF/JJY60) or 77.5 kHz (DCF77) atomic-clock receiver module
      - Airspy HF+ Discovery
      - Airspy YouLoop passive loop antenna
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  6.
    - **Name:** VLF/LF survey, sferics and lightning log
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Connect the HF+ Discovery and YouLoop (bias tee none/off), with the loop hung at least 5 m from the device. Ideally work at a site away from mains wiring; whistlers need very quiet sites (unverified at handheld scale).
      - 2. In SDR++, set the HF+ to cover 0-100 kHz (the full 768 ksps span) and record a waterfall. Sferics show as vertical broadband clicks; LF time stations as steady carriers.
      - 3. Step up to 190-535 kHz for NDBs (CW idents) and NAVTEX on 490/518 kHz.
      - 4. In parallel, log AS3935 events over SPI (time, distance estimate, energy) and time-match them to the sferics.
      - 5. Rule: if the AS3935 reports a storm within about 15 km, take down the outdoor wire and loop antennas.
    - **Needs:**
      - Airspy HF+ Discovery
      - Airspy YouLoop passive loop antenna
      - SparkFun Lightning Detector - AS3935 (SEN-15441)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  7.
    - **Name:** ADS-B (and US-only UAT) monitor with range map
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Set the dipole kit's short elements to about 6.5 cm, vertical. Put the 1090 MHz filtered preamp at the antenna, powered from the second V4L's bias tee.
      - 2. Run readsb --device-type rtlsdr --device <serial> --gain auto (or a fixed gain), with tar1090 as the local web UI. Pre-download the aircraft database and map tiles while online.
      - 3. Let it run 30-60 min. Export the tar1090 range outline and log the GNSS site position and antenna height.
      - 4. A/B: no preamp vs preamp; antenna at 1 m vs 2 m.
      - 5. US only: run dump978-fa --sdr driver=rtlsdr,serial=... with skyaware978 on 978 MHz. Use the SAWbird+ ADS-B if you want both bands from one antenna.
      - 6. Expected range with this small antenna: about 100-250 km for cruising aircraft (estimate, depending on the site horizon).
    - **Needs:**
      - Second RTL-SDR Blog V4L (the planned spare) as a parallel monitor receiver
      - Uputronics-design SAW-filtered preamps: 1090 MHz (ADS-B), 403 MHz (radiosondes), 162 MHz (AIS)
      - Existing RTL-SDR Blog multipurpose dipole kit, re-set per band (FM, DAB, AIS/NOAA WX, radiosondes, ADS-B)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  8.
    - **Name:** AIS and NOAA Weather Radio (coastal / US-Canada)
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Set the dipole arms to about 44 cm, vertical, as high as practical. Keep the FM band-stop in. The 162 MHz filtered preamp is optional.
      - 2. Run AIS-catcher -d:<serial>, which decodes 161.975 and 162.025 MHz, with its built-in web viewer on localhost. Log NMEA to file.
      - 3. Expected range: about 10-40 km from the shore, depending on antenna height (estimate).
      - 4. US/Canada: tune 162.400-162.550 MHz NFM in SDR++. Pipe the audio to multimon-ng -a EAS to log SAME headers; enable only the EAS decoder.
    - **Needs:**
      - Second RTL-SDR Blog V4L (the planned spare) as a parallel monitor receiver
      - Existing RTL-SDR Blog multipurpose dipole kit, re-set per band (FM, DAB, AIS/NOAA WX, radiosondes, ADS-B)
      - Uputronics-design SAW-filtered preamps: 1090 MHz (ADS-B), 403 MHz (radiosondes), 162 MHz (AIS)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  9.
    - **Name:** Radiosonde auto-track and chase (standalone)
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Build radiosonde_auto_rx natively against the patched librtlsdr2, or rebuild the Docker image with it. Check with ldd and look for 'Blog V4L' in rtl_test.
      - 2. In station.cfg: set the SDR serial, the 400-406 MHz scan range, the ppm offset from the WWV calibration, and turn the SondeHub, APRS and other uploaders off for offline use. Keep the ChaseMapper UDP output on.
      - 3. Use a dipole with 17.7 cm arms (vertical) and the 403 MHz filtered preamp at the antenna.
      - 4. Run gpsd on the LC76G UART. Run chasemapper with offline tiles (tile_server_enabled = True, cached to zoom 15) and car/handheld position from gpsd.
      - 5. Optionally send BNO085-derived bearings from a small handheld directional antenna as horus_udp 'Bearing' messages.
      - 6. Offline landing prediction needs cusf_predictor_wrapper and a downloaded GFS model; otherwise prediction requires internet.
      - 7. US: LMS6-1680 sondes can be received on the existing helicone + SAWbird+ GOES chain (1648-1728 MHz passband) with a second auto_rx instance.
    - **Needs:**
      - Second RTL-SDR Blog V4L (the planned spare) as a parallel monitor receiver
      - Uputronics-design SAW-filtered preamps: 1090 MHz (ADS-B), 403 MHz (radiosondes), 162 MHz (AIS)
      - Existing RTL-SDR Blog multipurpose dipole kit, re-set per band (FM, DAB, AIS/NOAA WX, radiosondes, ADS-B)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  10.
    - **Name:** FM-RDS and DAB+ coverage survey
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. FM: remove the FM band-stop and set the dipole arms to about 73 cm. Run rtl_fm -M fm -l 0 -A std -s 171k -F 9 -f <freq> | redsea, and log the JSON per station.
      - 2. Scan 87.5-108 MHz with a script. Store PI, PS and RadioText with signal level and GNSS position.
      - 3. Lower the gain if strong local stations overload the 8-bit RTL (birdies on empty channels).
      - 4. DAB+: set the arms to about 33-34 cm, vertical. Run welle-cli -c <channel> -w 7979 and log the ensemble and service list, SNR and FIC errors per site.
      - 5. US: replace step 4 with nrsc5 <freq> <program> for HD Radio.
      - 6. Build a coverage map from the logged positions.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - Existing RTL-SDR Blog multipurpose dipole kit, re-set per band (FM, DAB, AIS/NOAA WX, radiosondes, ADS-B)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  11.
    - **Name:** 21 cm hydrogen-line drift scan or pointed survey
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Bench: check the helicone's S11 at 1420 MHz with the VNA, conducted only. Re-trim the match or wind the 67 mm 1420 helix if S11 is worse than -10 dB.
      - 2. Fit the SAWbird+ H1 on the feed. Power it from the V4L tee (120 mA) or from micro-USB 5 V with a DC block when using the Lime.
      - 3. In the warm case, confirm the V4L holds PLL lock at 1420.4 MHz. If not, use the LimeSDR.
      - 4. Using GNSS and astropy/skyfield, point at galactic longitudes along the plane, about 20-30 degrees apart. Use the BNO085 for azimuth and elevation.
      - 5. Run Virgo (gr-osmosdr source) at 2.4 MS/s with 1024-4096 channels and 1-10 min per pointing. Take an off-plane 'cold' reference for the baseline.
      - 6. Expect a line a few K to tens of K above a Tsys of about 100-150 K. The radiometer equation gives about 0.2 K rms in 10 kHz after 1 min, so detection takes minutes (my estimate; baseline ripple and RFI are the real limit).
      - 7. Convert to LSR velocity and plot the rotation-curve tangent points (coarse with a 20-30 degree beam).
    - **Needs:**
      - Existing fold-flat petal helicone + L-band helix, reused as a 1420 MHz radio telescope and Sun-noise antenna
      - Nooelec SAWbird+ H1 (1420 MHz SAW + LNA)
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
  12.
    - **Name:** Sun-noise Y-factor and G/T check (no new hardware at 1.7 and 10.5 GHz)
    - **Steps:**
      - 1. Compute the Sun's azimuth and elevation from the GNSS fix and time (skyfield).
      - 2. Point the helicone with the existing SAWbird+ GOES (1.7 GHz) or the H1 (1.42 GHz) at cold sky about 30 degrees away from the Sun and galactic plane. Record total power with rtl_power or a SoapySDR script over 1-2 MHz for 30 s.
      - 3. Point at the Sun, using the BNO085 and a peak search, and record again. Y = P_sun / P_cold.
      - 4. Expected rise: about 0.7-1.5 dB at L-band with the 13-16 dBic helicone, and about 0.5-1.5 dB at 10.5 GHz with the 21-23 dBi gore horn + Bullseye LNB (my estimates from solar flux, effective area and Tsys).
      - 5. Repeat over days to track the antenna, LNA and feed health. A sudden drop in Y flags a failed LNA, a wet feed or a bad connector.
      - 6. Moon noise is NOT attempted (below 0.2 K with these antennas; see rejected).
    - **Needs:**
      - Existing fold-flat petal helicone + L-band helix, reused as a 1420 MHz radio telescope and Sun-noise antenna
      - Nooelec SAWbird+ H1 (1420 MHz SAW + LNA)
      - RTL-SDR Blog V4L in HF mode (existing primary SDR, reused; no external upconverter needed)
      - Receive software stack for Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64
- **Rejected:**
  1.
    - **Name:** External HF upconverter (Ham It Up, SpyVerter) or the LimeFEA HF Micro ($199)
    - **Why:** Redundant. The V4L datasheet lists 'HF Implementation: Upconverter with 28.8 MHz LO' from 500 kHz, and RTL-SDR Blog recommends the SpyVerter only for older dongles. The LimeFEA would cost about 5x the V4L to duplicate it.
  2.
    - **Name:** Mini-whip active antenna (PA0RDT design and clones)
    - **Why:** It is an E-field probe that needs a good ground and a mast, so a battery handheld with switching converters and an HDMI display near it is its own worst noise source. The rtl-sdr.com review says even the cheap MLA-30 loop is 'probably still better than using a miniwhip, especially in suburban/city environments'. Clones are commonly fed with about 12 V phantom power, not the 4.5 V tee (not verified per clone).
  3.
    - **Name:** Premium rigid active loops (Wellbrook class and similar)
    - **Why:** rtl-sdr.com puts them at '$300+'. They are rigid, about 1 m class, and break the fold rule (pieces at most 35 cm). The YouLoop + HF+ pair gives most of the low-noise benefit for $209.
  4.
    - **Name:** SDRplay RSP1B / RSPdx-R2 as the HF/LF receiver
    - **Why:** The audit records unreliable closed-API service behaviour on ARM Linux (hangs after boot or replug, Soapy activateStream failures). The HF+ Discovery is open source and natively supported by SDR++ and SatDump.
  5.
    - **Name:** rtlsdr-wsprd for HF WSPR
    - **Why:** Its README targets 'VHF/UHF bands' and says nothing about HF or V4/V4L upconverter mode. Use WSJT-X (noble arm64 package) through an SDR++ audio sink instead.
  6.
    - **Name:** Discovery Dish ($214) or a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi grid dish (about 100 x 60 cm) for the hydrogen line
    - **Why:** Dishes are excluded by the antenna rule. A 13 dBi homemade helix with a SAWbird H1 already showed the HI line (rtl-sdr.com), so the foldable helicone or a hinged horn is enough.
  7.
    - **Name:** Moon-noise measurements
    - **Why:** With antennas of 23 dBi or less, the 0.5 degree Moon fills about 5e-4 of the beam, so the rise is about 0.1 K (my calculation). That is undetectable; it needs a dish.
  8.
    - **Name:** Jupiter decametric / Radio JOVE dual dipole
    - **Why:** It needs two half-wave dipoles at about 20 MHz, roughly 7 m each (general knowledge), which the fold rule cannot meet. Shortened antennas lose too much.
  9.
    - **Name:** Meteor-echo counting on the GRAVES 143.050 MHz radar
    - **Why:** The transmitter is a French military space-surveillance radar, which is excluded by the project rule. Meteor pings on distant FM broadcast carriers with the telescopic dipole are an allowed alternative.
  10.
    - **Name:** ACARS, VDL2, HFDL, air-band and marine voice, pagers (POCSAG/FLEX in multimon-ng), DMR, TETRA, trunking
    - **Why:** These are private or operational communications, excluded by the rule and restricted by law in many countries. Only the public broadcast and beacon services listed (ADS-B, AIS, sondes, broadcast, weather, time, beacons) are included.
  11.
    - **Name:** rtl_433 general ISM-band decoding
    - **Why:** It decodes third-party devices (tyre-pressure sensors, doorbells, etc.), which raises privacy and tracking issues. Use it only for your own weather sensors, if at all.
  12.
    - **Name:** Blitzortung.org lightning-network station
    - **Why:** It is a fixed station that needs an internet uplink and site-specific antennas, not a standalone handheld. The AS3935 plus HF+ sferics cover local needs.
  13.
    - **Name:** HamSCI Grape WWV Doppler monitoring
    - **Why:** It needs a GPS-disciplined receiver clock. The V4L's free-running 1 ppm TCXO (about 10 Hz at 10 MHz) is far larger than the 0.1-1 Hz ionospheric Doppler being measured, and neither the V4L nor the HF+ has an external reference input (HF+ unverified).
  14.
    - **Name:** Ionosonde (chirp-sounder) reception
    - **Why:** It needs a receiver that captures most of the HF band at once. The V4L's 2.56 MHz and the HF+ Discovery's 660 kHz are far too narrow (bandwidth requirement inferred, not verified).
  15.
    - **Name:** DAB+ on the HF+ Discovery
    - **Why:** welle.io states 'Airspy HF+ is not supported due to limited bandwidth'. DAB+ stays on the V4L or the LimeSDR.
  16.
    - **Name:** UAT 978 MHz outside the US
    - **Why:** UAT is a US system (FAA; general knowledge, not fetched). Elsewhere there is nothing to receive, so dump978-fa and the dual-band SAWbird+ ADS-B are only worth it in the US.
  17.
    - **Name:** Unfiltered wideband LNA ahead of the V4L for ADS-B, sondes or HF
    - **Why:** The narrowband audit requires filter before gain. The V4L has only a diplexer, so broadband gain near FM, DVB-T or LTE desensitises it. Use the SAW-filtered preamps instead.
  18.
    - **Name:** Dedicated USB sound card for VLF
    - **Why:** It uses a scarce USB port and needs its own E-field preamp. The HF+ Discovery already covers VLF from 0.5 kHz and also does LF and HF.
- **Notes:** VERDICTS
  - **HF:** The RTL-SDR Blog V4L DOES cover HF with a built-in 28.8 MHz-LO upconverter from 500 kHz (verified in the V4L datasheet). No upconverter is needed; only an antenna. The core HF add-on is therefore just the MLA-30+ active loop (about $38-40 on eBay) plus thin coax and ferrites, with the $16.95 AM high-pass filter for city use.
  - **Below 500 kHz:** The V4L's limit is 500 kHz, so VLF/LF (DCF77/MSF/WWVB, sferics) and most NDBs need the Airspy HF+ Discovery ($169 list; EUR 232 incl. VAT at WiMo; 0.5 kHz-31 MHz verified) with the passive YouLoop ($39.95). The YouLoop needs a receiver with MDS of -140 dBm or better, so it suits the HF+ rather than the V4L.
  - **Hydrogen line:** It fits the antenna rule without a dish. Reuse the fold-flat helicone (C/lambda = 0.92 at 1420 MHz, about 13-14 dBic estimated) with a SAWbird+ H1 ($49.95, 120 mA, runs from the bias tee). A comparable 13 dBi homemade helix with a SAWbird H1 and an RTL-SDR has detected HI. A rigid 75 x 60 cm horn (18.5 dBi) is proven but complies only as a hinged flat-pack.
  
  USB AND PORT BUDGET (the binding constraint)
  - **USB 3.1 (blue):** primary V4L, or the NVMe enclosure. The compute and narrowband inputs disagree; settle it once on the bench.
  - **Shared USB 2.0 hub (3 ports, also used by Wi-Fi):** display touch, plus ONE of the second V4L or the HF+ Discovery. Swap them on one pigtail.
  - **Expansion:** a powered USB 2.0 hub on the filtered 5 V rail is possible but untested for RF noise.
  - **Bus load:** each V4L is about 4.8 MB/s at 2.4 MS/s, comfortable for one hub.
  - **Bias-tee current:** SAWbird+ H1 at 120 mA fits the V4L's 180 mA. The Uputronics preamp and MLA-30+ currents are unpublished, so measure them.
  - **GPIO/SPI:** the CANADUINO module (one GPIO) and the AS3935 (SPI plus IRQ) go on the 40-pin header at 3.3 V, alongside the GNSS UART and IMU.
  
  POWER
  - An HF, ADS-B or monitor session with the Lime idle and the display dimmed should be roughly 8-12 W at the pack, about 6-9 h on the 72 Wh 4S pack (estimate).
  - HF needs the charger off and battery-only operation.
  - Every new receive job is low power compared with the satellite modes.
  
  RF NOISE
  - At HF the handheld itself is the main noise source: Q6A bucks, the 12 V buck, the IP2368 charger, the 1080p HDMI link and the LimeSDR clocks.
  - Remote the loop by 5-10 m and choke the feed line.
  - Run the terminated-vs-antenna A/B test before trusting any HF result.
  - Mount the LF ferrite and the AS3935 away from the converters.
  
  SOFTWARE
  - Every package must link the patched V4L librtlsdr2.
  - Docker images and installers with their own older librtlsdr will be 'deaf'. Rebuild auto_rx natively, and check AIS-catcher and readsb with ldd.
  - Uploaders (SondeHub on by default, WSPRnet, PSK Reporter, ADS-B aggregators) stay off for standalone use.
  - Pre-cache map tiles: chasemapper is verified; tar1090 offline tiles are unverified.
  
  PERFORMANCE (estimates unless stated)
  - **ADS-B:** about 100-250 km with a 6.5 cm dipole and the 1090 MHz filtered preamp.
  - **AIS:** about 10-40 km from shore.
  - **Sondes:** typically well over 100 km while airborne. Line of sight; not verified for this antenna.
  - **FT8/WSPR:** continental or intercontinental, depending on propagation, if self-noise is controlled.
  - **NAVTEX on 518 kHz:** at the V4L's edge; the HF+ is better.
  - **Sun noise:** about 0.7-1.5 dB at L-band and 0.5-1.5 dB at 10.5 GHz.
  - **Moon:** not detectable.
  
  RECEIVE-ONLY / BENCH RULE
  - Every item here is receive only. The YouLoop is rated 250 mW maximum, and the Uputronics LNAs have no TX bypass.
  - Signal generators, VNAs or noise sources may only feed the SDRs, filters or LNAs conducted, through fixed attenuators (60 dB or more for MDS work) or into dummy loads. That covers MDS checks, S11 trims of the 1420 MHz helix and dipole lengths, and preamp gain checks. Never connect a generator to an antenna.
  
  LEGAL (generic, country unknown)
  - Reception rules differ by country. Some allow only broadcast, amateur, standard-frequency/time and meteorological signals.
  - Decoding, storing or publishing ADS-B or AIS data, or operating receivers near airports and harbours, can be regulated.
  - Never decode, record or share communications not intended for the general public. Leave the pager and voice decoders off.
  - Radiosonde recovery, land access and property rules vary; never enter restricted areas.
  - Data uploads to third-party networks are optional and subject to their terms.
  
  UNVERIFIED / MARKED
  - MLA-30+: loop size, current draw, and operation from the V4L's 4.5 V tee.
  - Whether the AM high-pass filter passes DC.
  - Uputronics preamps: the bias-tee voltage spec conflicts between sources (5 V max vs 5-26 V) and the current draw is unpublished.
  - HF+ Discovery current draw.
  - AS3935 Linux library on the Q6A.
  - CANADUINO 77.5 kHz price.
  - DWD RTTY frequencies, and NCDXF and WWV/CHU frequencies (general knowledge; the NCDXF table is JavaScript-generated).
  - tar1090 offline tiles.
  - The helicone's gain and S11 at 1420 MHz.
  - V4L PLL lock at 1420 MHz when hot.
  
  The radiofax frequencies were verified from NOAA's 'Worldwide Marine Radiofacsimile Broadcast Schedules' (7 March 2025): https://www.weather.gov/media/marine/rfax.pdf. NCDXF timing was verified at https://www.ncdxf.org/beacon/.

## lab:lab_software (run `wf_1dd437c5-0cf`)

- **Area:** Lab software on the Radxa Dragon Q6A (Radxa OS r2 / Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64): spectrum survey and logging, waterfall and recording, signal analysis, offline signal ID, SatNOGS option, calibration and measurement scripts, automation, data management, touch kiosk
- **Items:**
  1.
    - **Name:** rtl_power (from the rtl-sdr package, rebuilt for the V4L) + heatmap.py
    - **Category:** Spectrum survey / logging (RTL-SDR)
    - **Purpose in lab:** Swept power survey from 0.5 MHz to 1.766 GHz with the RTL-SDR V4L: occupancy logs, terminated-input self-noise baselines, A/B checks of EMI sources, long logs left running unattended. heatmap.py turns the CSV into waterfall PNGs.
    - **Key specs:** Hops are 2.4-2.56 Msps wide. Range and bin size are set with -f start:stop:bin, integration with -i, duration with -e, edge crop with -c. CSV lines hold date, time, f_low, f_high, step, samples and the dB bins. Commands from the audited plan: 'rtl_power -f 24M:1766M:100k -g 40 -i 10 -e 120 term_X.csv' and 'rtl_power -f 136.3M:138.7M:1k -g 40 -i 10 -e 2m A_137.csv'.
    - **Size weight power:** The rtl-sdr package installs 577 KB. CPU use on the Q6A is low but has not been measured. Output size is about (number of bins x ~6 bytes) per sweep line; compress with zstd.
    - **Interface and linux:** USB, through librtlsdr. Noble arm64 ships rtl-sdr/librtlsdr2 2.0.1-2build1, which has no V4L (R828S) support. Rebuild noble's source package with commit 0204c9c (keeps the librtlsdr.so.2 soname, so gr-osmosdr, SoapyRTLSDR and Gqrx keep working) or build osmocom 2.0.3. Blacklist dvb_usb_rtl28xxu.
    - **Price:** $0 (GPL-2.0)
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Use a fixed gain (-g) so logs can be compared. Always record a 50-ohm-terminated baseline first. librtlsdr gives one process exclusive use of the dongle, so stop SDR++, SatNOGS and similar before a sweep. Write to /srv/lab/survey/YYYY/MM/DD/. Known issue: soapy_power's 'rtl_power' output does not work with heatmap.py (soapy_power issue #24), so use real rtl_power CSV or convert first.
    - **Sources:**
      - http://ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports/dists/noble/universe/binary-arm64/Packages.xz
      - https://github.com/keenerd/rtl-sdr-misc/blob/master/heatmap/heatmap.py
      - https://github.com/xmikos/soapy_power/issues
      - /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/narrowband_sdr.json
      - /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/digest.md
    - **Availability:** apt (noble universe) plus a local rebuild for the V4L
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Already $0. 'soapy_power -d driver=rtlsdr' writes the same CSV through SoapySDR.
    - **Safety notes:** Receive only.
  2.
    - **Name:** lab-sweep: a small SoapySDR sweeper to write in Python, working like hackrf_sweep for the LimeSDR Micro
    - **Category:** Spectrum survey / logging (LimeSDR Micro, up to 3.8 GHz)
    - **Purpose in lab:** Wideband survey from 1.6 to 3.8 GHz (and lower) with the Lime. Output is rtl_power-compatible CSV plus Parquet, with GNSS position and chrony UTC on every sweep. The same script also works with driver=rtlsdr.
    - **Key specs:** Design, not an existing product: SoapySDR device 'driver=limesuiteng' (the name is verified in LimeSuiteNG plugins/soapysdr/Registration.cpp); RX-only CS16 stream; 30.72 Msps (the Micro's minimum is 7 Msps); explicit setBandwidth, because without -B LimeSDR users saw out-of-band signals fold in; 4096-point FFT (about 7.5 kHz bins); 20% edge crop, so about 24.5 MHz usable per hop; samples thrown away after each retune (settle time still to be measured); 20-50 ms dwell per hop. That is about 90 hops for 1.6-3.8 GHz, an estimate.
    - **Size weight power:** About 200-300 lines of Python on apt python3-soapysdr 0.8.1 and numpy 1.26.4. It FFTs only the dwell blocks, so the CPU load is a duty-cycled fraction of one A78 core (estimate, not benchmarked).
    - **Interface and linux:** PCIe, through la9310_limesdr and the LimeSuiteNG SoapyLMS plugin (limesdr-micro-staging branch, built from source per the software audit). RTL-SDR through SoapyRTLSDR 0.3.3.
    - **Price:** $0 (own code)
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Open only RX streams, never setupStream(SOAPY_SDR_TX). Write the same CSV columns as rtl_power so heatmap.py, DuckDB and notebooks treat both SDRs the same way. Stamp each sweep with UTC from chrony and lat/lon from gpsd. Reuse the RAM-ring recorder rules from the storage audit if raw IQ is also kept.
    - **Sources:**

      - /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/software.json
    - **Availability:** To be written; all dependencies are in apt or the LimeSuiteNG build
    - **Cheaper alternative:** soapy_power 1.6.1 (below), with no code to write but unmaintained

    - **Purpose in lab:** A ready-made frequency-hopping power logger for the Lime and the RTL until lab-sweep exists.

My test: 'pip install --no-deps soapy_power simplesoapy simplespectral' into a --system-site-packages venv on Ubuntu 24.04.5 x86_64 with Python 3.12.3, numpy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.11.4 and SoapySDR 0.8.   17.
    - **Name:** lab-cal: own measurement scripts (ppm, Y-factor NF, sky/ground Tsys, antenna pattern)
    - **Category:** Calibration / measurement
    - **Purpose in lab:** Repeatable, logged measurements that turn the receiver into an instrument.
    - **Key specs:** Y-factor: Y = P_hot/P_cold and NF = ENR(dB) - 10log10(Y-1) when T_cold is about T0 (Maxim/ADI note). In general F = (ENR_lin - Y(Tc/T0 - 1))/(Y - 1). Second-stage correction: F1 = F_sys - (F2 - 1)/G1, with G1 taken from the hot-minus-cold power deltas (Keysight AN 5952-3706). ppm: either GNSS-SDR user_clk_drift_ppm, or a linear fit of samples received against PPS-disciplined CLOCK_REALTIME over at least 30 minutes, restarted on any overflow. Pattern: per-satellite delta C/N0 (antenna under test minus reference), binned by antenna-frame angle using IMU attitude.
    - **Size weight power:** Python, small.
    - **Interface and linux:** Built on SoapySDR, gpsd, GNSS-SDR UDP protobuf, Skyfield, numpy and scipy, and the BNO085 USB-CDC puck.
    - **Price:** $0 (own code)
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Every script writes JSON plus CSV to /srv/lab/cal/<type>/<UTC>_<chain>.json with the full chain description and software versions. Each needs a warm-up step and a fixed gain (AGC off).
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.analog.com/en/resources/technical-articles/noise-figure-measurement-methods-and-formulas--maxim-integrated.html
      - https://www.keysight.com/us/en/assets/7018-06829/application-notes/5952-3706.pdf
      - https://gnss-sdr.org/docs/sp-blocks/pvt/
    - **Availability:** To be written
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Manual readings in SDR++ (much less repeatable)
    - **Safety notes:** Noise sources are conducted only: connect them straight into the LNA or SDR input, or into a terminated filter. Never connect one to an antenna.

  22.

  24.
    - **Name:** Receive-only guard (configuration plus a small lint script)
    - **Category:** Safety / compliance
    - **Purpose in lab:** Makes the 'receive-only on air' rule enforceable in software around a TX-capable LimeSDR Micro.
    - **Key specs:** (1) Build LimeSuiteNG with -DBUILD_PLUGINS_AMARISOFT=OFF; its plugins/CMakeLists.txt defaults it ON on UNIX, and it is an LTE base-station plugin. (2) Never run limeTRX with -i/--input or --looptx (its TX waveform flags in limeTRX.cpp). (3) A lint step rejects any .grc or .py flowgraph containing soapy/osmosdr/limesuiteng sink blocks or SOAPY_SDR_TX before the scheduler runs it. (4) URH without device backends. (5) A 50-ohm terminator on the Micro TX port.
    - **Size weight power:** Negligible.
    - **Interface and linux:** Shell/Python run as a pre-start step in the systemd units.
    - **Price:** $0
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Log the guard's verdict to the journal for every automated job.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://github.com/myriadrf/LimeSuiteNG/blob/limesdr-micro-staging/plugins/CMakeLists.txt
      - https://github.com/myriadrf/LimeSuiteNG/blob/limesdr-micro-staging/cli/limeTRX.cpp
    - **Availability:** To be written
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Discipline only
    - **Safety notes:** This is the software half of the receive-only rule; the TX-port terminator is the hardware half.
- **Capabilities added:**
  - Logged, geotagged swept spectrum survey from 0.5 MHz to 1.766 GHz (RTL-SDR V4L) and up to 3.8 GHz (LimeSDR Micro), in rtl_power-compatible CSV, Parquet and DuckDB
  - Self-interference and EMI baselines (terminated-input and per-subsystem A/B sweeps)
  - Live waterfall, listening and IQ/audio recording (SDR++, Gqrx; CyberEther for a 30-56 MHz GPU waterfall)
  - Offline signal analysis: bandwidth, symbol rate, burst timing, modulation, symbol extraction (inspectrum, GNU Radio Companion, Jupyter, optional URH in analysis-only mode)
  - Offline signal identification against a downloaded database of 500+ signals (Artemis 4.2.0)
  - Satellite recording and decoding, plus telemetry decoding (SatDump 2.0, gr-satellites 5.5, satnogs-decoders)
  - Frequency calibration of both SDRs traceable to GNSS (ppm and drift against temperature)
  - Bench noise-figure measurement by Y-factor with second-stage correction (conducted, noise source never on an antenna)
  - System noise temperature from sky/ground and Sun Y-factor on the real antenna (receive-only)
  - Relative antenna patterns from GNSS C/N0, satellite beacons, the QO-100 beacon and Sun drift scans
  - Unattended, gated pass scheduling, recording and post-processing
  - A standard SigMF data archive with checksums, catalog, retention and restic backup
  - Optional receive-only SatNOGS Network station when online
  - Touch kiosk operation, plus remote lab access from a laptop when docked
  - A software receive-only guard around the TX-capable LimeSDR Micro
- **Procedures:**
  1.
    - **Name:** P1. Self-noise baseline and wideband survey
    - **Steps:**
      - Fit a 50-ohm terminator on the RTL input and run 'rtl_power -f 24M:1766M:100k -g 40 -i 10 -e 120 term_base.csv'. Repeat with each Q6A subsystem switched on in turn (display, Wi-Fi, SSD writes, Lime streaming), following the state list in the antennas/display audits.
      - Lime: run 'lab-sweep --driver limesuiteng --rate 30.72e6 --bw 30e6 --fft 4096 --crop 0.2 --range 1.6e9:3.8e9 --gain <fixed> --out term_lime.csv' with a 50-ohm load (soapy_power '-d driver=limesuiteng -r 30.72e6 -k 20 -F rtl_power' as the interim tool).
      - Connect the band antenna, filter and LNA and repeat for the band of interest at the same gain, for example 'rtl_power -f 136.3M:138.7M:1k -g 40 -i 10 -e 2m A_137.csv'.
      - Import into DuckDB with time, lat/lon (gpsd), antenna and chain tags. Subtract the terminated baseline and flag bins more than 6 dB above it.
      - Render PNGs with heatmap.py and attach them to the survey record. List the flagged peaks for P8.
    - **Needs:**
      - RTL-SDR V4L with the patched librtlsdr2
      - LimeSDR Micro with LimeSuiteNG
      - rtl_power
      - lab-sweep or soapy_power
      - 50-ohm SMA terminators
      - DuckDB/pandas venv
      - gpsd/chrony
  2.
    - **Name:** P2. Frequency calibration against GNSS
    - **Steps:**
      - Method A (absolute): connect an active GNSS L1 antenna to the SDR under test; for the RTL use bias=1, whose bias tee gives 4.5 V/180 mA. Run gnss-sdr with Osmosdr_Signal_Source (osmosdr_args=rtl,bias=1; freq 1575420000; 2 Msps; AGC off), PVT.enable_monitor=true and Monitor.enable_monitor=true.
      - After the first fix, log user_clk_drift_ppm for at least 10 minutes and take the median. On the RTL the tuner and ADC share one 28.8 MHz TCXO, so this ppm also corrects tuning (standard RTL architecture).
      - For the Lime: record about 2-5 minutes of L1 IQ at 7.68 Msps cs16 into the RAM ring and process it offline with GNSS-SDR's file source (real time on the Q6A is unbenchmarked). limePPSDO does not support the Micro (its source lists only XTRX and Mini V2).
      - Method B (no extra antenna): with chrony locked to PPS (chronyc tracking RMS of a few us), stream the SDR for at least 30 minutes, timestamp every buffer, fit samples against time by least squares, and discard the run on any overflow. The slope error is the sample-clock ppm.
      - Write ppm, SDR temperature and Q6A thermal-zone readings to /srv/lab/cal/ppm.csv, and repeat cold and warm to build a ppm-vs-temperature table.
      - Apply the correction: rtl_* -p, SDR++ PPM correction, SATNOGS_PPM_ERROR, Gqrx frequency correction, and SoapySDR setFrequencyCorrection in the lab scripts. Check against a known stable carrier where one is receivable.
    - **Needs:**
      - GNSS-SDR (apt 0.0.19 or 0.0.22 from source)
      - Active GNSS L1 antenna (hardware area)
      - gpsd + chrony + PPS
      - lab-cal ppm script
  3.
    - **Name:** P3. Bench noise figure by Y-factor (conducted only)
    - **Steps:**
      - Connect noise source, then DUT (LNA or filter+LNA), then SDR, all by cable. Leave the antenna disconnected. A 50-ohm terminator stays on any unused port.
      - Set a fixed SDR gain with AGC off, the bias-tee state and the rate (RTL 2.048 Msps; Lime 7.68 Msps with explicit bandwidth). Pick measurement bins free of spurs and the DC spike, using the P1 baseline. Warm up for 15 minutes.
      - SDR alone first: switch the source ON/OFF (a GPIO-driven switch or by hand) in 2-5 s blocks for at least 60 cycles. Integrate power over the chosen bandwidth to get Y2, and compute F2 = (ENR_lin - Y2(Tc/T0 - 1))/(Y2 - 1), which is NF = ENR - 10log10(Y-1) when Tc is about 290 K.
      - Repeat with the DUT in line to get Y_sys and F_sys. Take G1 = (P_on - P_off with DUT)/(P_on - P_off without DUT), then F1 = F_sys - (F2 - 1)/G1.
      - Linearity check: change the SDR gain by 3-5 dB and confirm Y is unchanged within about 0.1 dB; otherwise the chain is compressing.
      - Store NF, uncertainty (ENR table uncertainty dominates and is unknown for uncalibrated sources), frequency, chain and software versions in /srv/lab/cal/nf/.
    - **Needs:**
      - Noise source with an ENR table (lab-instruments area; low output, conducted only)
      - Optional GPIO switch for the noise source's DC
      - SMA attenuators and 50-ohm terminators
      - lab-cal NF script (SoapySDR + numpy)
  4.
    - **Name:** P4. System temperature from sky/ground and Sun (receive-only, on the antenna)
    - **Steps:**
      - With the full chain on the antenna (for example the L-band helix plus SAWbird+ GOES), fix the gain and record 60 s pointing at cold sky (high elevation, away from the Sun and the galactic plane).
      - Record 60 s pointing at the ground (or a covered absorber, about 290 K). Y = P_ground/P_sky gives T_sys = (T_ground - Y*T_sky)/(Y - 1), with T_sky assumed at a few K at L-band (the assumption goes in the report).
      - Optional: point at the Sun and then at cold sky to get the Sun/cold ratio (the antennas audit expects about 0.5-1 dB at 1.7 GHz for a 13-15 dBic helix).
      - Log the results and compare before and after antenna or LNA changes; this checks P3 on the real antenna.
    - **Needs:**
      - lab-cal Tsys script
      - Fixed-gain SDR chain
      - IMU puck for pointing records
      - Skyfield (Sun position from GNSS time and QTH)
  5.
    - **Name:** P5. Relative antenna pattern from GNSS C/N0
    - **Steps:**
      - Mount the antenna under test (L-band patch or helix; L1 is near, not equal to, 1.7 GHz) on the boom with the BNO085 puck. Feed it through its LNA/bias tee to the RTL at 1575.42 MHz.
      - Run GNSS-SDR with the Monitor (CN0_dB_hz per channel) and the PVT monitor (azimuth_deg and elevation_deg per PRN). At the same time log LC76G reference C/N0 from gpsd SKY (ss in dB-Hz, az, el).
      - Either step the antenna in azimuth (for example 15 degrees, 2 minutes per step) at fixed tilt, or leave it static for 12-24 hours to sample the sky.
      - For each satellite and second compute delta = C/N0_AUT - C/N0_ref, convert az/el into antenna-frame angles with the IMU attitude, and bin into 5 x 5 degree cells. Normalise to the maximum to get relative gain in dB.
      - Caveats in the report: relative pattern only, C/N0 saturation near the receiver's upper limit, multipath, L1 only.
    - **Needs:**
      - GNSS-SDR
      - gpsd with the LC76G
      - BNO085 USB puck
      - lab-cal pattern script
      - Tripod/boom
  6.
    - **Name:** P6. Beamwidth and pointing from beacons (satellite pass, QO-100, Sun drift)
    - **Steps:**
      - Satellite pass: during a pass of a satellite with a continuous downlink (for example Meteor LRPT at 137 MHz), record IQ and log 1 s carrier or band SNR. Predict az/el and range with Skyfield from OMM, correct for free-space path loss, and plot SNR against off-boresight angle from the IMU attitude.
      - QO-100 (geostationary, only inside its footprint): with the Bullseye LNB and the 10 GHz patch or horn, sweep the antenna by hand through the beacon while logging IMU attitude and beacon SNR. Fit the -3 dB beamwidth and the pointing offset.
      - Sun drift scan: point ahead of the Sun's predicted track and let it drift through the beam while logging power. The drift time across the -3 dB points gives the beamwidth (the Sun is about 0.5 degrees across).
      - Store the cuts with the antenna ID in /srv/lab/cal/pattern/.
    - **Needs:**
      - SDR++ or lab-rec
      - Skyfield 1.55 + OMM snapshot
      - BNO085 puck
      - QO-100 chain (Bullseye LNB)
      - lab-cal pattern script
  7.
    - **Name:** P7. Unattended pass recording and decode
    - **Steps:**
      - When online, refresh CelesTrak OMM into /srv/lab/tle/YYYYMMDD.json. lab-sched reads the QTH from gpsd (3D fix plus the gates from the GNSS audit), otherwise the saved QTH.
      - Compute passes for the YAML targets above the minimum elevation, assign devices (RTL: 137/145/435 MHz; Lime: HRPT/AHRPT at 7-10 Msps per the software audit) and resolve overlaps.
      - Create a timer per pass with 'systemd-run --user --on-calendar=<UTC AOS-60s> --unit=pass-<norad>-<aos> lab-record <job.json>'.
      - At start: run the receive-only guard and the gates (chrony synced, free disk at least 1.5x the expected size, battery above the threshold, temperature below the limit). Then record with 'satdump legacy record ... --baseband_format cs16 --timeout <pass s>' or lab-rec into the RAM ring and mbuffer.
      - After LOS: 'satdump pipeline <id> baseband <file> <outdir>' at nice/ionice idle. Then write SigMF meta (sha512, geolocation, chain, ppm) and decode telemetry with satnogs-decoders where it applies.
      - Update catalog.sqlite and apply retention (keep products and meta; delete raw after a verified decode if configured). Push a summary to the launcher status bar.
    - **Needs:**
      - lab-sched
      - SatDump 2.0 (source)
      - SigMF tools
      - Skyfield/sgp4
      - Samsung T7 (wideband) / UFS (narrowband)
      - INA228 battery gauge readout
  8.
    - **Name:** P8. Identify an unknown signal
    - **Steps:**
      - From the P1 flagged peaks, record 10-60 s of IQ around the peak (SDR++ at Uint8/Int16 or lab-rec) and convert it to SigMF.
      - In inspectrum, measure occupied bandwidth, burst length and period, and symbol rate with the cursors; check the modulation from the amplitude, frequency and phase traces.
      - Search Artemis (offline) by frequency range, bandwidth and modulation; compare its waterfall and audio examples.
      - Write the result as a SigMF annotation (core:freq_lower_edge, core:freq_upper_edge, core:label, core:comment with the Artemis DB version and confidence).
      - If it is self-generated interference (it also appears in the P1 terminated or subsystem runs), log it as EMI and fix the hardware.
    - **Needs:**
      - SDR++/lab-rec
      - inspectrum 0.3.1
      - Artemis 4.2.0 with its database downloaded
      - sigmf 1.13.0
  9.
    - **Name:** P9. Data ingest, check and backup
    - **Steps:**
      - Every recorder writes to /srv/lab/<type>/YYYY/MM/DD/ with UTC-based names and a .sigmf-meta.
      - Run sigmf_validate on each new file and record sha512 in core:sha512 and in catalog.sqlite.
      - Compress survey CSV with zstd. Keep IQ uncompressed while it is still being analysed, then convert to .sigmf.xz or ZIQ if space is short.
      - Weekly: fio sanity check on the T7 and UFS life-time descriptors (storage audit), plus smartctl on the T7.
      - When docked, run 'restic backup /srv/lab --exclude raw-pending' to a laptop or NAS, then 'restic check'.
    - **Needs:**
      - sigmf 1.13.0
      - sqlite3/DuckDB
      - restic 0.16.4
      - fio 3.36
      - smartmontools 7.4
  10.
    - **Name:** P10. Optional SatNOGS session (online, fixed spot)
    - **Steps:**
      - Create or update the station in the SatNOGS Network with the current lat/lon/elevation from GNSS.
      - Start the librespace/satnogs-client:2.1.4 compose stack with SATNOGS_SOAPY_RX_DEVICE=driver=rtlsdr, the API token, station ID and ppm from P2, and /etc/localtime and /etc/timezone bind-mounted.
      - Inside the container, check 'SoapySDRUtil --probe' with the V4L. If the old librtlsdr is used, layer the patched librtlsdr2 into a derived image.
      - Stop the stack before going back to field mode (it takes the SDR exclusively).
    - **Needs:**
      - Wi-Fi with internet
      - Docker
      - SatNOGS account and station ID
      - RTL-SDR
  11.
    - **Name:** P11. Kiosk bring-up
    - **Steps:**
      - apt install labwc greetd wvkbd lisgd wlr-randr python3-pyqt6. Configure greetd autologin into a labwc session.
      - Set output scale 1 (1920x1080 at 7 in). Set QT_SCALE_FACTOR=1.75, GDK_SCALE=2, and SDR++ High-DPI 200%.
      - Create systemd --user units for each mode (sdrpp@<profile>.service using -r /srv/lab/sdrpp/<profile> --autostart, survey.service, lab-sched.timer, papermill-report@.service).
      - Write the launcher: big tiles that start and stop the units, plus a status bar (gpsd fix, chronyc tracking, INA228 state of charge, thermal zones, df, next pass). Map an edge swipe in lisgd to show or hide wvkbd.
      - Test with gloves and in sunlight, with Wi-Fi off. Confirm everything starts with no network.
    - **Needs:**
      - labwc 0.7.1
      - greetd 0.9.0
      - wvkbd 0.14.3
      - lisgd 0.3.7
      - PyQt6 6.6.1
      - systemd user units
- **Rejected:**
  1.
    - **Name:** hackrf_sweep
    - **Why:** It depends on HackRF firmware and the HackRF library and does not exist for the LimeSDR Micro. Its role goes to lab-sweep (SoapySDR) or soapy_power.
  2.
    - **Name:** QSpectrumAnalyzer 2.1.0
    - **Why:** Last PyPI release 21 Mar 2017 with no ARM packaging. It is only a GUI over rtl_power/soapy_power/hackrf_sweep, which the lab already drives directly.
  3.
    - **Name:** Ubuntu 'sdrpp' apt package and the SDR++ nightly .deb for the Micro
    - **Why:** Upstream says the Debian/Ubuntu package is incomplete and incompatible with official modules. The nightly .deb lacks the Soapy source and links the wrong libraries for the V4L and Micro (software audit).
  4.
    - **Name:** apt gr-limesdr 3.0.1, limesuite 23.11 and soapysdr0.8-module-lms7
    - **Why:** They link legacy LimeSuite 23.11, which cannot see the LimeSDR Micro, and clash with the LimeSuiteNG SoapyLMS plugin. Use gr-soapy or gr-limesuiteng.
  5.
    - **Name:** apt python3-skyfield 1.48 for OMM-based prediction
    - **Why:** Its sgp4lib has no EarthSatellite.from_omm (checked in the 1.48 wheel); 1.55 has it. Use pip Skyfield 1.55 and sgp4 2.27 (Alpha-5 NORAD IDs).
  6.
    - **Name:** apt package 'artemis' on noble
    - **Why:** It is the Sanger genome browser (18.2.0), not the radio Artemis. Use Flathub com.aresvalley.artemis.
  7.
    - **Name:** numpy 2.x in the same environment as apt GNU Radio/SciPy/SoapySDR
    - **Why:** apt SciPy 1.11.4 requires numpy below 1.28 (I observed the warning and a broken import), and the apt bindings are built against numpy 1.26. Pin numpy<2 in the venv.
  8.
    - **Name:** limePPSDO (LimeSuiteNG) for frequency discipline
    - **Why:** The limesdr-micro-staging source registers only LimeSDR XTRX and Mini V2 PPSDO registers, not the Micro. The audits also say GPSDO is not implemented for the Micro. Use the GNSS-SDR clock-drift method.
  9.
    - **Name:** kalibrate-rtl, gr-gsm, LTE cell scanners for ppm calibration
    - **Why:** They target cellular networks (gr-gsm is aimed at cellular communications), 2G is being shut down in many countries, and kalibrate-rtl is not in noble apt. GNSS-based calibration is better and stays clear of telecom signals.
  10.
    - **Name:** multimon-ng and pager/trunking/voice decoders
    - **Why:** They are aimed at the content of private communications, which is out of scope for this lab.
  11.
    - **Name:** SDR++ scheduler module
    - **Why:** The README marks it 'Unfinished' and OFF by default. Scheduling uses lab-sched plus the working rigctl_server AOS/LOS control.
  12.
    - **Name:** SatDump autotrack as the only scheduler on 2.0-alpha
    - **Why:** The 2.0 documentation does not cover autotrack (only legacy 1.1.4+ does, and that release changed the headless config format). Use lab-sched calling 'satdump legacy record' plus 'satdump pipeline'; revisit when 2.0 documents it.
  13.
    - **Name:** squeekboard and onboard on-screen keyboards
    - **Why:** squeekboard is not in noble arm64 apt. onboard is X11-only. wvkbd 0.14.3 is in apt and made for wlroots compositors.
  14.
    - **Name:** Browser-based kiosk (Chromium/Firefox)
    - **Why:** On noble both are snap transition packages, which are heavy for a battery handheld. A native PyQt6 launcher plus systemd units is lighter and works offline.
  15.
    - **Name:** Offline sigidwiki mirror via Kiwix/ZIM
    - **Why:** I found no published ZIM, and the site states no content licence. Artemis is the wiki's own designated offline companion.
  16.
    - **Name:** Gqrx AppImage
    - **Why:** The Linux AppImage is x86_64 only; the ARM64 builds are macOS DMGs. Use apt 2.17.4 or build 2.17.7.
  17.
    - **Name:** URH transmit, fuzzing and attack-simulation features
    - **Why:** Against the receive-only rule and the scope of the lab. URH is kept only as an optional offline analyser, and it is archived.
  18.
    - **Name:** rtl_433 and other consumer-device decoders
    - **Why:** Not needed for the satellite and RF-measurement lab, and they decode third-party devices. Left out by default.
- **Notes:** Method: versions come from the Ubuntu noble arm64 Packages indexes (ports.ubuntu.com, main/universe, noble and noble-updates, fetched 18 Oct 2026), PyPI JSON, Docker Hub and the Flathub API. Behaviour claims come from primary pages or source files, not forums: SDR++ rigctl_server, recorder, display and command_args; LimeSuiteNG limePPSDO.cpp, limeTRX.cpp, the Soapy Registration.cpp and plugins/CMakeLists.txt; the SigMF schema; the GNSS-SDR PVT, Monitor and Signal Source docs; gpsd JSON; Gqrx remote-control docs and releases. I used 6 web searches.
  
  Local tests: soapy_power 1.6.1 was installed and its PSD path exercised on an Ubuntu 24.04.5 x86_64 container (Python 3.12.3, numpy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.11.4, SoapySDR 0.8). That is not a Q6A, and no SDR was attached. Skyfield 1.48 vs 1.55 from_omm was checked in the PyPI wheels. Nothing in this list was run on the Q6A.
  
  Not verified:
  - GNSS-SDR real-time on 4x A78, and whether apt 0.0.19 already has user_clk_drift_ppm (the docs describe 0.0.22).
  - URH sdist build on aarch64.
  - Artemis Flatpak GPU acceleration on Adreno.
  - Whether the SatNOGS Docker image's librtlsdr supports the V4L.
  - wvkbd under the noble cage build.
  - SDR++ touch ergonomics.
  - What SDR++ does with WAV files above 4 GiB (RF64 is disabled in the source; 32-bit RIFF sizes imply a ~4 GiB limit).
  - LimeSDR Micro retune/settle time for lab-sweep.
  - Every Lime path depends on the unmerged la9310_limesdr driver and the 15 Dec 2026 board ship date (software audit).
  - The Gqrx 2.17.7 release page shows no year.
  - CyberEther ships releases every few days: pin one.
  
  Receive-only and legal: on air, the lab only receives. The LimeSDR Micro can transmit, so the software guard (no TX plugins or flags, sink-block lint, URH without the Lime backend) plus a 50-ohm terminator on its TX port enforce RX-only. Any signal-generating instrument (noise source, VNA, tracking or signal generator, calibrator) is for conducted bench tests only: into cables, attenuators, filters, LNAs or dummy loads, never into an antenna. Prefer low-output models and put attenuators in line.
  
  Rules on receiving, recording, decoding and publishing differ by country. Many jurisdictions allow reception of amateur, weather-satellite and broadcast signals, but restrict decoding, keeping or disclosing other communications, and some restrict SDR or scanner possession or use in vehicles or near sensitive sites. Check local law before use. SatNOGS observations are public, so do not upload anything you may not share.
  
  Budgets reused from the audits: 7 Msps cs16 is 28 MB/s, about 25 GB per 15-minute pass. Wideband IQ goes only to the Samsung T7 through a RAM ring and mbuffer. Record first and decode after the pass whenever the live real-time factor is above 0.5. SDR buffer timestamps are ms-level even with PPS.
  
  Version pins to hold:
  - Kernel 6.18.2-4-qcom with BIOS 260120.
  - librtlsdr2 rebuilt with the V4L commit 0204c9c.
  - LimeSuiteNG limesdr-micro-staging at 37cb183.
  - numpy<2 in the lab venv.
  - Skyfield 1.55 and sgp4 2.27.
  - sigmf 1.13.0, jupyterlab 4.6.4, papermill 2.7.0.
  - SatNOGS client 2.1.4, Artemis 4.2.0, CyberEther 1.15.0.
  
  All software is $0. The hardware the procedures need belongs to other areas: an active GNSS L1 antenna, a noise source with an ENR table, SMA terminators, attenuators and a TX-port load.

## lab:bench_tools (run `wf_1dd437c5-0cf`)

- **Area:** General portable lab tools: pocket DMM, USB-C/PD meter, USB scope plus logic analyzer (sigrok/PulseView on arm64), UART/SWD probe, UVC thermal camera, portable soldering, current-limited supply, ESD, hand tools, spares, notebook/labels, carry case, and how the instruments get power in the field
- **Items:**
  1.
    - **Name:** ANENG AN8008 pocket DMM (AN8009 is the variant with a thermocouple)
    - **Category:** multimeter
    - **Purpose in lab:** Continuity and polarity checks of the XT30, DC5525 and J21 3-pin leads. Rail checks: 9/12 V buck, Q6A 5 V and 3.3 V, LT3045 LNA rail, bias-tee output. uA standby and off-current of the pack chain. mA checks of LNA and bias-tee current against the V4L's 180 mA limit. Pack current up to about 4 A on the 10 A range. Diode and capacitance checks.
    - **Key specs:** 9999 counts, basic DC accuracy 0.5%. 9.999 mV range at 1 uV resolution. 99.99 uA (10 nA resolution) and 999.9 uA (0.1 uA). 999.9 mA, 9.999 A. 0.01 ohm mA shunt, so burden voltage is very low. DC current accuracy is +/-0.8%+3 on the uA ranges and +/-1%+3 on mA/A. Current ranging is manual and the ranges have gaps. AC bandwidth 3 kHz (-3 dB). The frequency counter reaches about 10 MHz at about 1.4 V. Resistance tops out at 9.999 Mohm. Continuity is latched and sounds at 40-50 ohm. 10 mm fuses. The printed 600 V CAT III / 1000 V CAT II rating is judged unlikely in practice by the reviewer. The AN8009 swaps the square-wave output for temperature sensing and NCV (retailer description only, not checked in detail).
    - **Size weight power:** Same case as the ANENG AN8002; exact size and weight are not published in the review (unverified). Runs on 2x AAA: 1.2-2 mA typical, 5.5 mA with backlight, 15 mA with the buzzer sounding. That works out to hundreds of hours per set (my calculation).
    - **Interface and linux:** None. It is standalone with no logging. Logging is covered by the INA228 in the device and by the FNB58.
    - **Price:** About GBP 15 delivered in the reviewer's purchase (older review). The current AliExpress/EU price is unverified; expect roughly $20-35 (unverified).
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Before inserting the meter in series, move the lead from the A jack to the uA jack (see the off-current procedure). Keep spare 10 mm fuses in the kit; open the meter to read their rating. Add a pair of mini-grabber leads (unverified price) so you can measure hands-free on 0.1 in headers. For hot-spot spot checks the AN8009's K-type thermocouple is a cheap complement to the thermal camera.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.markhennessy.co.uk/budget_multimeters/aneng_an8008.htm
      - https://budgetlightforum.com/t/test-review-of-dmm-aneng-an8008/47061
      - https://www.desertcart.sn/products/78091074
    - **Availability:** Widely sold on AliExpress and EU marketplaces. Live stock was not checked (unverified).
    - **Cheaper alternative:** ANENG AN8002: same case, but no 10 nA uA range (price unverified). Nothing cheaper keeps the 10 nA range.
    - **Safety notes:** Low-energy electronics only, never mains: the reviewer doubts the CAT ratings and finds the input protection minimal. Never leave a lead in the A/mA jack while measuring voltage on the 4S pack, because that shorts the pack through the shunt. The pack can deliver tens of amps.

Also cable resistance, e-marker reading and a ripple view.

Waveform logging at 2-100 sps; ripple drawing up to 4 Msps on the device itself. Ports: USB-A, micro-USB and Type-C. The product page does not name PD 3.1 or PPS.

The tool is pure Python, so it should run on the Q6A (arm64), but the author has not tested arm64 (unverified).

NEVER plug it into the Q6A's own USB-C port: that port is hard-wired to the 12 V input and back-feeds (power.json). Choose the Std variant so there is no 2.4 GHz Bluetooth radio near the 2.2 GHz receive chain.

  3.
    - **Name:** Hantek 6022BL USB oscilloscope plus logic analyzer
    - **Category:** USB oscilloscope / logic analyzer
    - **Purpose in lab:** 2-channel scope for converter ripple and spur attribution, using the known fundamentals from power.json: IP2368 250 kHz, SY81012 about 1 MHz, SY7120 1.04 MHz in PFM. Also LNA-rail noise, bias-tee voltage, fan PWM, and PPS and UART edge sanity. Its logic-analyzer mode handles UART, I2C and PPS.
    - **Key specs:** 2 channels, 8-bit, 20 MHz listed bandwidth, 1 Mohm || 25 pF, AC/DC coupling. 48 MS/s headline, but OpenHantek6022 caps it at 30 MS/s with CH1 only, because 48 MS/s USB streaming is unstable. Software trigger only, no onboard memory. Logic analyzer: 16 channels in hardware, 8 channels at up to 24 MHz in sigrok. It is a scope OR a logic analyzer, never both at once; the H/P button selects the mode at plug-in. Inside (per the sigrok teardown): CY7C68013A or CBM9002A, an AMS1117-3.3 LDO and a Mornsun A0505S 2 W isolated DC/DC.
    - **Size weight power:** Size and weight not verified. USB bus-powered. Its draw is not published; the 2 W isolated converter plus the FX2 suggest budgeting up to about 0.5 A at 5 V (my inference). Measure it with the FNB58.
    - **Interface and linux:** USB 2.0 HS. LA mode enumerates as 0925:3881 (the Saleae Logic ID) and uses sigrok's fx2lafw driver. Ubuntu noble universe has PulseView 0.4.2 for arm64 (libsigrok 0.5.2) and sigrok-firmware-fx2lafw 0.1.7 (arch: all); the firmware loads into RAM on every plug-in. Scope mode (04b4:602a) uses OpenHantek6022, which is Linux-first, has CI-built arm64 .debs, and offers a spectrum view, CH1/CH2/MATH software trigger, Vpp/RMS/frequency/THD measurements, cursors and offset calibration. The sigrok wiki says only the 6022BL's LA mode is supported, so do not plan on PulseView for its scope mode.
    - **Price:** GBP 110 ex VAT at The Debug Store UK (EUR 134.95 ex VAT in its FR store). About $126-135 in elecena's 2024 feed. AliExpress price unverified.
    - **Tier:** core
    - **Integration notes:** Plug it into a free port on the Q6A's USB 2.0 hub. A 30 MS/s stream is about 30 MB/s on the 480 Mb/s hub it shares with Wi-Fi and the RTL-SDR, so turn Wi-Fi off and don't record IQ while capturing. To measure ripple, use the x1 setting with a ground spring, or a short 50 ohm coax pigtail through a 1 uF DC block, with AC coupling.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://sigrok.org/wiki/Hantek_6022BL
      - https://sigrok.org/wiki/Hantek_6022BE
      - https://sigrok.org/wiki/Fx2lafw
      - https://github.com/OpenHantek/OpenHantek6022
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/pulseview
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/sigrok-firmware-fx2lafw
      - https://thedebugstore.com/products/hantek-6022bl-oscilloscope-analyser-uk
      - https://elecena.pl/product/25316954/rss
    - **Availability:** Sold by The Debug Store UK and Polish shops (gotronik.pl). SainSmart's listing is discontinued.
    - **Cheaper alternative:** Hantek 6022BE (scope only, about $85-120 on eBay or GBP 85 ex VAT, often sold out) plus a $10 fx2lafw LA. The total is similar, but you can run scope and LA at the same time and scope mode also works in sigrok.
    - **Safety notes:** Treat the probe ground as the Q6A's USB ground (inference: the isolated converter alone does not prove a floating input). Clip it ONLY to device GND (mid-plate or 40-pin GND). Never clip it to the high side of the INA228 shunt, a pack + terminal or a charger output; that shorts through the USB ground. Use x10 probes above the 5 V range.

    - **Category:** portable soldering iron

Open-source IronOS with these settings: Power source cutoff (DC=10 V, or S=3.3 V per cell); per-cell Minimum voltage (2.4-3.7 V for 4-6S); Power limit (on USB-PD the effective limit is the lower of this and the source's advertised wattage); PD Mode ('No Dynamic' disables EPR and PPS). Has BLE (app needs IronOS 2.21+).

On that lead set IronOS Power source to 4S and Minimum voltage to 3.4 V/cell (13.6 V), which matches the stack's Linux poweroff threshold. Stop SDR recording while soldering, because the heater PWM and the BLE radio are noise sources.
