- **Lost vs foldable:**
  1.
    - **Target:** QO-100 narrowband SSB from the strongest (beacon-level) stations
    - **Needed:** +3 dB in 2.7 kHz to barely copy needs about 23 dBi; +6 dB readable needs about 26 dBi; +10 dB comfortable needs about 30 dBi (calculated)
    - **Gap db:** Best small-tier horn (21.5 dBi) is 1.5 dB below the baseline 23 dBi horn and 6 dB below the 27.4 dBi lens. Strict (19.6 dBi) is 3.4 and 8 dB below. Bare LNB is about 13 dB below the horn.
    - **What would bring it back:** The 23 dBi horn (17.8 cm by about 28 cm) for barely-readable copy, or the 30 cm W1GHZ lens with a 17.5 dBi feed (about 65 cm deployed, packs flat) for readable copy, or a 35 cm dish (+9.5 dB). Software gains only 1-2 dB (narrower filter, noise reduction).
  2.
    - **Target:** QO-100 typical SSB stations 5-15 dB below the beacon
    - **Needed:** About 30-40 dBi (dish of 35-90 cm)
    - **Gap db:** 8-20 dB short in the small tier. The foldable baseline had only partial copy here: the lens reached about +2.5 dB for stations 5 dB down.
    - **What would bring it back:** A 35-60 cm dish only
  3.
    - **Target:** QO-100 multimedia beacon (8APSK, 7.2 kbit/s)
    - **Needed:** About 41 dB-Hz (estimate, assuming beacon-level power), which is about 27 dBi
    - **Gap db:** 5-8 dB short (small tier); about 16 dB short (bare LNB)
    - **What would bring it back:** The 30 cm lens (marginal) or a dish
  4.
    - **Target:** QO-100 wideband DATV beacon and stations
    - **Needed:** About 31-32 dBi for the beacon; a dish of 90 cm or more for user stations (BATC)
    - **Gap db:** 10-12 dB short (small tier). The foldable baseline could not decode this either.
    - **What would bring it back:** A dish of 45 cm or more only; no non-dish option reaches it
  5.
    - **Target:** Comfortable QO-100 pointing and SNR headroom (strict bare LNB versus horn)
    - **Needed:** 18-21.5 dBi horn
    - **Gap db:** 8-11 dB between the bare LNB and the small-tier horn. PSK beacon frames, beacon-level SSB and CW 10 dB below the beacon all depend on it.
    - **What would bring it back:** The 10-12 cm cone already fits the strict tier by its own dimensions. Only the overall length with the LNB (about 17-24 cm) pushes it into the small tier.
- **Borderline note:** BORDERLINE (excluded by the new size rule; for reconsideration only). The 23 dBi conical horn (17.8 cm mouth, about 28 cm long on the LNB collar, 37 cm slant) adds only about 1.5 dB over the best small-tier horn. With it, beacon-level SSB rises from about 0 dB to +3 dB, which is barely copyable. The 30 cm W1GHZ metal-plate lens is foam and foil, packs flat, and stands about 65 cm deployed with a 17.5-18 dBi feed horn. It adds about 6 dB: beacon-level SSB about +7.5 dB (readable) and the multimedia beacon marginal. Neither reaches DATV (31-32 dBi) or typical SSB stations (about 30 dBi or more). If listening to QO-100 SSB matters, the lens is the only item worth reconsidering. Otherwise the small tier loses little in this band.
- **Notes:** TIERS AS APPLIED. Strict: the bare LNB counts as strict (the rule says so explicitly), and so does a cone with mouth and length of 12 cm or less (about 19.6 dBi). Small: horns up to 15 cm by 18.5 cm (21.5 dBi). If the 11-14 cm LNB body must be counted in the overall length, the small-tier limit drops to an 11 x 8.3 cm cone (about 18.8 dBi). Excluded: dishes, flat panels (Selfsat H21D/H30D are about 47-52 cm and not specified below 10.7 GHz), the 23 dBi horn and the lens. I found no flat Ku panel of 20 cm or less with an LNB covering 10.489 GHz.
  
  ERROR FOUND IN THE INPUTS (corrected here). dish_replacement.json's QO-100 budget, 'beacon C/N0 is about 28 + G dB-Hz', is about 14 dB too optimistic. It gave the bare LNB a beacon C/N of 3-6 dB in 2.7 kHz, a 20/23 dBi horn 14/17 dB, and the lens 21 dB. The anchor it used, the BATC '>30 dB on 90 cm' snippet, must have been measured in a narrow FFT bin, not in 2.7 kHz.
  
  The primary measurement: EA4GPZ measured the BPSK beacon at about 45 dB-Hz on a dish he describes as comparable to 60 cm (about 34.2 dBi). After maintenance the beacons were about 3 dB stronger, and the beacon C/N0 against transponder noise was 56 dB-Hz. From that I derive, as a calculation: beacon C/N0 is about G + 14.6 dB-Hz (±2.5 dB), capped by transponder noise at 56 dB-Hz. This is the model behind every number above. It matches antennas.json's G/T model (-1 to +2 dB in 2.5 kHz for 20-23 dBi horns). It also matches the field evidence: the CW beacon was only just copyable on a bare LNB (OK1DX), and FT8 decoded at -11 to -15 dB, which is close to beacon level since the bandplan says users must stay 'not stronger than the Beacon'. The horn geometry and the DATV verdict do not change.
  
  PHYSICS. At 10.49 GHz the wavelength is 28.6 mm, so a 12 cm horn is 4.2λ across. It is not electrically short, and its aperture efficiency (about 0.52 for an optimum horn) carries no small-antenna penalty. What limits it is aperture area against a system temperature of about 100-150 K: the LNB's 0.5 dB NF (35 K) plus ground spillover. Sky noise at 32° elevation is small. Transponder noise only matters above about 35 dBi, and band noise from outside does not set the limit. Every +3 dB of gain costs 1.41x the mouth diameter and about 2x the length.
  
  CHAIN.
  - LNB: Bullseye (or QRO.cz at 12-15 V only). Use a regulated 13 V buck-boost through an injector; never the raw 4S pack, which reaches 16.8 V and can flip polarisation.
  - Then DC block, then a 10-20 dB pad, into the RTL-SDR V4L at 739.5-740 MHz.
  - Keep LNB DC away from the LimeSDR (its RX ESD protection is rated 5.3 V). The Lime also has a 737.28 MHz spur 2.2 MHz from the narrowband IF.
  - HDMI 1080p60 has a 5th harmonic at 742.5 MHz, close to the wideband IF. Use a 1080p52 EDID and shielding.
  - Cap the Bullseye's red F port: it is a +15 V serial calibration port.
  - The beacon tracker must acquire wide (about ±800 kHz around IF 739.625 MHz) before narrowing; this fixes the earlier acquisition bug.
  - Pointing: Kyiv 186°/32°, Lviv 178°/33°, Kharkiv 193°/32°, Odesa 187°/36°. Rotate the LNB for polarisation skew. Operate outdoors: window glass blocks 10 GHz.
  - Ku TV carriers above 11.516 GHz on the low band, and the high band (22 kHz tone), need the LimeSDR (ships 15 Dec 2026).
  
  CALIBRATION EXTRAS (calculated, assuming 250-400 sfu at 11 GHz). With the 12-15 cm horn the Sun gives about a 0.2-0.5 dB noise rise; with the bare LNB about 0.03 dB, which is not practical. A cold-sky versus ground comparison gives a quick check of the LNB and horn. Ku broadcasts from the 25.5-26°E cluster (Es'hail/Badr) might help confirm the QO-100 pointing, but whether their beams cover Ukraine is not verified.
  
  LEGAL AND SAFETY. Receive only.
  - Fine to receive: QO-100 amateur traffic, FTA broadcast carriers measured as RF power only.
  - Never: decrypt pay-TV or demodulate operator telemetry.
  - Excluded entirely: Starlink/OneWeb (private and military in Ukraine) and all military SATCOM.
  - Martial law: never publish geotagged spectra or photos, and do not set up near military or critical sites.
  - GNSS is widely jammed or spoofed, so enter your coordinates by hand and aim with the BNO085 plus the Sun or landmarks.
  - Fields may hold unexploded ordnance: if you find one, call 101.
  
  UNVERIFIED.
  - Bullseye dimensions and current draw.
  - Bare-LNB gain (9-12 dBi is an estimate).
  - How well a clamp-on cone mates to the scalar feed (±2 dB; check with an A/B beacon test, expect +6 to +11 dB).
  - Multimedia-beacon power.
  - Ku EIRP over Ukraine (48-53 dBW assumed).
  - Ku tracking-beacon frequencies.
  - Stability of the local Prom.ua LNBs.
  - Bullseye and WiMo shipping to Ukraine.
  - The OK1DX page returned HTTP 503 today, so its content comes from the earlier agents' reading.
  
  WebSearch used: 3 calls.

- **Ended or dead:**
  - NOAA-18: decommissioned 6 Jun 2025 17:40 UTC; APT 137.9125 MHz and HRPT 1707 MHz ended (NOAA OSPO).
  - NOAA-19: decommissioned 13 Aug 2025 18:55 UTC after a Battery 1A cell failure; APT 137.1 MHz and HRPT 1698 MHz ended (NOAA OSPO).
  - NOAA-15: decommissioned 19 Aug 2025 20:37 UTC; APT 137.62 MHz and HRPT 1702.5 MHz ended (NOAA OSPO). All 137 MHz APT is gone.
  - Metop-A: decommissioned (NOAA OSPO). Metop-B and Metop-C LRPT on 137 MHz are off (SatDump: off because of interference with HIRS; OSPO shows APT/LRPT red).
  - Meteor-M N2-2: LRPT inoperable after a micrometeorite strike in Dec 2019; in storage mode since Jul 2024 (SatDump).
  - FengYun-3A, 3B and 3C L-band AHRPT ended; FY-3C was the last, in Nov 2024. FY-3D to 3H AHRPT is X-band only (7.8 GHz, 6-38 Msym/s) and needs a dish (SatDump).
  - Elektro-L N2: no xRIT after a power-supply failure. Elektro-L N3: transmissions paused pending L5 commissioning. Elektro-L N5: LRIT/HRIT off for commissioning (SatDump, 2 Jul 2026). Not dead, but there is currently no geostationary L-band LRIT for Ukraine. The SatNOGS DB entry of 7 Apr 2026 conflicts.
  - EWS-G1 (GOES-13): ended 31 Oct 2023 (SatDump). GOES-East and West are below the horizon from Ukraine (calculation).
  - IO-117 GreenCube: no SatNOGS good observation after 25 Jul 2025, and stations stopped scheduling it after 5 Aug 2025. Presumed silent; cause unverified.
  - ISS VHF APRS on 145.825 MHz: no longer listed by ARISS (7 Oct 2026), which gives APRS on 437.825 MHz instead. Three AMSAT 'VHF Digi heard' reports on 17 Oct 2026 conflict.
  - ISS SSTV on 145.800 MHz: the latest listed ARISS event (Series 32, 8-12 May 2026) used 437.550 MHz Robot 36. The last 145.800 MHz events on the ARISS SSTV blog date from Oct-Nov 2024. No event is announced after May 2026.
  - Re-entered (SatNOGS DB; record-update dates are not decay dates): XW-2A, 2B, 2C, 2D, 2E, 2F and CAS-3G (KAITUO-1B); CAS-5A (FO-118); CAS-10 (HO-119); LilacSat-1 (LO-90); Nayif-1 (EO-88); HADES (SO-115); URESAT-1 (SO-120); HADES-D (SO-121); HADES-R (SO-124); HADES-ICM (SO-125); Tevel-1 to -8 (first generation); UVSQ-SAT; Geoscan-Edelveis; SONATE (the first one); INSPIRESat-1; INSPIRE-SAT 7; I-INSPIRE II.
  - Inmarsat-6 F2: drifting at about +2.5°/day (calculation from Celestrak elements); not a usable EGC source. Inmarsat-4 F2 now sits near 143.5°E (Celestrak SBAS group: SouthPAN PRN 122), out of view from Ukraine.
  - Degraded or intermittent rather than dead: AO-91 FM (2 'heard' against 7 'not heard', 13-18 Oct 2026); PO-101 and AO-27 (scheduled or part-time); CAS-3H FM repeater; TO-108; CAS-2T (last good 29 Aug 2026); Metop-B AHRPT (modulator problems).
- **Excluded private or military:**
  - Iridium: voice, SMS/SBD, pager traffic and ring-alert/paging frames, which carry subscriber identities with beam and satellite positions. Under martial law these could help locate users. Carrier and Doppler observation only; no demodulation guide.
  - Inmarsat: STD-C LES and private messages, FleetNET (commercial EGC), Aero ACARS, C-channel voice, Classic Aero, BGAN/GX. Only EGC SafetyNET maritime safety broadcasts are in scope.
  - Orbcomm: subscriber and user message content. Carrier and Doppler only.
  - Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper and other broadband constellations: all user data. These also need phased arrays or dishes.
  - Thuraya and other MSS voice and data in 1525-1559 / 1626-1660 MHz.
  - Military UHF SATCOM 240-320 MHz (UFO/FLTSATCOM, Skynet, Sicral, Syracuse and others) and MUOS around 360-380 MHz.
  - Military-operated or military payloads: EWS-G2 (GOES-15, US Space Force, 61.5°E; it also needs a dish), reconnaissance and military Kosmos satellites, and Russian military relay systems.
  - Encrypted or restricted GNSS signals (GPS P(Y) and M-code, Galileo PRS, GLONASS P). Do not map or publish GNSS jamming or spoofing sources, since that could reveal EW positions.
  - ISS non-amateur channels: Soyuz/Progress VHF-1/VHF-2 crew voice (143.625 / 130.167 MHz), EVA suit radios (121.x / 139.208 MHz), Dragon/Falcon/Kvant/TORU links. Only NA1SS/RS0ISS amateur modes are in scope.
  - COSPAS-SARSAT 1544.5 MHz repeater downlinks on Meteor-M and Metop, and 406 MHz distress beacons: distress identities and positions.
  - ARGOS/A-DCS (465.9875 MHz) and DCP downlinks of Elektro, Arktika, GOES and FengYun: user platform data such as animal tags and buoys.
  - Terrestrial military, drone or FPV video and telemetry, or police links heard incidentally while scanning: do not record, decode or share.
- **Legal rules:**
  1.
    - **Topic:** Receive-only equipment: licence and registration
    - **Rule:** I found no licence, permit or registration requirement for a receive-only receiver. NKEK's list of radio equipment requiring a frequency assignment (Resolution No. 361, 3 Jul 2024, under Art. 68 of Law 1089-IX) puts broadcast receivers under code ЗД-7: general authorisation, no entry in the frequency-assignment register. Assignments and registration apply to transmitting equipment. Nothing explicitly covers SDR or satellite receivers, so this is an inference. Ask the Ukrainian Amateur Radio League (ЛРУ/UARL) and NKEK in writing, as the inputs already advise.
    - **Source:** https://nkek.gov.ua/static-objects/nkek/sites/1/%D0%A0%D0%9E%20%D1%82%D0%B0%20%D0%92%D0%9F/dodatok-do-postanovy-361-03072024.pdf
  2.
    - **Topic:** Law on Electronic Communications (1089-IX)
    - **Rule:** Law 1089-IX of 16 Dec 2020 has been in force since 1 Jan 2022 and replaced the Law on the Radio Frequency Resource. Under Art. 64, each unit of radio equipment must come with an EU-style declaration of conformity, which matters for imported SDRs and LNBs. Its secrecy-of-communications article was not re-fetched, because zakon.rada.gov.ua returned 503 or reset the connection.
    - **Source:** https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/1089-20 (title only fetched); https://protocol.ua/ua/pro_elektronni_komunikatsii_stattya_64/ (search snippet)
  3.
    - **Topic:** Martial law: transmission ban
    - **Rule:** Art. 8 of Law 389-VIII 'On the legal regime of martial law' allows authorities to 'забороняти роботу приймально-передавальних радіостанцій особистого і колективного користування' (ban the operation of personal and collective transmit-receive radio stations) and to restrict information transmission over computer networks (item 11 in the edition checked). An amateur transmit ban has been reported since Feb 2022, and I found no source lifting it. So: receive only, never transmit or uplink (no SO-50 or ISS repeater access), and keep the LimeSDR TX port disabled and terminated.
    - **Source:** https://kodeksy.com.ua/pro_pravovij_rezhim_voyennogo_stanu/8.htm (2019 edition); https://www.arrl.org/news/ukraine-maintains-ham-radio-silence-in-state-of-emergency
  4.
    - **Topic:** Martial law: seizure of equipment
    - **Rule:** Art. 8 (item 12 in the edition checked) allows seizure of telecom equipment, TV, video and audio equipment, computers and 'інші технічні засоби зв’язку' (other technical means of communication) from people who violate the martial-law regime. Expect the receiver to be inspected or seized if it raises suspicion. Carry a Ukrainian-language explanation that it is a receive-only hobby device.
    - **Source:** https://kodeksy.com.ua/pro_pravovij_rezhim_voyennogo_stanu/8.htm
  5.
    - **Topic:** Martial law: term
    - **Rule:** Martial law runs until 31 Oct 2026 under Decree No. 596/2026: 90 days from 05:30 on 2 Aug 2026, approved by Law No. 4928-IX on 14 Jul 2026 and in force from 25 Jul. Another extension is expected but was not found as of 18 Oct 2026. Re-check after 31 Oct.
    - **Source:** https://nfront.org.ua/?p=62502 (secondary); https://www.president.gov.ua/documents/5962026-60509 (returned 403)
  6.
    - **Topic:** Secrecy of communications: Constitution
    - **Rule:** Constitution Art. 31 guarantees the secrecy of correspondence, telephone conversations, telegraph and other correspondence; exceptions are made only by a court in cases set by law. Private satellite traffic is therefore out of scope (see the excluded list). The text was not re-fetched this run because zakon.rada.gov.ua was unavailable.
    - **Source:** https://zakon.rada.gov.ua/laws/show/254к/96-вр (not re-fetched)
  7.
    - **Topic:** Secrecy of communications: Criminal Code Art. 163
    - **Rule:** Violating the secrecy of correspondence, telephone conversations, telegraph or other correspondence sent by means of communication or by computer is punishable by a fine of 50-100 untaxed minimum incomes, correctional labour up to 2 years, or restriction of liberty up to 3 years. Part 2 (repeat offences, or use of special means for covert information removal) carries 3-7 years' imprisonment. This is why Iridium, Inmarsat LES/ACARS and Orbcomm user data are excluded.
    - **Source:** https://urst.com.ua/kku/st-163 (mirror, 05.01.2022 edition)
  8.
    - **Topic:** Special technical means: Criminal Code Art. 359
    - **Rule:** Illegally acquiring, selling or using special technical means for covert information gathering is punishable by a fine of 200-1000 untaxed minimum incomes or up to 4 years; parts 2-3 carry 4-10 years. Whether a general-purpose SDR counts is not settled in commentary. Keep the device a general receiver for public broadcasts, and do not configure, describe or sell it as an interception tool.
    - **Source:** https://urst.com.ua/kku/st-359 (mirror, 05.01.2022 edition)
  9.
    - **Topic:** Publishing receptions: Criminal Code Art. 114-2
    - **Rule:** Added in March 2022 and amended by Law 2178-IX. It punishes unauthorised dissemination, under martial law, of information on the movement of weapons into Ukraine and on the movement or location of the Armed Forces and other formations (part 1: 3-5 years). Part 2 covers locations identifiable on the ground that the General Staff or MoD has not published, and courts have imposed 10 years under part 3. So: no live streams or geotagged photos. Do not publish exact station coordinates (SatNOGS publishes station latitude and longitude; AMSAT reports include grid squares). Do not post imagery or recordings that show or locate strike damage, infrastructure, or military or drone signals.
    - **Source:** https://i.factor.ua/ukr/law-455/section-1525/article-33548/; https://court.gov.ua/press/news/1797902
  10.
    - **Topic:** GNSS jamming and spoofing
    - **Rule:** Ukrainian anti-drone EW spoofs GPS. The General Staff acknowledged that it disrupts smartphone GPS and clocks (2024), and NovAtel (Sep 2025) reported spoofed receivers in Ukraine showing a future GPS week. Do not trust GNSS time or position. Use the RTC and a manually entered locator for pass prediction. Never publish GNSS-derived positions or analyses of interference sources.
    - **Source:** https://therecord.media/ukraine-anti-drone-gps-spoofing-affects-civilian-mobile-phones; https://novatel.com/support/bulletins-alerts-release-notices/technical-update-gnss-spoofing-attacks-in-ukraine
  11.
    - **Topic:** Field safety: unexploded ordnance
    - **Rule:** Set up only on known-safe ground: your own property, paved areas, or areas cleared by the State Emergency Service (ДСНС/SES). Do not enter fields, forest edges or former combat areas, and do not touch suspicious objects. Call 101 (ДСНС). Avoid infrastructure, checkpoints and military sites, where pointing antennas attracts attention.
    - **Source:** Required by the task; 101 = ДСНС emergency number (general knowledge, not re-verified this run)
- **Notes:** INTERPRETATION OF THE 18 OCT 2026 RULE (applied throughout):
  - STRICT tier: largest deployed dimension at most about 12 cm (patches, chip/ceramic antennas, a bare LNB with its own feed, stubby or helical-loaded whips, small loops).
  - SMALL tier: at most about 20 cm (short loaded whips, rubber ducks, a 20 cm patch or loop).
  - EXCLUDED: dishes of any size and anything with a deployed size of about 20-25 cm or more, even if it folds (Yagis, helicone, full telescopic V-dipoles, the 47 cm helix, the 23 dBi horn, the 300 mm lens).
  
  QUARTER-WAVE LENGTHS (calculation, free space):
  - 137.1/137.9 MHz: 54.7/54.3 cm. 145.8-145.96 MHz: about 51.4 cm.
  - 436.8-437.8 MHz: 17.1-17.2 cm (half wave 34 cm).
  - 1544-1700 MHz: 4.4-4.9 cm.
  - Consequences: all VHF targets (Meteor LRPT, AO-91, PO-101, AO-7 mode B, JO-97, AO-73, Orbcomm, SONATE-2 APRS/SSTV) need electrically short antennas in both tiers, and I have not quantified those losses here. That is for the antenna/link agent; at 137-146 MHz, external noise rather than antenna efficiency may set the limit. UHF 435-438 MHz fits the SMALL tier at full quarter-wave size and is about 0.7 of a quarter wave in the STRICT tier. L-band and GNSS are naturally STRICT-tier.
  
  BIGGEST STATUS CHANGES AFFECTING THE RULE:
  (1) ISS APRS is now 437.825 MHz (ARISS, 7 Oct 2026), and the latest ISS SSTV series used 437.550 MHz (May 2026). Both now sit in the small-antenna-friendly UHF band.
  (2) All NOAA APT ended in 2025. 137 MHz weather now means only Meteor-M N2-3 and N2-4 LRPT, both observed on 137.900 MHz this week.
  (3) There is no geostationary L-band LRIT for Ukraine right now. Elektro-L3 is paused and L5 is off for commissioning (SatDump, 2 Jul 2026). This contradicts the inputs' plan to validate antennas on Elektro-L5 LRIT; use FengYun-2H (79°E, 16.6° elevation, linear polarisation) as the reference carrier instead.
  (4) GreenCube IO-117 has been silent since about Aug 2025.
  (5) Inmarsat-4 F2 has moved to about 143.5°E and is out of view. Inmarsat-C EGC for Ukraine must come from Alphasat (24.9°E) or I-6 F1 (83.8°E); which one is unverified.
  
  REACHABILITY HINTS (reusing input numbers; not new link budgets):
  - QO-100 narrowband: the bare TCXO LNB is STRICT-tier (beacon, CW, FT8 documented). The 20 dBi horn (126 mm mouth, 147 mm cone) is SMALL-tier. DATV is lost.
  - Meteor HRPT: only the 4-5 turn helix on an 18 cm plate (11.6-12.0 dBic modelled, 19-22 cm tall, about +5 dB margin) sits at the SMALL-tier edge. A STRICT-tier patch of about 7-8 dBic (aperture estimate) would cut the inputs' roughly 7 dB average SNR to about 1-2 dB against 0.5 dB needed. That is my estimate, assuming SNR scales dB for dB with gain: marginal, high passes only, and unverified.
  - Metop AHRPT and AWS are out of reach in both tiers.
  - Inmarsat EGC SafetyNET and GNSS are STRICT-tier with patches.
  
  METHOD:
  - SatNOGS Network API (good observations, 30 Sep-18 Oct 2026, most with European stations and decoded frames). SatNOGS DB 'alive' flags are often stale, so I relied on observations instead.
  - AMSAT status page, parsed for 13-18 Oct 2026 (the JSON API returned empty).
  - SatDump sat_list.json (last commits 2 Jul 2026); NOAA OSPO Metop (3 Sep 2026) and POES pages.
  - ARISS status (7 Oct 2026) and the ARISS SSTV gallery.
  - Celestrak element sets (17 Oct 2026). GEO longitudes and elevations are my calculations, good to about ±0.5°.
  
  GAPS:
  - zakon.rada.gov.ua returned 503 or reset, so the legal texts come from mirrors with old editions (Criminal Code 05.01.2022; martial-law law 2019 edition). Item numbers and penalties may have changed; re-check on the official site.
  - No 2026 primary source for Inmarsat EGC configuration, Iridium ring-alert frequency, ISS SSTV after May 2026, the martial-law extension past 31 Oct 2026, any lifting of the amateur transmit ban, or LilacSat-3 activity.
  - The president.gov.ua and NAVCEN pages returned 403.
  
  Budget: 12 WebSearch calls. Raw downloads are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/status_dl and scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/status_scripts.

- **Sdr decision:** HOW I APPLIED THE 18 OCT 2026 RULE
  - STRICT: largest deployed dimension about 12 cm or less. This covers patches, the bare LNB, stubbies, the 12 cm loop, the 12 cm loaded whip and the 2-turn helix on a 12 cm disc.
  - SMALL: about 20 cm or less. This covers the 20 cm loop, NA-701/SRH-701-class whips, the 17 cm whip, the 4-turn helix on a 20 cm disc, and the LNB with an 11 cm cone at 20 cm or less overall.
  - EXCLUDED: every dish, and anything about 20-25 cm or more when deployed, even if it folds. That rules out the 92 cm V-dipole, the WB2HOL/N2SPI Yagis, the 47 cm helix, the 44 cm helicone, the 23 dBi horn, the 30 cm lens and the 2x2 array.
  - Coax leads are not counted as antenna size. The default build uses SMALL-tier antennas; STRICT swaps are listed with their cost in dB.
  
  DECISION: drop the LimeSDR Micro and cancel the pre-order before it ships on 15 Dec 2026 (full refund before shipment). The RTL-SDR Blog V4L becomes the only SDR type, with two units in use.
  - Range: 500 kHz-1.766 GHz and 2.56 Msps stable, per the V4L datasheet.
  - What it covers, all at 2.56 Msps or less:
    - 137.9 MHz LRPT at 1.024 Msps.
    - 145.8-146 and 435-438 MHz signals, all under 0.2 MHz wide.
    - The QO-100 NB transponder at a 739.5-740 MHz IF.
    - Inmarsat-C at 1537-1545 MHz and GNSS L1.
    - Meteor HRPT at 1700 MHz, at 2.4-2.56 Msps.
  
  What the Lime alone would still reach with allowed antennas:
  - Reliable, with a 12 cm S helix plus LNA and cavity: Black Kite-1/2 S-band 38k4 GMSK telemetry (2286/2288 MHz) and the CARTOSAT-3 CW carrier (2224.797 MHz).
  - Opportunistic only: AWS at 1707 MHz (needs at least 3.6 Msps), PHASMA, S-band science humps, the HamTV carrier, Ku high-band carrier humps above 11.516 GHz, and full-band Iridium.
  - Metop AHRPT, Elektro-L LRIT and QO-100 DATV are out of reach in both tiers with any SDR.
  
  That is two niche reliable targets for about $310-320 landed, plus a riser, a cooling path of 10 W or more, an unmerged arm64 driver and an S-band LNA with a EUR 65.45 cavity.
  
  Two V4Ls give something the Lime cannot: its RX1/RX2 share one LO, so it receives one band at a time.
  - RTL-A on the blue USB 3.1 port: 137/145/435 MHz.
  - RTL-B on a hub port with Wi-Fi off: L-band and the QO-100 IF.
  - Example: LRPT and HRPT from the same Meteor N2-4 pass.
  - If S-band is wanted later, add a USB module (ADALM-PLUTO, $253.32 at DigiKey, in stock) instead of reviving the PCIe design.
  
  STILL REACHABLE (band studies, models ±3 dB)
  - Reliable:
    - ISS SSTV on 437.55 MHz (Series 34, 22-25 Oct 2026, confirmed on ARISS today), ISS APRS on 437.825 MHz and the FM repeater on 437.800 MHz, receive only.
    - AO-73/JO-97 BPSK telemetry and the AO-7 beacon.
    - RS-44 and FO-29 CW beacons (reliable to marginal).
    - Inmarsat-C EGC SafetyNET, GNSS and EGNOS.
    - QO-100 NB beacons, CW and FT8 on the bare LNB, plus BPSK beacon frames with the cone.
    - Meteor-M N2-4 HRPT with the 20 cm helix, from about 13-18° elevation.
  - Marginal:
    - Meteor-M N2-4 LRPT: 20 cm loop from about 17°, 12 cm loop from about 20°. No published decode with an antenna under 20 cm exists.
    - Meteor HRPT on the STRICT 2-turn helix, above about 22-28°.
    - 1 W 9k6 UHF CubeSats on passes above about 40-45°.
  - Opportunistic: Meteor N2-3 LRPT, SO-50 (overhead passes), SSB on the linear transponders, VHF APRS digipeaters, AO-91, and the FY-2H carriers.
  - Lost: Metop AHRPT, Elektro LRIT (also switched off), QO-100 SSB from typical stations, DATV and the multimedia beacon, 0.5 W and 19k2+ CubeSats, and most low passes. All APT is gone because NOAA POES ended in 2025.
  - Legal: Iridium and Orbcomm are limited to carrier and Doppler only, because the input files conflict on this.
  
  PHYSICS
  - A quarter wave is 54.5 cm at 137.5 MHz and 17.2 cm at 436 MHz.
  - 137.5 MHz antennas:
    - 20 cm loop: Rr 1.36 Ω, efficiency -0.9 to -1.5 dB, about +0.3 dBi.
    - 12 cm loop: Rr 0.18 Ω, -3.0 to -3.8 dB, about -2 dBi.
    - 12 cm loaded whip: Rr 1.2 Ω, -6.6 to -9.7 dB.
  - At 137 MHz, rural man-made plus galactic noise is about 2000-2300 K. Noise rather than efficiency is then the limit, so the 20 cm loop loses only 0.3-1.3 dB of SNR against the V-dipole. The penalty is larger at a truly quiet site.
  - At 436 MHz the 17 cm whip is full size (Rr about 24 Ω). Its 11 dB gap to the Yagi is lost directivity, which noise cannot hide.
  - At L-band and 10.5 GHz, 12-20 cm is 0.7 λ or more. Efficiency stays above 90%, and only aperture limits gain.
  - My calculation: the loop's own selectivity (Q about 98) rejects 88-108 MHz by about 34-39 dB.
  
  BORDERLINE (EXCLUDED, listed only for reconsideration)
  - 70 cm Moxon (25x10 cm): about +5.4 dB. 1 W CubeSats work from about 15-20° elevation, and SO-50 and SSB improve.
  - 4-element 70 cm Yagi (29x34 cm): within 1.5 dB of the 6-element.
  - WB2HOL (105x51 cm): brings back VHF FM, APRS and SSB, plus about 6 dB at 137 MHz.
  - 44 cm helicone or 47 cm helix: +5-8 dB at 1.7 GHz. HRPT from about 5°, and Metop or AWS on high passes.
  - 33 cm S cone: +4-6.5 dB.
  - 23 dBi horn (+1.5 dB) or 30 cm lens (+6 dB): QO-100 beacon-level SSB becomes copyable.
  - 92 cm V-dipole: only +0.3-1.3 dB over a good 20 cm loop. Bring it back only if the loop fails validation.
- **Compute decision:** Keep the Radxa Dragon Q6A, but buy the 8 GB board from TinyTronics NL: EUR 121 incl. NL VAT, or EUR 100 ex VAT (about $116-140), 20+ in stock on 18 Oct 2026 per compute.json. It replaces the 12 GB board at $189.99 from Allnet.
  
  Why 8 GB is enough:
  - Every reason for 12 GB and PCIe Gen3 is gone: no 61-160 Msps bursts, no 8 GiB mlocked RAM ring, no M.2 SDR.
  - The new worst case is two RTLs at 2.56 Msps 8-bit (about 10 MB/s), live SatDump HRPT/LRPT, gr-satellites, an SDR++ waterfall and an optional small classifier.
  - Board power at that load is about 4-6 W. Idle is 2.9 W and full stress 9.3-10.1 W (Geerling/sbc-bench).
  
  Why not a cheaper board:
  - Smaller boards could run this load, but none is a clear win.
  - A733 boards (Radxa Cubie A7A $50-75, Orange Pi 4 Pro $48-71) have BSP 5.15 kernels and an undocumented NPU SDK.
  - The RK3576 ROCK 4D 6 GB costs $98.99 and needs an RKNN port.
  - Any switch saves only about $20-90. It would throw away the verified Q6A integration: pinned kernel, HDMI/EDID fixes, UART6 GNSS bring-up, the J21 3S power path, the USB/hub topology and the STEP-based case.
  - A Raspberry Pi 5 8 GB is $175 MSRP (compute.json) and has no NPU.
  
  Changes to the Q6A setup:
  - Use path A: Radxa OS r2 on BIOS 260120, kernel 6.18.2-4-qcom held, the Samsung 128 GB UFS and the golden NPU set.
  - Out-of-tree work is gone: no out-of-tree module, no LA9310 PCI class-code quirk, no SMMU identity group, no isolcpus/nohz_full real-time thread.
  - The NPU stays optional, with the CPU ONNX classifier as the default.
  - Leave the M.2 slot empty and covered. A 2230 NVMe can go in later if ever needed.
  - Keep active cooling: the SoC still throttles at about 90 °C under full load, and the 2000-nit display heats the box.
  - USB plan: RTL-A on the blue USB 3.1 port. Touch, IMU puck and RTL-B on the three USB 2.0 hub ports. GNSS on UART6.
  
  Revisit the board choice only if the NPU goal is dropped.
- **Display power mechanical impact:** DISPLAY: keep the Wisecoco 7in 2000+ nit HDMI kit with USB touch. The antenna rule does not change the sunlight requirement.
  - It is now the largest single load: about 3.6-4.8 W at 60% brightness and 6-8 W at full, i.e. 30-45% of typical draw. The RP2040/VEML7700 auto-dimmer is the biggest runtime lever.
  - RFI matters more, because the small antennas pick up little noise of their own:
    - Use the 1080p52 128.7 MHz EDID if the board accepts it. At 1080p60 the 148.5 MHz clock sits 2.7 MHz above 145.8 MHz, and its 5th harmonic (742.5 MHz) sits 2.5 MHz above the QO-100 NB IF.
    - Use a short shielded HDMI cable with ferrites.
    - Keep every antenna and LNA on 0.5-1 m of coax with a choke, away from the box.
  - Option if size and power matter more than sun readability: the Waveshare 5DP-CAPLCD-B (5in, 800 nits, 4.2 W, $47-55). It brings the case to about 160x100x55-60 mm and 0.85-0.95 kg (mechanical estimate).
  
  POWER (my calculation):
  - At the pack: typical about 11-17 W (was about 25-28 W), peak about 24-32 W (was about 45-52 W).
  - Load is now:
    - Q6A: 4-6 W.
    - V4L: about 1.3 W each.
    - LNA: 0.7-0.85 W each.
    - Fans: 0.8-2 W.
    - GNSS and IMU: about 0.3 W.
    - LNB in QO-100 mode: 1.4-3.6 W.
    - Conversion losses: 8-12%.
  - The Lime's M.2 3.3 V allowance (up to 8.25 W) leaves the Q6A's roughly 17 W internal 5 V_PERI budget.
  - Recommendation: 3S1P Molicel P50B (54 Wh) wired straight into J21 (pack, 7.5 A fuse, INA228, #2813, SMBJ14A, 220 µF, J21):
    - This is the power study's budget topology. J21 sees only about 1.5 A peak, because the display, LNAs and LNB run from their own regulators.
    - Strap the IP2368 for 3S at 4.10 V/cell.
    - Runtime: about 2.8-4.0 h typical, against about 2.2-2.4 h before on 72 Wh.
    - Keeping the 4S1P pack (72 Wh, about +$45, about +75 g) gives about 3.7-5.3 h.
  - The LNB needs only a fixed 13 V, from a GPIO-switched MT3608/XL6009-class boost on the 3S pack. There is no 18 V branch.
  
  MECHANICAL/THERMAL:
  - Removed:
    - The R44SF riser, its clamp bar and the windowed female board.
    - The Lime pedestal and gap pad, and the Lime part of the plate fins.
    - The MHF4 pigtails and the I-PEX tool.
    - The internal T7 SSD.
  - J21 no longer needs desoldering, which was only for the riser path. Still fit a keyed, latched housing.
  - Internal heat falls from about 25-35 W to about 11-17 W typical and 24-32 W peak, including the display. The Q6A fin stack, its fan and the display blower stay; the Lime's 10 W conduction path goes.
  - The FR4 shield bay now holds two V4Ls in their own aluminium cases bonded to the plate, plus three injectors.
  - SMA panel: RTL-A (VHF/UHF), RTL-B (L-band/IF), and an F-type 13 V LNB port with a guarded switch and LED.
  - Size: the footprint stays display-limited at about 205-215 x 130-140 mm; at best about 10 mm shorter without the top-edge Lime strip (estimate). Thickness stays about 50-55 mm (about 45 mm with a low-profile cooler), because the panel, plate and cooler set it.
  
  GNSS/IMU: unchanged parts.
  - Mount the puck on the antenna in use. On the loop, keep the satellite in the loop plane, because the nulls lie along the axis.
  - On the helix and cone, take elevation from gravity and peak on the signal.
  - Dropping the steel tape elements improves the compass.
  
  STORAGE: the 128 GB UFS only. It holds about 5 h of raw IQ at 18.4 GB/h, or keep products only.
  
  SOFTWARE:
  - Removed: the Lime stack.
  - Added: a SafetyNET-only Inmarsat-C decoder, WSJT-X, Direwolf (no iGate), an SSTV decoder, and a two-RTL SatDump configuration.

- **Size weight power before after:** Device box:
  - Before: about 205-215 x 130-140 x 50-55 mm, about 1.2-1.4 kg (mechanical_thermal.json; bare panel plus driver board). Add about 70 g for the internal T7 and its cable.
  - After: about 200-215 x 120-140 x 45-55 mm, about 1.05-1.25 kg (my estimate). The changes are: Lime under 20 g, riser 15 g, pigtails about 10 g, pedestal and fins 20-40 g, T7 and cable about 70 g and one cell about 70 g removed; a second V4L of about 30 g added.
  - The footprint stays set by the 7-inch display, and the thickness by the panel, plate and cooler stack.
  
  Antenna kit (estimates):
  - Before: about 1.4-2.0 kg. The largest deployed pieces were the 92 cm V-dipole, the 105 cm 2 m Yagi elements and the 44-47 cm L-band antenna.
  - After: about 0.7-0.9 kg, with nothing over about 20 cm deployed. Breakdown:
    - 20 cm loop with its SAWbird: about 200-280 g
    - NA-701: about 15 g
    - Helix on a 20 cm disc with its LNA: about 210 g
    - LNB plus cone: about 200-250 g
    - Four thin leads: about 100 g

  - Before: typical about 25-28 W, peak about 45-52 W, internal heat about 25-35 W.
  - After: typical about 11-17 W, peak about 24-32 W.
  
  Runtime (85% of nominal capacity usable):
  - Before: about 2.2-2.4 h typical on 72 Wh.
  - After, 3S1P 54 Wh: about 2.8-4.0 h typical, about 1.4-1.9 h at peak.
  - After, 4S1P 72 Wh kept: about 3.7-5.3 h typical.
- **Risks:**
  - Meteor LRPT with antennas under 20 cm is model-based only (±3 dB); no published decode exists. Validate on 2-3 high Meteor N2-4 passes and A/B the loop against the NA-701 by SatDump SNR. If it fails, the only fix is a borderline item: the 92 cm V-dipole or the 137 MHz tape Yagi.
  - Host self-noise is now the likely real limit. Small antennas have low antenna temperatures, and the Q6A, HDMI, IP2368, display boost and USB sit within centimetres. Run terminated-input and antenna-on noise sweeps with each source switched on and off at 137.9, 145.9, 437, 739.5, 1542 and 1700 MHz. Keep antennas on 0.5-1 m choked coax, switch Wi-Fi off, and use the 1080p52 EDID if the board accepts it.
  - Tuned loops detune with hands, temperature and nearby metal. The 20 cm loop's roughly 1.4 MHz bandwidth tolerates a fixed tuning; the STRICT 12 cm loop (0.1-0.55 MHz) must be peaked every pass on sky noise. A varactor instead of the air trimmer costs about 2.7 dB more.
  - The whole receiver now depends on one end-of-life tuner (R828S, stock expected to last about a year). Buy both V4Ls now, back up their EEPROMs, fit GPIO VBUS-cut pigtails for the 'stuck noisy until replug' fault, and keep a V3/V3c fallback, which is 2-3 dB worse. Meteor HRPT at 2.56 Msps against a 2.7 MHz main lobe is a marginal sample rate (software.json).
  - L-band interference: LTE Band 3 uplink (1710-1730 MHz) falls inside the SAWbird+ GOES passband. The smaller, wider-beam helix has less margin than the 47 cm helix, and GNSS jammers near the front may raise the 1.5-1.6 GHz noise floor (plausible, unverified). Choose shielded sites and keep the LNA at the feed.
  - The 70 cm chain has no band filter: the Uputronics 435 CubeSat preamp is out of stock (Kubii stock alert, 18 Oct 2026). A broadband LNA V2 on a broadband whip near DVB-T2, LTE 800 or pagers can overload the 8-bit RTL. Run the 3 dB-pad test and use the Flamingo+ at strong-FM sites.
  - 3S directly into J21 has no public long-term bench test (Radxa staff give 4.5-16 V; the docs say 12 V). The Wisecoco board's input voltage is unknown, and a 12 V-only board would need a buck-boost from 3S. Measure hot-plug overshoot and J21 heating, or keep the 4S1P pack and the D36V50F12.
  - Cancelling the Lime loses S-band (Black Kite-1/2, CARTOSAT-3) and AWS. Lime pricing has moved before ($199 to $249), so a later re-order may cost more. The ADALM-PLUTO alternative is unverified on the Q6A and for shipping to Ukraine.
  - Satellite status: Meteor N2-3's VHF antenna is partly undeployed. ISS SSTV runs only during events (Series 34 is 22-25 Oct 2026, times TBD). Which satellite serves the EMEA Inmarsat-C NCS (Alphasat or I-6 F1) and its exact frequency are unverified, so scan 1537-1545 MHz. Elektro-L LRIT is off, so use the Inmarsat carrier as the fixed L-band reference.
  - Corrections to the inputs: (1) the status agent wrote that no ISS SSTV event after May 2026 was posted, but ARISS lists Series 33 (2-6 Oct) and Series 34 (22-25 Oct 2026); (2) the SAWbird+ prices are $49.95, not $44.95; (3) the earlier conflict over who uses the blue USB 3.1 port (RTL or T7) disappears now that the T7 is gone.
  - Legal frame: receive only, with the LimeSDR/Pluto TX never configured. Under martial law, which runs to 31 Oct 2026 and an extension is expected, do not iGate or publish APRS positions, geotagged images or station coordinates (Art. 114-2). Filter Inmarsat to SafetyNET only. The inputs conflict on Iridium and Orbcomm (system frames versus carrier/Doppler only), so use carrier and Doppler only. Military, Starlink, Cospas-Sarsat and private traffic are excluded. Expect GNSS spoofing. Watch for UXO at field sites and call 101 if you find any.

## small:verify_stack_legal (run `wf_41027870-8e7`)

- **Lens:** STACK AND LEGAL. I checked the remove, keep and add decisions, the cost, size and power deltas, satellite statuses, and whether anything excluded slipped into the reachable lists. Searches used: 4 WebSearch calls. Pages read with WebFetch or curl: ARISS, Crowd Supply, Nooelec, the RTL-SDR V4L datasheet, iridium-toolkit, SatNOGS and Celestrak. I also re-ran the stack's bom.py, bom2.py and pwr.py.
- **Refuted:**
  1.
    - **Claim:** Keep list and BOM: 'SMA bias-tee injectors with TPS2553 load switches ... two for RTL-B: 5 V for the L-band SAWbirds and 13 V for the LNB'; BOM line '3 SMA bias-tee injectors, 3 TPS2553 switches ... 13 V boost'.
    - **Why:** The TI TPS2553 is a 2.5-6.5 V USB-class power switch; the project's own rf_frontend.json gives '2.5-6.5 V input'. It cannot switch the 13 V LNB feed, and it cannot switch the boost's input either, because that is the 9-12.6 V 3S pack. Used on either side it would be destroyed.
    - **Correction:** Keep TPS2553 switches only on the 5 V LNA injectors. Switch the LNB rail with a part rated for at least 16-20 V. A second Pololu #2813 (4.5-40 V, 6 A, already chosen in power.json) in front of the boost works, or an eFuse or high-side switch of the same rating (exact part not verified).
    - **Source:** /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/rf_frontend.json; https://www.ti.com/product/TPS2553 (not re-fetched)
  2.
    - **Claim:** The LNB gets a fixed 13 V 'from a GPIO-switched MT3608/XL6009-class boost on the 3S pack'.
    - **Why:** MT3608/XL6009-class boosts are non-synchronous and have no output disconnect. With EN pulled low, the output still sits at the pack voltage minus one diode drop, about 8.5-12 V through the inductor and Schottky. The LNB therefore stays powered, which selects vertical polarisation, wastes 1.4-3.6 W and leaves DC on the F port when it is meant to be off.
    - **Correction:** Put a real load switch before or after the boost (see the previous item), or use a boost with true output disconnect. Verify with a meter that the F port reads 0 V when switched off.
    - **Source:** Circuit-topology reasoning (general knowledge, not a fetched source)
  3.
    - **Claim:** Add list: a 20 cm loop with one fixed tuning at 137.9 MHz 'covers both Meteors (and Orbcomm) with no motor'.
    - **Why:** Calculation using the stack's own Q, about 98 (1.4 MHz 3 dB bandwidth), and a single-tuned response. Tuned to 137.9 MHz, the loss is 3.6 dB at 137.1 MHz (the Meteor alternate) and 2.7 dB at 137.25 MHz. On a link already rated marginal, 3.6 dB is enough to lose the decode. Today both Meteors use 137.900 MHz: SatNOGS observations 15230698 (N2-4, 18 Oct) and 15229039 (N2-3, 17 Oct) were good at 137.900 MHz. Caveat: these were IQ-recording observations, so they show the transmitter entry, not that 137.1 MHz is unused.
    - **Correction:** Fixed tuning at 137.9 MHz is fine while both satellites stay there. If one moves to 137.1 MHz, retune, or centre the loop at about 137.5 MHz, which costs about 1.2 dB at each frequency. Orbcomm is carrier/Doppler only and does not justify any tuning.
    - **Source:** https://network.satnogs.org/api/observations/15230698/ ; https://network.satnogs.org/api/observations/15229039/ ; calculation
  4.
    - **Claim:** L-band band study: 'Iridium constellation: ring-alert and system broadcast frames (IRA/IBC) ... reachability reliable ... strip TMSI'. Its bottom line also lists 'Iridium system frames' as reliable at STRICT tier.
    - **Why:** iridium-toolkit's FORMAT.md shows IRA frames carry 'PAGE(tmsi:... msc_id:...)' subscriber paging entries. IBC frames carry channel assignments that answer terminal access requests (Rid). Decoding either captures private-communications metadata, which Constitution Art. 31 and Criminal Code Art. 163 protect. 'Stripping' fields after demodulation does not avoid the interception. Iridium is also heavily used by military users in Ukraine. The stack decision already restricts Iridium to carrier/Doppler, but it gives the wrong reason ('because the input files conflict'), and the band study still lists frame decoding as reachable.
    - **Correction:** Remove 'Iridium system frames' from every reachable list. Iridium is carrier and Doppler observation only: no gr-iridium or iridium-toolkit frame decoding. Also drop 'full-band Iridium' from the list of capabilities lost with the Lime, since it should not be counted as a capability at all. Apply the same carrier/Doppler-only rule to Orbcomm. The VHF study's claim that Orbcomm user messages are 'encrypted' is unverified, and it does not matter: they are excluded either way.
    - **Source:** https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muccc/iridium-toolkit/master/FORMAT.md
  5.
    - **Claim:** L-band band study: 'The MEAS Inmarsat-4 satellite near 64°E is at about 24° elevation' from Ukraine.
    - **Why:** I used Celestrak element sets with 16-17 Oct 2026 epochs and an approximate longitude calculation (good to about ±1°). Inmarsat 4-F2 is at about 142.5°E, 4-F1 at about 177°E, 6-F1 at about 83°E, and 6-F2 is drifting about +2.5°/day. The only Inmarsat object near 62°E is 5-F1, which is Ka-band GX with no L-band. This agrees with the status agent and contradicts the band study.
    - **Correction:** Inmarsat-C EGC from Ukraine comes from Alphasat (about 25°E, about 32° elevation from Kyiv) or Inmarsat-6 F1 (about 83°E, about 14° elevation). Which one carries the EMEA NCS is still unverified, so scan 1537-1545 MHz.
    - **Source:** https://celestrak.org/NORAD/elements/gp.php?NAME=INMARSAT&FORMAT=TLE ; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/verif_stack/geo_lon.py
  6.
    - **Claim:** Stack decision, 'STILL REACHABLE ... Reliable': 'Meteor-M N2-4 HRPT with the 20 cm helix, from about 13-18° elevation'.
    - **Why:** The L-band study's own evidence field says 'Calculated only, with no field precedent. Validate first on a high pass.' The rating rests on an NEC model (±1.2 dB optimism) plus an unverified Meteor EIRP (±2-3 dB). Meteor LRPT, which has the same kind of evidence, is rated 'marginal'.
    - **Correction:** Rate it 'expected reliable (model, ±3 dB), not yet validated'. Promote it to reliable only after 2-3 decoded passes.
    - **Source:** Internal: L-band band study, entry 'Meteor-M N2-3 and N2-4 HRPT, SMALL tier'
  7.
    - **Claim:** Default 2 m/70 cm antenna: 'Nagoya NA-701 ... (21 cm, at the SMALL limit)'.
    - **Why:** 21 cm is over the stated SMALL limit of about 20 cm. The rule says 'about', so this is borderline rather than a clear violation. The band study's own W9MDB figures put the 16.8 cm Baofeng A-V85 ahead of the NA-701 at 146 MHz (-0.8 vs -2.3 dB against the NA-771; I did not re-fetch the PDF). The NA-701 also has a documented clone problem (one clone measured -10.3 dB).
    - **Correction:** Default to an antenna clearly under 20 cm: the SRH-701 (19 cm) or A-V85 (16.8 cm) for 2 m, plus the DIY 17 cm quarter-wave for 70 cm. List the NA-701 as a rule-edge alternative. Check whichever you buy with the NanoVNA.
    - **Source:** https://www.miklor.com/COM/pdf/AntennaTestingW9MDB.pdf (as cited by the VHF study)
  8.
    - **Claim:** Power at the pack: 'typical about 11-17 W', runtime about 2.8-4.0 h on 3S.
    - **Why:** pwr.py's typical case has one RTL, one LNA and no LNB. QO-100 mode adds 1.4-3.6 W for the LNB plus conversion loss. The headline dual-RTL mode (LRPT and HRPT in the same pass) adds about 1.3 W for the second RTL plus 0.7-0.85 W for a second LNA. Those modes run at about 13-21 W.
    - **Correction:** Give power per mode. For QO-100 or dual-RTL sessions, typical is about 13-21 W and runtime about 2.2-3.5 h on 3S1P (46 Wh usable). The peak figure of 24-32 W, which already includes the LNB and two LNAs, is correct.
    - **Source:** /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/smallstack/pwr.py
- **Confirmed:**

The V4L datasheet gives R828S, 500 kHz-1.766 GHz, '2.56 MHz stable (up to 3.2 MHz with drops)', 250-270 mA draw and a 4.5 V / 180 mA bias tee. That covers 137.9 MHz, 145.8-146 MHz, 435-438 MHz, the 739.5-740 MHz QO-100 IF, 1537-1545 MHz, GNSS L1 and 1700 MHz HRPT.   - Removing the Samsung T7 and the 12 GB board is consistent: the largest remaining stream is 2x 2.56 Msps 8-bit, about 10 MB/s.
  - Inmarsat-C: no 2026 retirement or EMEA NCS change notice was found (one search). SafetyNET remains a valid public GMDSS safety broadcast target.
  - Legal sweep of the stack decision's own 'STILL REACHABLE' list: it contains only amateur, weather, navigation, public-safety (SafetyNET) and science or telemetry targets, with no private, military or Starlink content. The excluded lists cover Iridium and Inmarsat user traffic, ACARS, Orbcomm user data, Starlink/OneWeb, UHF military SATCOM at 240-320 MHz, MUOS, military payloads, Cospas-Sarsat and ARGOS/DCP. The APRS no-iGate rule, the no-geotag rule, the Art. 114-2 warning, the GNSS spoofing warning and the UXO/101 warning are all present.
  - Added parts that are verifiably real: V4L ($37.95; RTL-SDR Blog serves Ukraine through its AliExpress store, per narrowband_sdr.json); SAWbird+ iO ($49.95); NA-701 (950 UAH on Prom.ua per the band study). The ADALM-PLUTO, TinyTronics, Nooelec, WiMo and DigiKey are still unverified for delivery to Ukraine.
- **Missed targets or parts:**
  - Not mentioned among the costs of dropping the Lime: dynamic range. The V4L has an 8-bit ADC, 'poorer overload behaviour than the V4 near FM, DAB or TV transmitters', and a 'diplexer front end with no notch filter' (narrowband_sdr.json). The 70 cm chain will have no band filter, because the Uputronics preamp is out of stock. With the Lime gone, overload is the main technical risk. A 70 cm band-pass filter at the LNA V2 should be added to the BOM; I did not verify a specific part.
  - Legal benefit of the decision not credited: dropping the Lime removes the only transmit-capable device. The kit (RTL-SDRs, LNB, LNAs) becomes physically receive-only, which is the easiest position to defend under martial-law Art. 8 (transceiver-station ban and seizure power). The optional ADALM-PLUTO would bring a transceiver back. If S-band is ever wanted, document the TX as disabled, or look for a receive-only downconverter plus RTL route (no product verified).
  - Savings are avoided spend only. The stack does not say which parts are already bought. The 12 GB Q6A, the T7, the 4th cell and the D36V50F12 save nothing if they are already in hand; keep the T7 as a backup in that case. The Lime is refundable only as a pre-order or stock order.
  - The 11 cm x 8.3 cm cone plus Bullseye LNB being 20 cm or less overall rests on an unverified LNB length (estimated 11-14 cm), so the real total could be 19-22 cm. Measure it. If it is over, use the 10 cm x 6.3 cm cone (about 18 dBi).
  - AO-73 'reliable' depends on an ASSUMED 0.3 W EIRP. FUNcube-1's beacon power has a low-power mode (from memory, not verified). If it is 10 dB lower, the margin at 10° drops from +5 dB to about -5 dB, so its rating should carry that assumption.
  - CARTOSAT-3 is used as one of the two 'reliable' reasons for the optional S-band module. It is a civil ISRO Earth-observation satellite, but its imagery is also used for defence. Carrier logging is harmless; still, given the military-exclusion frame, list it as dual-use or drop it from the justification.
  - Small note: a NanoVNA sweep into an antenna radiates a µW-level signal across the 137 MHz, 435 MHz and GNSS L1 bands. Tune indoors or briefly, and not near sensitive sites.
  - Dual-RTL 'LRPT and HRPT in the same pass' needs both antennas pointed at once (the loop in the satellite's plane and the helix on target). A single handheld operator needs one of them on a fixed mount or tripod. This is operationally hard, not impossible.
- **Notes:** Overall verdict: the remove, keep and add decisions are sound. The LimeSDR can be dropped safely: everything still reachable fits the V4L's 0.5-1766 MHz range at 2.56 Msps or less, and the S-band and AWS losses are honestly listed. Three corrections are needed before the stack is final. (1) The 13 V LNB switching is wrong: a TPS2553 cannot take 9-13 V, and a plain boost without output disconnect cannot switch the LNB off. (2) Iridium IRA/IBC frame decoding must be removed from the L-band reachable list, because iridium-toolkit documents TMSI paging entries in IRA frames. (3) The 'MEAS I-4 at 64°E' Inmarsat-C source is out of date: from Ukraine it is Alphasat at about 25°E or I-6 F1 at about 83°E. Smaller fixes: rate Meteor HRPT on the 20 cm helix as model-only, not 'reliable'; prefer an antenna clearly under 20 cm to the 21 cm NA-701; give power per mode, since the LNB and dual-RTL operation are missing from 'typical'; and if the 4S pack is kept, keep the D36V50F12 buck and change the SMBJ14A. The cost, size and storage numbers reproduce from the stack's own scripts. Note the pending abolition of the EUR 150 parcel exemption (autumn 2026) and the 31 Oct 2026 martial-law expiry, with an extension expected. Files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/verif_stack/geo_lon.py (GEO longitude from TLEs) and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/verif_stack/dl/inm.tle.

## small:verify_rf_link (run `wf_41027870-8e7`)

- **Lens:** RF link budgets: short antennas at 137.9/145.9/437 MHz (efficiency, pattern, counterpoise, external noise), the L-band helix/patch against HRPT/AHRPT/LRIT/EGC, and the bare LNB or cone against the QO-100 modes. My own NEC2 (PyNEC) runs and Python budgets are calculations: free space, no hand or body model, ITU-R P.372 coefficients as I recall them. Scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/ (whip_nec.py, whip2.py, loop_nec2.py, lb_check.py).
- **Refuted:**
  1.
    - **Claim:** Whip margins that grow with elevation. Examples: 1 W 9k6 UHF CubeSats '+2.0/+3.6/+4.8 dB at 45/60/90 deg, so only passes above about 40-45 deg work'; RS-44/FO-29 CW beacons up to '+11/+13 dB' at 90 deg; AO-73/JO-97 '+15/+19 dB at 90 deg' on the NA-701; the stack's '1 W 9k6 CubeSats only above about 40-45 deg'.
    - **Why:** small_ant/lb.py and sats.py give every whip a fixed 1.8-2.0 dBi of directivity at all elevations. A vertical monopole has a null at zenith. My NEC2 model of a plain 17 cm whip held vertically on a 13x20 cm case at 437 MHz gives realised gain of +0.5 / -2.0 / -5.1 / -9.3 / -16.0 dBi and a null at 10 / 30 / 45 / 60 / 75 / 90 deg. With the band study's own CubeSat budget (EIRP 27 dBm, 4.5 dB losses, Tsys 340 K, 51.8 dB-Hz needed, h 500 km), the margins become -5.3 / -2.4 / -3.1 / -5.7 / -11.5 / -35 dB. They are never positive. So the high-pass margins are 5-40 dB optimistic for a vertical whip.
    - **Correction:** The numbers hold only if the whip is tilted so the satellite stays broadside to it, using the IMU as is already done for the loop. Tilted, NEC gives margins of -5.3 / +0.1 / +2.5 / +4.1 / +5.0 / +5.3 dB. Add 'keep the whip perpendicular to the line of sight' to the operating procedure. Without it, rate 1 W 9k6 CubeSats as not reachable, and treat RS-44/FO-29/AO-73 zenith margins as void. ISS SSTV survives either way: a vertical whip still gives 18.8-22 dB CNR in 15 kHz from 10 to 60 deg.
    - **Source:** /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/whip_nec.py; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/lb_check.py; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/small_ant/lb.py
  2.
    - **Claim:** The stack mounts the NA-701 (about -3 dBi at 145.8 MHz, about 0 dBi at 436 MHz, from W9MDB) and the 17/12 cm whips 'on four thin 0.5-1 m coax leads with ferrite chokes, LNA at each feed, away from the box', while keeping 'AO-73/JO-97 telemetry reliable' and 'ISS/CubeSats via NA-701 + LNA V2'.
    - **Why:** A monopole needs a counterpoise, and W9MDB measured these whips on an HT body. My NEC2 model (ideal choke, no hand): a 21 cm whip loaded to resonate on a 6x12 cm HT body is 10.6+j0.3 ohm and -4.1 dBi realised at 10 deg. Moved to a 5x3 cm LNA box it becomes 8.2-j341 ohm, with an 18.7 dB mismatch, and is -22.2 dBi realised. That is still an SNR penalty of -10.1 dB (rural, 2000 K) or -12.9 dB (quiet, 600 K) after allowing for the external-noise effect. A plain 17 cm whip on the LNA box at 437 MHz is 24.5-j175 ohm with an 8.7 dB mismatch, -7 to -10 dBi realised. Real clip-on ferrites are imperfect, so the coax shield becomes the counterpoise. That is exactly the host-noise path the leads were meant to remove. The band study itself assumed the 17 cm whip 'on the case', so the stack contradicts it.
    - **Correction:** Choose one of two options.
  (a) Mount the whips directly on the case. NEC puts the NA-701-type whip only about 1 dB (rural) to 1.9 dB (quiet) below the HT-body case, and the 17 cm whip at +0.5 dBi at 10 deg. Accept the host-noise risk and measure it.
  (b) Use balanced antennas on the remote lead, which need no counterpoise: the 20 cm loop retuned to 145.8-146 MHz (NEC +1.1 dBi), and for 70 cm a 7 cm tuned loop (NEC +1.2 dBi, tuning capacitance about 0.5 pF) or a loaded 17 cm dipole.
  With the NA-701 on a remote choked lead, AO-73/JO-97 drop from reliable (+5/+10/+15) to about -5/0/+5 dB (marginal), and VHF FM/APRS become not reachable.
    - **Source:** /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/whip2.py; https://www.miklor.com/COM/pdf/AntennaTestingW9MDB.pdf
  3.
    - **Claim:** Stack: the 20 cm loop has 'about 1.4 MHz 3 dB bandwidth, so one fixed tuning to 137.9 MHz covers both Meteors (and Orbcomm) with no motor'. Band study: tuning capacitance 3.5 pF.
    - **Why:** At C/λ = 0.29 the analytic small-loop inductance is too low. Converged NEC2 (16/24/32 segments) gives X ≈ 514 ohm, tuning capacitance ≈ 2.2 pF, unloaded Q ≈ 330, so the matched 3 dB bandwidth is about 0.84 MHz and SWR stays under 1.5 over only about 170 kHz. With 2.2 pF in total, a 0.05 pF hand or stray change moves resonance by about 1.6 MHz, which delivers about -12 dB. Even with external noise cushioning it, the SNR cost is about -2.5 dB (rural) to -5.4 dB (quiet). That exceeds the modelled 0-4 dB LRPT margin at 17-40 deg. VK5BR (13.3 cm 2 m loop) reports that 'it can be put off tune by hand capacitance', even with the dial operated at arm's length.
    - **Correction:** Keep the band study's stepper-driven trimmer, or at least peak on sky noise just before every pass. Enclose the capacitor, use an insulating mast, and keep hands more than 2 diameters away. The rest of the loop result survives and is slightly better than claimed: NEC gives +1.07 dBi in-plane and efficiency about -1.4 dB, against +0.3 dBi claimed.
    - **Source:** /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/loop_nec2.py; https://www.qsl.net/v/vk5br/LoopAntennas/VHFLoopAntenna.htm
  4.
    - **Claim:** Meteor-M N2-3/N2-4 HRPT is 'reliable' with the SMALL 4-turn helix 'from about 13-18 deg, margin +3.4 to +4.7 dB', and 'marginal above 22-28 deg' with the STRICT 2-turn helix or 12 cm patch.
    - **Why:** There is no reception evidence. My search found no decode of HRPT on a small handheld helix. The anchor is soft. The metislair page gives 'average SNR being at around 7 dB' for an 11-turn helix but no pass elevation and no helix gain, and that setup had a G4DDK VLNA ahead of the SAWbird. The '12.75 dBic' anchor is an assumption in lband_small/scripts/budget.py, so the '-1.2 dB NEC optimism' correction is circular. Scaling SNR dB for dB with gain also ignores the higher Tsys of a 50-70 deg beam (ground spill of +30-60 K, about -1.3 to -1.8 dB) and the loss of the VLNA (about -0.3 dB). Redone: the 4-turn helix averages about +1.5 to +3 dB margin and decodes above about 25-30 deg; the 2-turn helix or patch is about -0.5 to +1 dB, about 38-45 deg or higher.
    - **Correction:** SMALL 4-turn helix: marginal, passes above about 30 deg, unvalidated. STRICT 2-turn helix or 12 cm patch: opportunistic, near zenith only. Validate on a high pass before relying on it. The stack's 'HRPT reliable from 13-18 deg' should not be used as a selling point.
    - **Source:** https://blog.metislair.com/docs/Radio/Creating%20a%20helix%20for%20direct%20satrx.html; /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/lband_small/scripts/budget.py
- **Confirmed:**
  - External noise at VHF (my calculation, ITU-R P.372 formulas as recalled): rural man-made noise plus galactic gives 2354 K at 137.9 MHz and 2026 K at 145.9 MHz; quiet sites give about 600 / 527 K; at 437 MHz it is about 113 K rural and 250 K residential. This matches the band study's 2300/2000 K and its point that at VHF the noise floor, not antenna efficiency, sets the limit; at UHF lost directivity costs dB for dB.
  - 20 cm tuned loop electrical performance (NEC2): +1.07 dBi in-plane; tuned resistance 1.57 ohm including 0.34 ohm of capacitor ESR at Q 1500; efficiency about -1.4 dB. This supports 'within about 1 dB of the V-dipole in rural noise'. Meteor-M N2-4 LRPT as 'marginal (model)' is reasonable, and real omni-antenna decodes support it: SatNOGS station VK4ATW (discone) decoded N2-4 LRPT imagery (63 product files) on a 67 deg pass on 17 Oct 2026, https://network.satnogs.org/observations/15225852/ (station antenna listed as discone 135-148 MHz).
  - 12 cm STRICT loop (NEC2): -1.1 dBi (slightly better than the -2 dBi claimed), 3 dB bandwidth about 0.41 MHz. VK5BR's measured 100 kHz at SWR 1.5 implies about 0.5 MHz at 3 dB, so the band study is right that it needs peaking every pass.
  - ISS SSTV on 437.55 MHz is reliable. ARISS lists Series 34 for 22-25 Oct 2026 (times TBD) on 437.55 MHz, Robot 36; Series 31 lists 'ISS transmit power: 10 watts' (https://www.ariss.org/upcoming-sstv-events.html). My CNR in 15 kHz: a vertical whip on the case gives 18.8/22.0/21.4/18.8 dB at 10/30/45/60 deg; even a whip on a remote box keeps 11-16 dB. Field evidence: SatNOGS users decoded 12 of 12 images in April 2026, one at about 3 deg elevation (https://community.libre.space/t/iss-sstv-event-from-2026-04-10-to-2026-04-14/14542?page=2).
  - AO-73 BPSK telemetry is decodable with omni-class antennas. The SatNOGS Sofia SAT Club VHF turnstile decoded 30 frames per pass, including passes peaking at 23 and 30 deg (13-14 Oct 2026). The SatNOGS API listing for NORAD 39444 has status=good; station 4272 antenna is a turnstile. So 'reliable' holds with a 20 cm loop retuned to 145.9 MHz (NEC about +1 dBi), but not with the NA-701 on a remote choked lead (refuted above).
  - Inmarsat-C EGC on small L-band antennas has real reception reports. The rtl-sdr.com tutorial says the RTL-SDR Blog patch 'does a very good job', the modified GPS antenna is 'just on the edge of being able to decode', and a helix or dish gives the highest SNR (https://www.rtl-sdr.com/rtl-sdr-tutorial-decoding-inmarsat-std-c-egc-messages/). A 7-9 dBic 2-turn helix (+7.5 dB of G/T margin) and the 4-turn helix (+10 dB) are therefore plausible.
  - The L-band patch is out of band for 1700 MHz HRPT, and Metop AHRPT and Elektro-L LRIT are unreachable at 20 cm or less. This is consistent with metislair, where even the final 11-turn helix reached only 'about 1.5 dB on LRIT'.
  - QO-100 beacon model C/N0 ≈ G + 14.6 dB-Hz. It is consistent with EA4GPZ: the BPSK beacon measured 'around 45 dB-Hz' on a 95 cm dish 'comparable to a 60 cm dish' (about 34 dBi) (https://destevez.net/2019/03/qo-100-beacons-power/), and the beacons were about 3 dB stronger after maintenance. This confirms the band study's correction that dish_replacement.json's '28 + G' was about 14 dB optimistic.
  - QO-100 CW beacon on a bare LNB: OK1DX writes 'I was able to copy CW beacon just without any dish, with LNB just pointed to QO100!' He needed about 20 dB of attenuation before the RTL and found glass blocks the signal (http://ok1dx.cz/techinfo/qo100/qo100.html, fetched 18 Oct 2026). This matches the calculated bare-LNB C/N0 of about 23.6-26.6 dB-Hz, i.e. about +6 dB in 50 Hz.
  - QO-100 FT8 on a bare LNB: RigExpert TBR-AN-1 lists 'Satellite dish – you do not need it!' and shows WSJT-X decodes (https://rigexpert.com/files/product_documentation/gpsdo/TBR-AN-1.pdf). Note that its LNB was GPSDO-locked; the Bullseye TCXO depends on the beacon-lock tracker for an equivalent result.
  - QO-100 limits: SSB on a bare LNB is not reachable (about -10 dB in 2.7 kHz), the DATV beacon is not reachable (-17 dB bare, -9 to -5 dB with a horn), and the multimedia beacon is not reachable. All are consistent with the G+14.6 model and the BATC MER table.
  - 11 x 8.3 cm cone: an optimum conical horn of 11 cm aperture at η 0.52 gives 18.8 dBi, and the geometry is consistent (slant length 14.1 cm from the apex). BPSK beacon frames have about +7.4 dB nominal margin (±2.5 dB model, ±2 dB feed mating), so they stay positive in the worst case. That makes 'reliable' plausible, but it is calculation-only: run the A/B beacon test.
  - Black Kite S-band 38k4: a real decode exists. SatNOGS 'Pi Station 1' (listed antenna: discone, 25 MHz-3 GHz) decoded a frame on an 18 deg pass (https://network.satnogs.org/observations/15185665/). So a reliable link with an 8-9 dBic helix is supported, but only for the optional Pluto module.
  - Ku broadcast carrier humps: my calculation with an assumed EIRP of 50 dBW gives about -12.7 dB C/N in 27.5 MHz for a bare LNB, a hump of about 0.2 dB, so 'opportunistic' is right; a 19-21 dBi horn gives a visible hump of 1.5-5 dB.
- **Missed targets or parts:**
  - The 1080p52 EDID pixel clock of 128.7 MHz has its 12th harmonic at 1544.4 MHz. That is inside the Inmarsat-C receive band (1537-1545 MHz) and next to the excluded Cospas-Sarsat 1544.5 MHz. The 1080p60 3rd harmonic (445.5 MHz) is 8 MHz above 437 MHz. Add both to the terminated-input sweep (my calculation).
  - When a whip is badly mismatched, the LNA's own noise temperature rises well above its nominal NF. I did not quantify this; it would make the mismatch penalties above worse, not better.
  - The V-dipole baseline (lb.py) is also flat at 2.0 dBi at all elevations, with no ground reflection. A horizontal V-dipole at about 1-1.5 m (about 0.5 λ) has a reflection notch near zenith. This affects how the LRPT EIRP was calibrated (±2 dB).
  - Meteor LRPT and HRPT EIRPs are still unverified. The LRPT EIRP was calibrated to an assumed V-dipole performance. The HRPT anchor has no stated elevation.
  - A SatNOGS 'good' status on 'IQ recording' transmitters means only that a signal was seen. I checked demoddata for the LRPT, Black Kite and AO-73 observations cited here. The other agents' 'good' citations are not proven decodes.
  - Receiving LRPT on the loop and HRPT on the helix in the same pass needs one operator to point two antennas: the loop oriented by hand and the helix manually tracked at about 1 deg/s on a tripod. This is not a link issue, but it bounds the 'two V4L' benefit.
  - Hand and body loss were not in my NEC runs, and real ferrite-choke impedance at 145 MHz (a few hundred ohms) sits between my 'ideal choke' and 'no choke' cases.
- **Notes:** Four refutations, in order of importance:
  (1) Whip budgets assume no zenith null.
  (2) Monopole whips on remote choked leads have no counterpoise. NEC shows -10 to -13 dB of SNR at 2 m, which contradicts the stack's integration plan.
  (3) The 20 cm loop's '1.4 MHz bandwidth, no motor' claim does not hold. NEC gives 0.84 MHz bandwidth and a 2.2 pF tuning capacitance, so it is very sensitive to hand capacitance.
  (4) Meteor HRPT 'reliable' on the 20 cm helix has no evidence behind it and a circular anchor. Downgrade it to marginal above about 30 deg.
  
  The core physics in the band studies is sound: rural VHF noise of about 2000-2300 K masks efficiency loss, the 20 cm loop is efficient, and the QO-100 beacon model is right.
  
  Actionable fixes:
  - Use balanced antennas (tuned loops) on remote leads; whips only on the case.
  - Tilt whips broadside to the satellite using the IMU.
  - Keep the motorised or per-pass-peaked loop trimmer.
  - Treat HRPT as a high-pass experiment.
  
  Validation order: ISS SSTV 22-25 Oct, then AO-73 on the retuned loop, then a high Meteor N2-4 LRPT pass, then an HRPT test on a pass above 40 deg.
  
  Downloads are kept in separate untrusted folders: dl_sn, dl_ok1dx and dl_rigexpert, under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/rfverify/. Searches used: 4 WebSearch, plus WebFetch and curl on primary pages (rtl-sdr.com, ARISS, EA4GPZ, metislair, VK5BR, OK1DX, RigExpert, SatNOGS API).

## small:final (run `wf_41027870-8e7`)

- **Verdict:** Once every dish and every antenna larger than about 20 cm deployed is removed, the receiver still works, but for fewer things.
  
  RELIABLE (with evidence or a large margin):
  - ISS on 70 cm (receive only): SSTV pictures on 437.55 MHz (Series 34 runs 22-25 Oct 2026), the APRS digipeater on 437.825 MHz and the FM repeater on 437.800 MHz. These work even with a 12 cm whip.
  - Inmarsat-C EGC SafetyNET maritime safety text on 1537-1545 MHz, with a 12 cm L-band helix.
  - GNSS and EGNOS time and position.
  - QO-100 narrowband beacons, CW and FT8 on the bare LNB. With an 11 cm clamp-on cone the BPSK beacon frames and weaker CW also become reliable.
  
  MARGINAL (model only; validate before relying on it):
  - Meteor-M N2-4 LRPT weather images on a 20 cm antenna, decoding from about 17-24 deg elevation.
  - Meteor-M N2-3/N2-4 HRPT on the 20 cm helix, passes above about 25-30 deg only.
  - 1 W UHF CubeSat telemetry, passes above about 30 deg, and only if the whip is held broadside to the satellite.
  - AO-73/JO-97 BPSK telemetry, and the AO-7/RS-44/FO-29 CW beacons.
  
  OPPORTUNISTIC: Meteor N2-3 LRPT, SO-50, AO-91, VHF APRS digipeaters, linear-transponder SSB, QO-100 SSB from beacon-level stations, and FY-2H carriers.
  
  LOST:
  - Metop AHRPT, AWS, Elektro-L LRIT.
  - All S-band (unless the optional Pluto module is added).
  - QO-100 readable SSB, the multimedia beacon and DATV.
  - Most FM-voice and SSB listening, low passes, and 0.5 W or 19k2+ CubeSats.
  
  STACK: the LimeSDR Micro, its riser and cooling, the T7 SSD and the 12 GB board tier are removed. Two RTL-SDR Blog V4Ls cover everything that is still reachable.
  - Avoided spend: about $650-665.
  - Peak power: from about 45-52 W down to 24-32 W.
  - Antenna kit: nothing over about 20 cm, about 0.6-0.9 kg.
  
  VERIFIER FIXES APPLIED:
  - Whips have a zenith null, so they must be tilted broadside using the IMU.
  - Monopole whips must sit on the case. On a remote choked lead they have no counterpoise and lose 10-13 dB.
  - The 20 cm loop has only 0.84 MHz bandwidth and 2.2 pF of tuning capacitance, so it needs a stepper or peaking before every pass.
  - HRPT is downgraded to marginal (20 cm helix) and opportunistic (12 cm helix).
  - Iridium is carrier and Doppler only.
  - The 13 V LNB rail needs a switch rated above 16 V; neither a TPS2553 nor the enable pin of a plain boost converter can do it.
  - My own check: AO-73 is in transponder mode with low-power telemetry (30 mW design level), so its margin is about 10 dB lower than the 0.3 W the band study assumed.
  
  CONFLICT TO RESOLVE: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/user_requirements.md was created at 02:18 today, after this run started. It says the user banned all loop antennas, allows foldables that are larger when deployed, and is not in Ukraine. I therefore made a loop-free 137 MHz antenna the default (a 20 cm helical whip on the case, about 2 dB worse than the loop in rural noise and about 4.5 dB worse at a quiet site). The loop is listed as optional.
- **Size rule used:** HOW I READ THE RULE (18 Oct 2026, "remove what needs dishes or antennas tens of cm in size")
  - STRICT tier: largest deployed dimension about 12 cm or less. Covers patches, chip antennas, the bare LNB with its own feed, stubby or helical-loaded whips, a 12 cm loop, and the 2-turn helix on a 12 cm disc.
  - SMALL tier: about 20 cm or less deployed. Covers 17-19 cm whips, a 20 cm helical whip, the 20 cm loop, the 4-turn helix on a 20 cm disc, and the LNB plus cone at 20 cm or less overall.
  - EXCLUDED: every dish, and anything about 20-25 cm or more when deployed, even if it folds. That rules out the 92 cm V-dipole, the WB2HOL and N2SPI Yagis, the Moxon, the 47 cm helix, the 44 cm helicone, the 23 dBi horn, the 30 cm lens and the 2x2 array. These appear only as labelled borderline notes.
  - The 21 cm NA-701 is treated as rule-edge. Coax leads are not counted as antenna size.
  
  PHYSICS (calculations)
  - A quarter wave is 54.3 cm at 137.9 MHz, 51.4 cm at 145.9 MHz and 17.2 cm at 437 MHz. So every 137-146 MHz antenna here is electrically short, while a 17 cm 70 cm whip is full size.
  - 137.9 MHz antennas:
    - 20 cm tuned loop: radiation resistance 1.36-1.57 ohm, copper loss 0.06 ohm, capacitor ESR 0.22-0.34 ohm. NEC2 gives about +1.1 dBi in the loop plane and about -1.4 dB efficiency.
    - 12 cm loop: radiation resistance 0.18 ohm, about -1.1 dBi (NEC).
    - 20 cm normal-mode helical whip: radiation resistance 3.3 ohm on an ideal ground; Q 60-150 coil loss 2.4-6 ohm, so efficiency -2.7 to -4.7 dB and about -4 dBi realised on the case.
    - 12 cm helical whip: radiation resistance 1.2 ohm, efficiency -6.6 to -9.7 dB.
    - 20 cm loaded short dipole (balanced): radiation resistance 1.7 ohm, reactance about -1455 ohm; coil loss at Q 150-300 gives -8.3 to -5.9 dB.
    - An unloaded short whip has a reactance of 400-1200 ohm and loses 24-45 dB to mismatch, so loading is mandatory.
  - External noise usually sets the VHF limit. ITU-R P.372 (as recalled) gives about 2350 K rural, 6600 K residential and 450-600 K quiet at 137.9 MHz, against about 100 K for an LNA at the feed. So the SNR cost compared with the 92 cm V-dipole is:
    - 20 cm loop: about +0.3 / +0.4 / -0.4 dB (rural / residential / quiet).
    - 20 cm helical whip: -1.9 / -0.9 / -4.9 dB.
    - 12 cm helical whip: -4.4 / -2.2 / -9.1 dB.
  - At 437 MHz the sky is only about 110-420 K. The 11 dB gap to the 6-element Yagi there is lost directivity, which external noise cannot hide.
  - At L-band and 10.5 GHz, 12-20 cm is 0.7 wavelength or more. Efficiency stays above 90%, and only aperture limits gain:
    - 12x12 cm: 6.8 / 7.6 dBi at 1.54 / 1.70 GHz.
    - 20x20 cm: 11.2 / 12.1 dBi.
    - At 10.49 GHz a 12 cm horn is 4.2 wavelengths across; an 11 cm cone gives about 18.8 dBi.

  12.
    - **Target:** Remote-mounted whips
    - **Capability lost:** Monopole whips can no longer sit on a remote choked lead away from the host. NEC shows a 21 cm whip on a 5x3 cm LNA box at 8.2-j341 ohm and -22 dBi, which is -10 to -13 dB of SNR. So whips sit on the case, close to the Q6A, HDMI and DC-DC noise.
    - **Needed:** A counterpoise or a balanced antenna
    - **What would bring it back:** Balanced antennas on the lead: the 20 cm loop (if allowed), a 20 cm loaded dipole at 137/145 MHz (about -6 to -8 dB efficiency), or a 17 cm loaded dipole at 70 cm (about -1 dB, calculation)
- **Excluded by law or ethics:**
  - Iridium voice, SMS/SBD, pager traffic, and ALL frame decoding including IRA ring alerts (iridium-toolkit FORMAT.md shows TMSI paging entries) and IBC. Carrier and Doppler only.
  - Inmarsat: STD-C LES and addressed messages, FleetNET, Aero/ACARS, C-channel voice, Classic Aero, BGAN/GX. Only EGC SafetyNET and bulletin-board packets are in scope.
  - Orbcomm subscriber and user message content. Carrier and Doppler only.
  - Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper and other broadband user data. Starlink is a front-line military system in Ukraine: do not record, track, characterise or publish it.
  - Thuraya and other MSS voice and data in 1525-1559 / 1626-1660 MHz; Globalstar 2483.5-2500 MHz downlinks.
  - Military UHF SATCOM at 240-320 MHz (UFO/FLTSATCOM, Skynet, Sicral, Syracuse) and MUOS at about 360-380 MHz.
  - Military payloads: Yunhai-1 01-04 (1704 MHz, encrypted), DMSP F17/F18, Coriolis, EWS-G2, OPS 5644, EMISAT, military Kosmos and Russian relay systems.
  - CARTOSAT-3 carrier logging, dropped as a target: a civil ISRO Earth-observation satellite also used for defence (dual-use).
  - Encrypted GNSS codes (GPS P(Y)/M, Galileo PRS, GLONASS P). Also any mapping or publishing of GNSS jamming or spoofing sources.
  - ISS non-amateur channels: Soyuz/Progress VHF voice (143.625 / 130.167 MHz), EVA suit radios, Dragon/Kvant/TORU links.
  - Cospas-Sarsat 1544.5 MHz relay downlinks and 406 MHz beacons (distress identities and positions).
  - ARGOS/A-DCS (465.9875 MHz) and DCP user-platform data from Elektro, GOES and FengYun.
  - Pay-TV decryption, demodulation of Ku operator telemetry or tracking beacons, and contribution feeds.
  - Terrestrial military, drone/FPV video or telemetry and police links heard while scanning: do not record, decode or share.
- **Borderline options:**
  - BORDERLINE, NOT IN THE STACK: 21 cm Nagoya NA-701 (genuine, 950 UAH on Prom.ua). It is at the 20 cm edge and gives no gain over the SRH-701 or A-V85; W9MDB measured the 16.8 cm A-V85 1.5 dB better at 146 MHz. Clone risk: one unit measured -10.3 dB.
  - BORDERLINE: a 48-52 cm telescopic quarter-wave whip for 2 m. G4ILO measured about +3 dB over a stock HT whip. It roughly recovers the whip-vs-loop difference at 145.9 MHz, but it must stay on the case.

It adds about +1.9 dB (rural) to +4.9 dB (quiet) over the 20 cm helical whip, but only 0 to 0.4 dB over a well-tuned 20 cm loop.
  - BORDERLINE: 70 cm wire Moxon (25 x 10 cm, 31 g, 5.4 dBi modelled). It adds about +5.4 dB over the 17 cm whip: 1 W 9k6 CubeSats from about 15-20 deg, and SO-50 and SSB 5 dB better. This is the single most useful borderline item.
  - BORDERLINE: 4-element 70 cm Yagi (29 x 34 cm deployed, packs into 17 cm pieces, 9.5 dBi). It comes within 1.5 dB of the old 6-element Yagi.
  - BORDERLINE: WB2HOL 2 m tape Yagi (105 x 51 cm, 7.9 dBi). The only option that brings back VHF FM, APRS and SSB, plus about +6 dB at 137 MHz.
  - BORDERLINE: 44 cm fold-flat helicone (15.7 dBic modelled; packs to about 19 x 19 x 4 cm) or the 47 cm 11-turn helix. Adds +5-8 dB at 1.7 GHz: Meteor HRPT from about 5 deg, Elektro LRIT back at threshold when it transmits, Metop and AWS possible on high passes.
  - BORDERLINE: 33 cm S-band fold cone (15.5 dBic). Adds +4-6.5 dB for PHASMA-class 400 kbps CubeSats and science dumps (needs the optional Pluto as well).
  - BORDERLINE: 15 x 18.4 cm cone (21.5 dBi; about 29-32 cm overall with the LNB). Adds about +2.7 dB over the 11 cm cone, making beacon-level QO-100 SSB about +1.7 dB (barely copyable).
  - BORDERLINE: 23 dBi horn (17.8 cm mouth, about 28 cm long) gives beacon-level SSB at about +3 dB. The 30 cm W1GHZ lens with a 17.5 dBi feed (about 65 cm deployed) gives about +7.5 dB, readable copy. Neither reaches DATV.
  - BORDERLINE: 56-60 cm 2x2 spring-helix array (17-18 dBic). The only non-dish route to Metop AHRPT; it also needs an SDR above 2.56 Msps.
