  - WISECOCO-COMPATIBILITY HYPOTHESIS UNSUPPORTED AND VISUALLY CONTRADICTED: the FPC in Wisecoco's rear photo (wp-content/uploads/2026/05/7-inch-1920-1200-lcd-2-2.webp) has two green rigid islands with inductors, a board-to-board connector, a flex tail and the label '8813070'. It has no separate backlight wires. Youritech's FPC is a different wide flex with a top-edge connector (it looks marked '30', unconfirmed) and has external backlight wires. Different FPC means a different pinout and power scheme. Wisecoco's 40-pin adapter and HDMI-to-MIPI board cannot be assumed to work. The only things that match are the text outline 160.8x98.7 and the -10~60 / -30~70 C temperatures. Those hint at a shared base glass with a re-backlit module, but that is not proven.
  - Contrast differs: Youritech says 1200:1 and Wisecoco says 1100:1. Not decisive, but more evidence the documents are not for the same part.
  - 1500 nits is vendor marketing and a table value only. Youritech lists a same-outline sibling at 1350 nits (ET070WU10-O). There is no datasheet minimum and no measured value from anyone.
  - The backlight field '9~11v' is garbled: no current is given, and it is unclear whether a driver is on board. The external 2-wire lead suggests a bare LED string that needs a constant-current driver. Assuming 3S x 15P (an inference from 45 LEDs and 9-11 V), current would be about 300-600 mA. Unverified.
  - No HDMI path exists for this panel. Youritech advertises driver boards in general but none for this part. The Q6A's MIPI-DSI only supports Radxa panels, so the panel cannot be driven directly.
  - No touch, which fails a hard requirement.
  - No community reports, teardown, or luminance review found. Not on prom.ua (search for 'ET070WU07' returns nothing). No Alibaba or Made-in-China listing found.
- **Touch reaches host as usb hid:** no
- **Q6a mode line and link check:** Calculated, assuming some unknown HDMI-to-MIPI bridge sits in front of the panel. The Q6A cannot drive this MIPI panel directly.
  
  Width and blanking: 1200 px is under the 2400 px DPU linewidth, so no virtual planes are needed.
  
  Standard modes and their harmonics:
  - CVT-RBv2 1200x1920@60: htotal 1280, vtotal 1975 (55 lines vertical blanking, meets the 24-line rule). 151.68 MHz, 3.64 Gbps. Fits 2-lane HBR (4.32) and HBR2 (8.64). The 15th harmonic, 2275.2 MHz, falls in 2200-2300.
  - CVT-RBv1 @60: htotal 1360, vtotal 1975, 161.0 MHz, 3.86 Gbps. The 14th harmonic, 2254 MHz, falls in 2200-2300.
  - JDI LT070ME05000-style native timing (from memory of the mainline panel driver, not verified): 1340x1934@60, 155.49 MHz, only 14 lines of vertical blanking. If a bridge's EDID copied this, it would break the 24-line DP rule. Its 11th harmonic, 1710.4 MHz, sits on the 1690-1710 edge.
  - RBv2 @50: 125.82 MHz. The 18th harmonic, 2264.8 MHz, falls in 2200-2300.
  
  Harmonic-clean custom modes (up to the 20th harmonic, calculated):
  - 1360x2042@60: 166.63 MHz, 4.0 Gbps, 122 lines vertical blanking. Nearest harmonic is 20.6 MHz from any band. Fits HBR.
  - 1304x1994@60: 156.01 MHz. Only 6 MHz margin: the 11th harmonic is 1716.1 MHz.
  - 1296x1986@50: 128.69 MHz, 3.09 Gbps. Same clock as your known-clean 1080p@52 mode.
  
  These modes only help if the bridge's EDID or scaler accepts custom timings. The bridge's own DSI clock is free-running: about 455-483 MHz at 4 lanes x ~0.9-0.97 Gbps. At 151.68 MHz input its 5th harmonic is about 2275 MHz, which is in band. Its scaler and DDR clocks are also uncontrolled and need sniffing with the receiver itself.
- **Rf harmonics check:** All figures calculated.
  - CVT-RB 60 Hz modes (151.68 and 161.0 MHz) land in 2200-2300 MHz at the 14th-15th harmonic.
  - A JDI-like 155.49 MHz timing hits 1710.4 MHz.
  - 50 Hz RBv2 (125.82 MHz) hits 2264.8 MHz.
  - Clean choices: 1360x2042@60 at 166.63 MHz (at least 20 MHz margin), or 1296x1986@50 at 128.69 MHz (8.3 MHz margin).
  - The bridge board adds its own DSI HS clock (about 455-483 MHz; at 455 MHz the 5th harmonic is 2275 MHz) plus scaler and DDR clocks the host cannot control. Real emissions are broadband around these lines, so a near-field scan with the SDR across all six bands is mandatory.
- **Sunlight readability estimate:** Calculated ambient contrast (ACR) in 100 klx sun, with diffuse reflectance Rd:
  - At the claimed 1500 nits: about 5.7 with the bare hard-coat (Rd about 1%), about 3.4 with an air-gapped add-on CTP (Rd about 2%), about 10 with a bonded AR cover (Rd about 0.5%).
  - If real luminance is only 750-1000 nits (plausible, given the 1350-nit sibling and no minimum spec): about 3.3-4.1 bare, and about 2.2-2.6 with an air-gapped touch panel.
  - Readable in direct sun only if the 1500 nits is real and any touch layer is optically bonded. The hard-coat (non-AR) surface gives strong specular glare.
- **Power and thermal:** Estimated, not from a datasheet.
  - Backlight: assuming 45 LEDs as 3S x 15P at 9-11 V (inference) and 20-40 mA per string, about 3-6.6 W.
  - Panel logic: 5.5 V x 60 mA = 0.33 W (Youritech figure).
  - HDMI-to-MIPI scaler or bridge board: about 1-2.5 W (estimate).
  - Total: about 4.5-9 W, roughly 0.35-0.7 A from the 4S pack.
  - An external constant-current LED driver is probably needed. A buck driver from the 12 V Pololu rail has only about 1 V of headroom at an 11 V string voltage, so a buck-boost or SEPIC CC driver from the pack is safer.
  - Heat: about 75-80% of backlight power becomes heat inside a thin module. Full sun adds about 14.3 W incident on the active area (1000 W/m2 x 0.0143 m2, calculated).
  - Youritech's own catalog line rates operating temperature at only -10~60 C. That is easy to exceed in a closed handheld in Ukrainian summer sun. Expect forced derating of the backlight and possible LC blackening near the clearing point.
- **Real price and shipping to ukraine:** Unknown. Youritech publishes no price: both ET070WU07-O pages are quote-only B2B with MOQ not stated. For reference, the Wisecoco 500-nit kit is $69.00 with the HDMI-to-MIPI 40-pin board (verified on wisecocodisplay.com). Its compatibility with this panel is not established. No Ukrainian seller: prom.ua search for ET070WU07 returns nothing. Shipping would be express courier from Shenzhen (cost not verified). Budget for customs and VAT, and confirm the current Ukrainian duty-free threshold. Add the cost of a separate LED driver, a bridge board and a bonded PCAP with a USB controller, none of which is quoted.
- **Questions for seller:**
  - Send the full spec-approval datasheet for ET070WU07-O, with minimum and typical luminance, the measurement method, and the LED configuration (series/parallel, Vf, If per string, total power).
  - Your two ET070WU07-O pages conflict. Which outline is correct: 160.8x98.7x1.97 mm or 107.98x163.8 mm (and what thickness)? Which temperature range: -20~70 C or -10~60 C? Which technology: a-Si or LTPS?
  - Who makes the base glass and what is its part number? Which driver IC? What is the FPC pin count, pinout and mating connector part number? Please provide the DSI init sequence and the native timing (HFP/HBP/HSA, VFP/VBP/VSA, pixel clock).
  - Is the backlight a bare LED string on a separate cable? Which constant-current driver and dimming method (PWM frequency) do you recommend?
  - Do you supply an HDMI-to-MIPI board proven with this exact panel? Which bridge chip? What EDID (preferred mode, portrait 1200x1920 input or scaled 1920x1200)? Does it accept custom timings such as 1360x2042@60 at 166.6 MHz or 1296x1986@50 at 128.7 MHz, with at least 24 lines of vertical blanking? What are its supply and power?
  - Can you optically bond a PCAP with a USB-HID controller (give the controller IC and USB VID:PID) and an AR or AG cover glass? Price and MOQ?
  - Can you provide a luminance measurement report from a production sample at rated current, plus backlight derating versus temperature and the LC clearing point?
  - What are the sample price, MOQ and lead time? Is there DDP or DAP shipping to Ukraine, and what warranty applies?

- **Reason:** Drop. The candidate fails a hard requirement: it has no touch. It has no HDMI path; the only proposed path, Wisecoco's 40-pin HDMI-to-MIPI board, rests on a text outline that Youritech's own dimension drawing (107.98x163.8 mm) and FPC photos contradict. The FPC differs from Wisecoco's panel and the backlight uses separate wires. Its specs conflict across Youritech's own two pages (-20~70 vs -10~60 C, a-Si vs LTPS, 1.97 mm thickness against a 4.05 mm, 1350-nit sibling of the same outline). The 1500 nits is a vendor table and banner value only, with no datasheet. There is no price or availability, and nothing sold in Ukraine. The 1200x1920 resolution itself would fit the Q6A, which is why the receiver could cope with it given a known bridge. If Youritech is pursued at all, ask instead about ET070WU01-HLT (7 in 1200x1920, 2000 nits typ, in-cell touch, listed on the Youritech site). It still needs a bridge and a USB-HID touch path, so it would need its own check.

- **Verdict:** The Wisecoco 7in 1920x1080 2000+ nit HDMI kit stays the main pick, but buy it only after the seller confirms two things in writing: the touch reaches the host as USB HID (with VID:PID), and the cover glass is optically bonded. If the seller cannot confirm both, buy the 4D Systems 4DHDMI-70-1280-800-CT-EAR-1000 instead: 1000 nits, optical bonding stated in the datasheet, USB-C touch, 12 V input, in stock in Ukraine at 9,520 UAH. I found no buyable plug-and-play kit above 1920x1080 at 1000 nits or more in 5.5-8in. The closest is a bring-up project around the bare Midas MDT0700F1IHHC-MIPI (1200x1920, up to 2500 nits): EUR 324.37 ex VAT at Farnell, 12-week lead time, plus a bridge board, an LED driver and a touch bridge. At 30-35 cm, going above FHD gains almost nothing visible (7in FHD is already 315 PPI, against an acuity limit of 249-291 PPI). It costs money, time, about 1-3 W and Q6A mode risk. By my calculation, optical bonding, an AR film and a hood improve sun contrast more than another 1000 nits does.
- **Main pick:**

- **What above fhd costs us:** All figures are my calculations unless stated. Script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final_calc/fc.py
  
  COSTS:
  1) Brightness.
  - Every buyable above-FHD 5.5-9in kit is 287-706 nits: Waveshare 9in about 350; Wisecoco 2.5K 500; Sharp 7.9in QXGA kits 460 per listing; Legion Go 413 and AYANEO KUN 678 measured by Notebookcheck.
  - At 100 klx with a bonded AR-film front (1.2% reflectance) that gives about 2.3-3.2:1, against 6.2:1 at 2000 nits.
  - The bright above-FHD glass exists only as bare MIPI panels.
  2) Power.
  - A 2000-nit 1200x1920 build is about 8-10 W: 6.4 W of LEDs per the Midas datasheet, plus about 1 W for the bridge, plus logic.
  - That compares with about 6-8 W estimated for the Wisecoco FHD kit.
  - Runtime with 15 W for the rest of the system and 61 Wh usable: about 2.5 h against about 2.8 h. An 8.4in 2.5K 2000-nit panel at about 10 W gives about 2.4 h.
  3) GPU fill.
  - 1200x1920 is 1.11x the FHD pixel count; 1600x2560 is 1.98x.
  - Portrait-native panels also need a full-screen rotation pass in the compositor.
  4) Q6A mode risk.
  - No above-1080p display has been reported stable on Q6A HDMI.
  - Portrait panels 1200 or 1600 px wide avoid the 2400-px DPU split. A landscape 2560-wide mode needs msm.dpu_use_virtual_planes=1 on the held 6.18.2.
  - Bridge EDIDs often have fewer than the required 24 lines of vertical blanking (JDI-class 1200x1920 native is 14), so a custom EDID is needed. The bridge vendor must flash the firmware.
  - 1600x2560 RB at 276.9 MHz uses 77% of the 2-lane HBR2 link; 348.5 MHz CVT is out.
  - RF: CVT-RB 1200x1920 at 161.0 MHz hits 2254 MHz and RBv2 at 151.68 MHz hits 2275 MHz. The HX8279-style 156.458 MHz timing is clean in the six RX bands, but its 10th harmonic lands at 1564.6 MHz in the GNSS band.
  5) Money and time.
  - Midas EUR 324.37 ex VAT, plus about EUR 50-120 of bridge, LED and touch electronics (estimate), plus about EUR 56 UA duty and VAT, plus a 12-week lead time and unbounded bring-up.
  - Compared with $132 under the EUR 150 threshold and a plug-in HDMI kit.
  
  GAINS:
  - The 1-arcminute acuity limit is 291 PPI at 30 cm and 249 PPI at 35 cm.
  - 7in FHD is already 315 PPI. 7.02in 1200x1920 is 322.5 PPI, only 2.5% denser linearly and invisible. 8in 1200x1920 is 283 PPI, actually less dense. 8.4in 2560x1600 is 359 PPI, beyond acuity.
  - The only real gain is 11% more pixels on the short axis (1200 vs 1080) for UI space, or a physically larger 8-8.4in face.
  
  NET: not worth it for a sunlit handheld. Spend the effort on bonding, AR, a hood and auto-dimming.

  3.

- **Q6a settings:**
  - Kernel: stay on Radxa 6.18.2-x-qcom. Hold it with: sudo apt-mark hold linux-image-radxa-dragon-q6a linux-headers-radxa-dragon-q6a embloader (confirm the names with dpkg -l | grep -E 'linux-image|embloader'). Add the same names to Unattended-Upgrade::Package-Blacklist. Keep the old boot entry, a dd+zstd golden image and a USB-UART cable; measure the header voltage first.
  - Inspect the panel before choosing a mode: edid-decode /sys/class/drm/card1-HDMI-A-1/edid; cat /sys/class/drm/card1-HDMI-A-1/modes; modetest -M msm -c. The chosen mode needs VFP+VSW+VBP of at least 24 lines. If dmesg shows 'low vbp+vfp', shearing or underrun, edit the EDID.
  - Wisecoco bring-up: append video=HDMI-A-1:1920x1080@60 to /etc/kernel/cmdline, then sudo kernel-install add $(uname -r) /boot/vmlinuz-$(uname -r) and reboot. This is CEA 148.5 MHz, which hits 742.5 and 2227.5 MHz, so use it for bring-up only.
  - Wisecoco field mode, RF-clean (calc): Modeline "1920x1080_52" 128.700 1920 2008 2052 2200 1080 1084 1089 1125 +hsync +vsync. That is 45 lines of vertical blanking and 3.09 Gbps, 36% of 2-lane HBR2. Clean alternative: 135.760 1920 1968 2000 2080 1080 1083 1088 1111 (58.75 Hz, 31 lines). Avoid 1080p CVT-RB at 138.5 MHz: its fundamental sits 0.5 MHz above the 137-138 MHz band.
  - Apply the clean mode by EDID override:
  1. cp /sys/class/drm/card1-HDMI-A-1/edid edid.bin
  2. python3 -c "b=bytearray(open('edid.bin','rb').read());b[54:56]=(12870).to_bytes(2,'little');b[127]=(-sum(b[:127]))&255;open('wisecoco52.bin','wb').write(b)". This only gives 52 Hz if DTD#1 totals are 2200x1125. Otherwise choose a pixel clock in 127.85-129.35 or 135.4-135.95 MHz for the real totals.
  3. Check the result with edid-decode, then sudo cp wisecoco52.bin /lib/firmware/edid/.
  4. Add 'drm.edid_firmware=HDMI-A-1:edid/wisecoco52.bin video=HDMI-A-1:1920x1080@52' to /etc/kernel/cmdline.
  5. Add the file to the initramfs with an initramfs-tools hook, then run kernel-install add.
  - Portrait 1200x1920 bridge (above-FHD route): set the bridge EDID to Modeline 156.458 1200 1250 1274 1340 1920 1934 1936 1946 (60 Hz, 26 lines, 43% of the link; clean in the RX bands, but the 10th harmonic is at 1564.6 MHz in GNSS). RF-quiet option: 128.500 1200 1250 1274 1340 1920 1944 1946 1956 (49.0 Hz, 36 lines; panel and touch tolerance unknown). Rotate in GNOME Settings > Displays > Orientation, or under X11: xrandr --output HDMI-1 --rotate right plus xinput map-to-output <id> HDMI-1.
  - Virtual planes: not needed for any recommended mode, since all are 1920 px wide or less. Only for a landscape 2560-wide test on 6.18.2: append msm.dpu_use_virtual_planes=1, run kernel-install add, and check that cat /sys/module/msm/parameters/dpu_use_virtual_planes prints Y. Use 2560x1600 CVT-RB at 268.6 MHz (totals 2720x1646, 75% of the link); never the 348.5 MHz CVT mode.
  - 4D 1280x800: video=HDMI-A-1:1280x800@60 (CVT 83.77 MHz, 31 lines). Its only hits are weak high-order harmonics: the 19th at 1591.5 MHz (GNSS) and the 27th at 2261.6 MHz. Auto-dim by having an RP2040 pull the OSD button-board lines (10-pin 2.0 mm: Menu, Down, Up, Enter, Power) through open-drain GPIOs.
  - Newhaven 1024x600: replace the stock 62.00 MHz EDID with Modeline 52.000 1024 1184 1204 1344 600 612 622 645 (60.0 Hz, 45 lines). The TFP401A has no scaler, so the panel itself must accept this timing.
  - Touch: run only D+/D-/GND from the display board to a Q6A USB 2.0 port, and power the board's VBUS from its own 12 V or 5 V buck so it never back-feeds the Q6A. Check with lsusb, sudo libinput list-devices and sudo evtest. Map it in GNOME with: gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.peripherals.touchscreen:/org/gnome/desktop/peripherals/touchscreens/<vid>:<pid>/ output "['VEN','Product','Serial']".
  - SDR++/SatDump touch (GLFW has no Wayland touch support): launch them with Exec=env XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11 sdrpp and Exec=env XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11 satdump-ui so they run under XWayland.
  - DDC brightness test, expected to fail on cheap boards: sudo modprobe i2c-dev; sudo ddcutil detect --verbose; ddcutil --bus N setvcp 10 30. Otherwise use the RP2040 PWM or button route with a VEML7700 lux sensor and NTC derating.
- **Sunlight measures:**
  - Optical bonding first. The 100 klx model (calc) at 2000 nits: air gap 1.5:1, bonded plain glass 2.4:1, bonded plus a 1.2% AR film 6.2:1, factory bonded AR 9.9:1. At 1000 nits the same cases give 1.2, 1.7, 3.6 and 5.5:1. Reject an air-gapped front; check by holding a pen tip on the glass at a grazing angle, where a doubled reflection means an air gap.
  - Add an AR front: an AR screen film of about 0.7% reflectance (vendor claim class, e.g. TELESIN) or AR-coated cover glass. Do not use matte AG on a 315-PPI panel, because it sparkles and softens the image. Ask 4D or Wisecoco whether AR cover glass is available as a custom option.
  - Hood: 25-35 mm deep, matte-black interior, hinged so it folds down as a lid. Tilt the screen so it mirrors the hood interior or dark clothing, not the sky or a white shirt: a sunlit white shirt is about 25,000 cd/m2, which becomes about 1000 nits of glare at 4% reflectance (calc). In 20 klx shade the bonded 2000-nit panel reaches 8.1:1 with plain glass and 26.5:1 with AR film; the 4D reaches 4.6:1 and 13.9:1 (calc).
  - Polariser: ask the seller for the transmission-axis angle. Test with polarized sunglasses at 0, 45 and 90 degrees before fixing the panel orientation in the case. If the axis is wrong, use non-polarized glasses; a quarter-wave retarder film (Relec and Digiwise sell TFTs fitted with one) makes the output circular, but I found no tested DIY sheet.
  - Thermal:
  - Light-coloured ASA case, never PLA.
  - A fan pulls air through a 4-6 mm gap behind the backlight frame into the Q6A heatsink.
  - 1 mm aluminium plate, doubling as RF shield and heat spreader.
  - NTC on the frame: derate to 50% above 60 C and 20% above 68 C (panel rated -20 to 70 C).
  - IR-rejecting film only if it shows no rainbow effect against the LCD polariser.
  - Brightness discipline:
  - Auto-dim from a VEML7700 behind a diffuser facing the same way as the screen.
  - Run at 30-50% most of the time and full only in direct sun.
  - Never exceed the datasheet LED current; the Midas 2500-nit point is rated only at room temperature in open air.
  - Use DC/analog dimming or 20-25 kHz PWM-to-analog, not burst PWM, for RF.
  - Do not rely on transflective or e-paper: the VIEWE 8in transflective has 15-20% NTSC colour and 300:1 contrast indoors, and e-paper smears a scrolling waterfall.
- **Acceptance tests:**
  - Luminance: show full white in a dark room and press a lux meter flat on the glass (L is about E/pi). Pass: Wisecoco at least 5600 lx (about 1800 nits); 4D or Newhaven at least 2800 lx (about 900 nits). Expect about 25% error; return the unit if it fails.
  - Touch: lsusb shows the touch VID:PID (WCH boards use 1a86). dmesg shows hid-multitouch bound. evtest shows ABS_MT_SLOT with the advertised number of points and X/Y ranges matching the panel. Touch must keep working at the 52 Hz clean mode.
  - EDID: edid-decode shows the preferred mode and its orientation, with VFP+VSW+VBP of at least 24 (or the edited EDID is accepted). The board must show no flicker, shear or colour fault at 128.70 MHz.
  - Boot robustness on held 6.18.2: the correct mode on 20 cold boots, 20 reboots and 10 HDMI re-plugs. Log head -1 /sys/class/drm/card1-HDMI-A-1/modes from a boot service each time.
  - Power on the 12 V rail with a 1.5 A limit: Wisecoco 9 W or less at full white; 4D about 6.5 W or less (datasheet 540 mA). Record the current at minimum and at full brightness.
  - Back-feed: with the display powered and the Q6A off, the USB VBUS at the Q6A side must read 0 V.
  - Optics: the pen-tip test shows no doubled reflection (bonded), and the polarized-sunglasses test passes at the chosen mounting orientation.
  - Thermal: a 30-minute full-white soak, then a 45-minute noon test face-on to the sun with hood and fan. Pass: frame 60 C or less, glass 65 C or less, no darkening or retention, no case deformation.
  - RF A/B: rtl_power sweeps (130-150, 430-440, 735-755, 1685-1715 MHz) and LimeSDR averaging (2200-2300 MHz), first into a terminator, then on the antenna. Compare display off, minimum, full, black screen, white screen and each mode. Pass: 1-2 dB or less rise. Also check u-blox UBX-MON-RF and C/N0 change by 1 dB-Hz or less.
  - Application: SDR++ and SatDump launched with XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11 tune by tap and drag. With the screen rotated, a touch in a corner lands in the same corner.
- **Ukraine purchase:** - **Bought locally:** the only module with 1000 nits or more, optical bonding and USB touch that is stocked in Ukraine is the 4D Systems range from neostore.in.ua on prom.ua (in stock, 12-month warranty, Nova Poshta, cash on delivery):
    - 7in 1280x800 1000-nit: 9,520 UAH
    - 8in 1280x800 1000-nit: 10,060 UAH
    - 7in 1024x600 1000-nit: 8,140 UAH
  
    prom.ua has no Wisecoco 7in FHD kit, no Lilliput 719, and nothing for ET070WU01 or ET070WU07. Its field monitors (Portkeys, SmallHD, FEELWORLD) have menu-only touch.
  - **Wisecoco:** order direct (wisecocodisplay.com, 'Add to cart' at $132) or from the Wisecoco AliExpress store. Ask for DHL or FedEx with a correct invoice under EUR 150.
  - **Customs (searches, Oct 2026):** Ukraine still applies the EUR 150 duty-free limit per international shipment. Above it, 10% duty and 20% VAT are charged; my understanding is that this applies to the amount over EUR 150, so verify on the order date. The Cabinet re-approved bills in Sept 2026 to charge VAT from EUR 0 (non-commercial up to EUR 45 exempt). Reports say not before July 2027, but the Rada has not passed them, so check before ordering.
  - **Midas:** Farnell export, EUR 324.37 ex VAT, 12 weeks. Expect about EUR 56 duty and VAT (calc) plus courier and broker fees; confirm Farnell ships to Ukraine at checkout.
  - **US items (Xenarc $429, Newhaven $120.20):** use a forwarder with a US warehouse such as Nova Poshta Global or Meest, or the vendor's own international shipping if quoted.
  - **Payment:** PayPal or card for buyer protection.
  - **Quality check:** get luminance and touch photos or video from the seller before shipping, and run the acceptance tests within the dispute window. AliExpress generally ships to Ukraine, but the SURENOO item could not be checked.
- **Open questions:**
  - Wisecoco: what is the panel part number? Is it the in-cell ET070FH01-HT-class glass (6.97in, active area 154.368x86.832 mm)? Is the 4500-nit backlight variant available, and can the board's LED driver supply it?
  - Wisecoco: which touch controller, and does the HDMI board output USB HID? Please give the lsusb VID:PID and the number of touch points. Is a separate USB cable included in the $132?

  - Wisecoco: board input voltage range and current at full brightness? Backlight driver IC, PWM frequency, and how brightness is set (keys, PWM pad or DDC/CI)?
  - Wisecoco: is the cover glass fully laminated (OCA/OCR) or air-gapped? AR or AG treatment, cover thickness, polariser transmission axis, and the LC clearing point or high-Tni rating?
  - Wisecoco: DHL or FedEx cost to Ukraine, invoice value, DDP option, and warranty or DOA policy?

    - **Subsystem:** Compute (Q6A)
    - **Topic:** Power input (J21 header)
    - **Current decision:** Feed J21 (pin 1 = 12 V, 2 = GND, 3 = PWR key) from a fused, reverse-protected, regulated buck at 9 V or 7.5 V, at least 3 A. Never power USB-C at the same time (Q5 back-feed). Never apply the raw 16.8 V 4S pack.
    - **Key numbers:** Header accepts 3.6-16 V (Radxa staff). SY81012 buck is a 16 V-class part. No fuse, TVS or reverse protection on the header. Use Pololu D36V50F9 or F7 (#4093 is the F7; the F12 is #4095). SMBJ13A clamps near 21 V, so it does not protect below 16 V; use an OVP eFuse near 13.5 V.
    - **Evidence:** forum.radxa.com/t/30400; schematic v1.21 DC-IN page; pololu.com.
    - **Status:** verified
    - **Conflicts or errors:** The research claim '12 V only, 5/9 V will not start' was refuted. The pack is undecided: small_antenna_stack accepts 3S (9-12.6 V) direct to J21, but the lab UI thresholds and its 12.0 V LDO assume 4S.
    - **Needed action:** Decide 3S vs 4S, then fix the buck and the UI thresholds.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://forum.radxa.com/t/30400
      - https://www.pololu.com/product/4095

    - **Topic:** LNB rail switching and regulator topology
    - **Current decision:** A buck-boost (or a boost with true output disconnect) set to 13.2 V. The rail is switched by a part rated 20 V or more (a second Pololu #2813 or an eFuse), plus an LC filter, a ferrite and a polyfuse. Never put the raw pack on the LNB.     - **Evidence:** small_antenna_stack verifier (topology reasoning); dish_replacement and rf_frontend.
    - **Status:** verified

Lens: +6..+9 dB. Typical SSB stations 5-15 dB below the beacon: -3 to -13 dB at 23 dBi. DATV beacon needs about 31-32 dBi (about a 45 cm dish); DATV stations need a 90 cm or larger dish.

Physics vs wish: readable typical SSB needs about 26 dBi and DATV needs 31-32 dBi, which only a dish provides; the closest compliant option is the 23 dBi gore horn plus the lens on a tripod.
    - **Needed action:** Run the A/B test (bare / cup / 3 gores / 6 gores) on 10489.500 and 10489.750 MHz to settle the model. Remove the optimistic figures from dish_replacement.

- **Open questions:**
  - Which country or region is the user in? It decides whether QO-100 (25.9°E) is visible at all, which Inmarsat-C NCS (Alphasat or I-6 F1) and LF time station (DCF77/MSF/WWVB/JJY) to use, whether Elektro-L/FY-2H can serve as references, legal limits, and landed prices.
  - Do small rigid antennas whose pieces are all 20-23 cm or less (17 cm whip, SRH-701/A-V85, 20 cm helical whip, 2/4-turn helices, bare LNB with cone) count as allowed alongside patch/chip and folding antennas?
  - LimeSDR Micro: keep the cancellable pre-order as a gated optional (decision gate 31 Jan 2027)? Is the order a refundable store pre-order or a campaign order? Which parts (12 GB Q6A, T7, 4th cell) are already bought?
  - S-band: if the Lime is dropped, is a TX-capable ADALM-PLUTO (TX unconfigured and terminated) acceptable, or should only a receive-only downconverter route be pursued?
  - May a VNA be swept into an antenna briefly indoors for S11 tuning, or must antenna tuning be strictly receive-only (sky/Sun noise, beacon C/N, GNSS C/N0)?
  - Does the no-loop rule also cover H-field near-field test probes and the AS3935 ferrite coil? The default is to exclude them.
  - Is the standard crossed Yagi with 35 cm boom halves and 34 cm elements acceptable, or must the ultra-compact (≤17-20 cm pieces, longer setup) build be the default?
  - Pack: 3S or 4S? This determines how the 13.2 V LNB and 12.0 V Boni-Whip rails are built.
  - Bench values still unpublished: Bullseye LNB current at 13.2 V and its length and waveguide ID; HF+ Discovery and Boni-Whip currents; Boni-Whip housing length; Balun One Nine DC path; Uputronics 435/403/1090 bias-voltage range.
  - On-air status checks before spending on the array or an AHRPT-rate SDR: Metop-B/C AHRPT at 1701.3/1707 MHz, AWS at 1707 MHz, and Elektro-L5 LRIT at 1691 MHz.
  - Which 70 cm band-pass filter or filtered preamp is actually purchasable? This is the main overload risk on the 8-bit V4L.
  - Which HDMI timing will the Q6A drive the Wisecoco panel at, and does a custom EDID avoid all lab-band harmonics (including AIS 162, ADS-B 1090 and Inmarsat-C 1544)?
  - Q6A RAM: the NPU design's 6-8 GiB IQ ring (Lime LIME-W 56 Msps) is incompatible with the small stack's 8 GB board downgrade. Keep 12 GB if the Lime stays?
  - Does ISS SSTV Series 34 (22-25 Oct 2026) run at 10 W like Series 31? This is the assumption behind the 'reliable on a 12 cm whip' rating.
- **Notes:** All 18 named final JSON files exist (plus foldable_partial.json and digest.md). The P1b register final/report_research.json does not exist yet. Most of the minute-log and summaries are in Ukrainian; I read them in full or in targeted excerpts.
  
  Biggest cross-file problems:
  1. small_antenna_stack applied a superseded deployed-size rule. Its removals (Lime, T7, 12 GB board, all foldables, 18 V branch) must be re-decided for the two-tier rule.
  2. Loops remain in small_antenna_stack (optional 20 cm loop and loop alternatives in its tables) and as conditional H-probes in radio_lab.
  3. Several files prescribe VNA S11 sweeps into antennas, which conflicts with the conducted-only rule.
  4. Three incompatible librtlsdr recipes.
  5. Four USB port maps.
  6. The 3S vs 4S pack choice breaks either the Boni-Whip 12 V LDO or the TVS.
  7. The SAWbird+ bias source, LNB voltage and current limit, and polyfuse ratings are inconsistent.
  8. The Lime frequency range is still misquoted as 30 MHz-3.8 GHz in two final texts.
  9. QO-100 and all geostationary targets assume a European location; the user's region is unknown.
  
  Objective position on the Lime: no reliable patch-tier target needs it. In the foldable/full-lab tier it is the only in-stack S-band path and the basis of the NPU wideband design. Keep it as a gated optional and keep the core (2x V4L + HF+) independent of it. The Airspy Mini is the cheaper receive-only route for L-band at 3.6-6 Msps (AWS/Metop), and the Pluto is the either/or S-band fallback.
  
  Physics vs wishes:
  - Patch/chip antennas cannot serve 137-146 MHz usefully. The closest options are the foldable V-dipole, or the experimental 20 cm helical whip.
  - QO-100 DATV (about 31-32 dBi) and readable typical SSB (about 26 dBi) need dish-class gain. The closest options are the 23 dBi gore horn plus the 300 mm lens.
  - No-loop HF is noise-limited near the handheld. The closest option is the wire with a 9:1 transformer, fed 5-10 m away.
  - Metop AHRPT needs about 16-19 dBic plus an SDR above 2.56 Msps. That means the experimental 2x2 fold array, and the target status is itself contested.
  
  Web checks (6 WebSearch, 5 WebFetch):
  - ARISS pages (fetched): Series 33 (2-6 Oct) and Series 34 (22-25 Oct 2026) are on 437.55 MHz, Robot 36. APRS is on 437.825 MHz and the FM repeater on 437.800 MHz (7 Oct status).
  - V4L datasheet (I extracted the PDF text): 500 kHz-1.766 GHz, 2.56 MHz stable, 4.5 V/180 mA bias tee, diplexer.
  - SAWbird+ GOES page: $44.95 Barebones, 180 mA nominal.
  - Crowd Supply: no Lime update after 17 Jun 2026.
  - Elektro-L5: rtl-sdr.com says commissioned, WMO says commissioning, SatNOGS lists it as unconfirmed.
  - Metop: OSPO shows Metop-C AHRPT 'No'; NOAA retires its Metop HRPT ground products on 1 Sep 2026.
  - Pluto: DigiKey prices vary by region ($197-$429).
  
  All link margins and antenna gains in the report are NEC or formula models (±1-3 dB, with EIRPs mostly assumed) until the on-air A/B tests are done.

## labui:hf_receiver (run `wf_fceb75d0-87e`)

- **Area:** HF receiver (about 100 kHz-30 MHz, plus LF/VLF where possible) for the Radxa Dragon Q6A handheld receive-only lab, with a small folding or collapsing NON-LOOP antenna. Per the user's latest request, no loop antennas, loop amplifiers, loop frames or loop-specific chokes are included.
- **Options:**
  1.
    - **Name:** Airspy HF+ Discovery (RECOMMENDED dedicated HF/LF/VLF receiver)
    - **What it is:** Pocket-size HF + VHF SDR with sigma-delta ADCs, an 18-bit DDC and band-tracking preselectors. Open-source driver (libairspyhf).
    - **Key specs:** HF 0.5 kHz-31 MHz and VHF 64-260 MHz. Up to 768 ksps IQ, 660 kHz alias-free. MDS -140 dBm (HF, 500 Hz). IIP3 +15 dBm at max gain (HF). Blocking dynamic range 110 dB on HF (WRTH estimates about 116 dB at 10 MHz). HF preselection: switched high-pass at about 0/5/10/17 MHz and low-pass at 5/31 MHz. Max input +10 dBm. 0.5 ppm clock. Single 50-ohm SMA input. No bias tee is listed on Airspy's page or RigPix.
    - **Linux arm64 support:** Good and open source. Ubuntu noble universe has airspyhf, libairspyhf1 and libairspyhf-dev 1.6.8-4build1 for arm64, so no source build is needed. SDR++'s ubuntu_noble aarch64 nightly is built against libairspyhf-dev, so airspyhf_source is included. SatDump has an airspyhf plugin and SDRangel has a plugins/samplesource/airspyhf plugin (SDRangel has no verified arm64 binary; build it from source). SoapyAirspyHF (pothosware) is not packaged in noble, so build it from source. The USB load is about 3.1 MB/s (768 ksps x 4 bytes), far below the roughly 30 MB/s measured on a Q6A USB 2.0 port, so it can share the black-port FE1.1s hub with Wi-Fi.
    - **Price:** $169 list (iTead; ships from EU/US warehouses in 3-6 days, otherwise from China). It was $135.20 in Airspy's 20% summer sale, Jun 27-Jul 4 2026.
    - **Pros:** Best HF strong-signal handling per dollar. WRTH: 'Best value SDR'; Guy Atkins found it 'close to identical' to the $899 Elad FDM-DUOr; Leif SM5BSZ ranked it second only to the Perseus in most tests. Covers VLF/LF down to 0.5 kHz. Very small and USB 2.0 only. Open driver in apt. Double duty: its 64-260 MHz range with 95 dB VHF blocking dynamic range can back up the V4L for 137 MHz LRPT or 145.8 MHz near strong FM.
    - **Cons:** Only 660 kHz of usable bandwidth: it cannot show the whole HF spectrum at once, so the NPU classifier must sweep or work in narrow windows. The case is plastic (WRTH: 60x42x12 mm plastic box) and a community comment says the HF+ picks up EMI from its host, so it needs shielding inside the handheld. No bias tee is listed, so an active antenna needs an external injector. Current draw is not published (unverified; measure it).
    - **Sources:**
      - https://airspy.com/airspy-hf-discovery/
      - https://www.itead.cc/product/airspy-hf-discovery/
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/?p=66258
      - https://airspy.com/downloads/WRTH2020Features_Airspy_Discovery_review.pdf
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/airspy-hf-discovery-collection-of-tests-and-reviews/
      - https://swling.com/blog/2019/08/airspy-hf-discovery-first-impressions-on-medium-wave-vs-elad-fdm-duor/
      - https://packages.ubuntu.com/search?keywords=airspyhf&searchon=names&suite=noble&section=all
      - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AlexandreRouma/SDRPlusPlus/master/docker_builds/ubuntu_noble/do_build.sh
      - https://github.com/pothosware/SoapyAirspyHF
      - https://github.com/f4exb/sdrangel/tree/master/plugins/samplesource
      - https://rigpix.com/miscrx/airspy_hfplusdiscovery.htm
    - **Community reports:** WRTH 2020: 'truly a pocketable item and ideal for portable use'; listening tests showed it 'barely distinguishable' from the Excalibur Pro. G4ELI: 'virtually immune to strong signals' on Band II. A portable build of the original HF+ with a Raspberry Pi 3 and the 7-inch touch LCD got about 3.5 h from a 13000 mAh bank; the builder had to tackle noise from the Pi's USB bus, and a commenter said the HF+ picks up EMI from the host (rtl-sdr.com). A RadioReference user runs a PA0NHC Mini Whip with the Discovery for VLF. A reviewer reports that early-prototype overload above 19 MHz was fixed in production units.
    - **Size weight power:** 45x60x10 mm (Airspy) or 60x42x12 mm plastic (WRTH). iTead lists 75x45x10 mm and 105.6 g (that figure may include packaging; unverified). 5 V USB bus power. Current not published by Airspy or RigPix; icholakov measured it on video but the numbers are not in the text.
  2.
    - **Name:** RTL-SDR Blog V4L built-in HF mode (BUDGET / fallback; use a second V4L)
    - **What it is:** The V4L already in the lab. It has a built-in upconverter with a 28.8 MHz LO, so you tune HF directly. Direct sampling is not used.
    - **Key specs:** Datasheet: 500 kHz-1.766 GHz, 'Upconverter with 28.8 MHz LO', diplexer front end, no notch filter, 8-bit RTL2832U, 2.56 MS/s stable, 4.5 V / 180 mA bias tee, 250-270 mA. The HF upconverter path covers about 0.5-28.8 MHz (earlier-stage reading). HF MDS is 'significantly improved' over V3 direct sampling: about -135 dBm versus -115 to -120 dBm, read from the chart by the earlier stage. Its two-tone (95 MHz blocker) results are 'identical to the V3'. Datasheet: 'very strong reception may still require front end attenuation/filtering'.
    - **Linux arm64 support:** Already planned. Use the patched librtlsdr (osmocom 2.0.3 / commit 0204c9c) with SoapyRTLSDR, SDR++, SatDump and GNU Radio, as in narrowband_sdr.json. Without the updated driver the V4L gives no signal.
    - **Price:** $0 extra if it timeshares the existing V4L. A dedicated second unit costs $37.95 (official store), or about $34.20 on the official AliExpress listing.
    - **Pros:** Cheapest. 2.4 MHz windows feed the NPU classifier better than the HF+'s 660 kHz. Has a bias tee. Same software stack as the satellite chain.
    - **Cons:** No LF/VLF (500 kHz floor). 8-bit: overloads near MW/SW broadcast transmitters with a long wire, so add the AM band-stop or attenuation. Spur families from 28.8 MHz (shared TCXO and LO). Users report an HF noise floor about 1-1.5 dB higher than the V4. The main V4L is committed to 137/145/435 MHz and the QO-100 IF, so HF at the same time needs a second V4L on a black USB 2.0 port (about 4.8 MB/s). The R828S stock is finite.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/RTLSDR_V4L_Datasheet4.pdf
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/V4L
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/rtl-sdr-blog-v4l-lite-now-available-for-purchase/
      - https://www.reddit.com/r/RTLSDR/comments/1pfnvqa/rtlsdr_creates_fake_signals_that_spread_from_288/
    - **Community reports:** r/RTLSDR: spur families spreading from 28.8 MHz even with no antenna; fixes are lower LNA gain and setting gain stages separately. RTL-SDR Blog: activating direct sampling on a V4 'will yield no results'. A few users report the V4L's HF noise floor about 1-1.5 dB above the V4 (narrowband_sdr.json forum stage).
    - **Size weight power:** Dongle size, aluminium case. 250-270 mA at 5 V (about 1.3 W).
  3.
    - **Name:** LimeFEA HF Micro add-on for the LimeSDR Micro M.2
    - **What it is:** Companion board that adds a third, direct-sampling 0-30 MHz RX path to the LimeSDR Micro M.2 2280 (Basic or GNSS). The base Micro covers only 30 MHz-3.8 GHz.
    - **Key specs:** 0-30 MHz direct sampling into the second pair of LA9310 analogue baseband inputs over a 15-pin FPC. 90 dB gain, 72 dB step attenuator, MW broadcast notch, filters at 0-2 MHz LPF, 2-12 MHz BPF and 12-30 MHz BPF ('relatively basic band filtering'; Lime says an external preselector may help). Includes two FPC cables and five MHF4-to-SMA transitions; I2C is used for control.
    - **Linux arm64 support:** Unverified for the HF path. Crowd Supply names LimeSuiteNG (with a SoapySDR plug-in) only for the product in general. No HF-path support is documented in the limesdr-micro-staging branch that the lab already depends on.
    - **Price:** $199 pre-order plus $18 worldwide shipping. Orders placed now ship Dec 15, 2026.
    - **Pros:** Uses no USB port (it rides on the M.2/PCIe Lime). Direct sampling captures the whole HF range, which is attractive for the NPU waterfall. Has a built-in MW notch and step attenuator.
    - **Cons:** Not shipping until Dec 15, 2026, and HF software support is unproven. It adds a board, FPC cables and MHF4 transitions inside the handheld. It costs more than the HF+ Discovery and has weaker preselection. Its channel concurrency with the Lime's RF RX (shared LA9310) is unverified. The LimeSDR Micro itself is a transceiver, so TX must stay disabled in the menu.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.crowdsupply.com/lime-micro/limesdr-micro
    - **Community reports:** No user reports were found (the product is not shipping yet).
    - **Size weight power:** Size and power are not published.

    - **What it is:** 14-bit, 1 kHz-2 GHz single-tuner SDR with an 11-band preselector.

The Linux .run installer contains an arm64 library: SDR++'s noble aarch64 CI copies arm64/libsdrplay_api.so.3.15 from API 3.15.2. SDRplay says Linux is 'only tested and supported on Ubuntu LTS distributions up to 24.04 LTS', which fits the held noble image but blocks a move to 26.04. SoapySDRPlay3 needs API 3.15 or later.     - **Name:** ANTENNA A (RECOMMENDED primary): wire on a winder + 9:1 unun (Tecsun AN-05 7 m reel or a 10-15 m DIY wire on a winder + Nooelec Balun One Nine v2)
    - **What it is:** Passive random-wire HF antenna. The wire winds onto a small reel, and a 9:1 transformer at the feed point drives 3-5 m of thin 50-ohm coax back to the handheld.

A 49:1 transformer is meant for end-fed wires near a half wave (for example about 20 m for 7 MHz or about 10 m for 14 MHz); for a broadband random wire, 9:1 is the usual choice (engineering judgement, not measured).

    - **Cons:** Needs a support (tree, branch or pole) and a few minutes to deploy. It is not usable while walking. It is weak at LF/VLF with only 7 m. Long wires build static, so discharge the wire before connecting and never use it in thunderstorms (the balun's varistor is a last line of defence).

    - **Linux arm64 support:** N/A. Feed the bias tee from a filtered 12 V rail made from the 4S pack (12.8-16.8 V) with a low-noise linear regulator and a polyfuse (engineering recommendation).
    - **Price:** Moonraker US$123.95 (was $134.95), £109.95, €127.27. WIMO €135-159 incl. VAT. One WIMO page says available from 20.11.2026.
    - **Pros:** Fits the antenna size rule (under 20 cm). Covers VLF to 300 MHz. Ships with its injector, so no DIY bias tee. Weatherproof. Can take the lab's 23 cm-1 m telescopic elements as a longer radiator (thread compatibility unverified).
    - **Cons:** Like every small E-field antenna, it receives the voltage between its element and its ground or coax shield, so performance depends on mounting and grounding. Mounted on or near the handheld, local noise will dominate. Needs about 2 m+ height and a ground stake or counterpoise. Costs about 5x a clone.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.wimo.com/en/18067
      - https://moonrakeronline.com/us/bonito-boni-whip-active-antenna
      - https://www.pa3fwm.nl/technotes/tn07.html
      - https://pa3fwm.nl/technotes/tn09d.html
    - **Community reports:** No user reports were opened for the Boni-Whip (retailer data only). General active-whip physics from PA3FWM: received signal is 'directly proportional to the height of the antenna above ground'; 'if the antenna is only grounded in the shack, via the coax cable, much noise can be picked up'; a fully isolated system receives 'nothing'.
    - **Size weight power:** Radiator 14-17 cm, 189 g, 9-15 V via the included bias tee (current not published).
  9.
    - **Name:** ANTENNA B-budget: PA0RDT-type miniwhip clone (10 kHz-30 MHz)
    - **What it is:** Small PCB-plate active E-field antenna (PA0RDT design family), sold as clones and kits.
    - **Key specs:** Passion Radio listing: 10 kHz-30 MHz, built-in preamp, 9-15 V via bias-T (12 V nominal), SMA female, install 'outdoors... away from all metal sources and at a height of at least 2 metres'. A plate of about 2 pF gives a useful signal (PA3FWM).
    - **Linux arm64 support:** N/A. Needs a bias tee rated down to about 10 kHz. A generic RF bias tee rated from MHz upward will not pass LF/VLF properly (engineering note). Use the kit's own injector or a DIY one with a large choke and large coupling capacitor.
    - **Price:** Passion Radio 'Active 0-50 MHz mini antenna' €25.90 incl. VAT, in stock. The 10 kHz-30 MHz item's price was not captured. Tindie and AliExpress kits not verified (Tindie returned 403).
    - **Pros:** Very cheap and very small. Good LF/MF/low-HF coverage when mounted correctly.
    - **Cons:** Clone quality varies: a RadioReference user found the ra0sms mini whip produced noise spikes every 10 kHz and '100% static'. Same grounding and placement sensitivity as the Boni-Whip. Needs a separate 12 V injector.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.passion-radio.com/sdr-antennas/mini-whip-1012.html
      - https://forums.radioreference.com/threads/problems-with-ra0sms-mini-whip-antenna.354968/
      - https://www.rtl-sdr.com/an-opensource-mini-whip-antenna-and-upconverter-design-for-rtl-sdrs/
      - https://www.pa3fwm.nl/technotes/tn07.html
    - **Community reports:** rtl-sdr.com open-source mini-whip guidance: install it 'up high and preferably away from the house' because mini-whips are 'quite susceptible to local noise pickup', and they 'need to have a good ground connection'. PA0NHC's installation guide says to run the ground wire to the PCB GND point, not to the coax.
    - **Size weight power:** PCB about 10-20 cm in a tube (typical, unverified). 12 V at tens of mA (unverified).
  10.
    - **Name:** ANTENNA C (quick look only): telescopic whip, reusing the lab's RTL-SDR Blog dipole-kit elements (23 cm collapsed, 1 m extended, M5)
    - **What it is:** A passive short whip or short dipole on the 50-ohm SDR input.
    - **Key specs:** A whip is about 10 pF per metre (PA3FWM). Into 50 ohms, a 1 m whip loses roughly -50 dB at 1 MHz, -30 dB at 10 MHz and -20 dB at 30 MHz compared with a high-impedance buffer (my estimate from Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C) with C = 10 pF; not measured).
    - **Linux arm64 support:** N/A.
    - **Price:** $0 (already in the BOM as the 137 MHz dipole kit, $17.95).
    - **Pros:** Instant to deploy and already carried. Adequate for strong SW broadcast and 10-30 MHz in daytime.
    - **Cons:** Too inefficient below about 5 MHz on a 50-ohm input, and very close to the device's noise. As the main HF antenna it is rejected; use it as the radiator on an active buffer (Antenna B) instead.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://www.pa3fwm.nl/technotes/tn07.html
      - /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-lizbeth307/f89a86b4-fa51-5ce8-96da-e73d5f771cf3/scratchpad/final/foldable_antennas.json
    - **Community reports:** None specific; the figures are a physics estimate.
    - **Size weight power:** 23 cm collapsed. 0 W.
- **Recommendation:** Add an Airspy HF+ Discovery (about $169 list, $135 in Airspy's sales) as the dedicated HF/LF/VLF receiver (0.5 kHz-31 MHz):
  - Plug it into one of the Q6A's black USB 2.0 ports. It needs about 3.1 MB/s, which the FE1.1s hub can share with Wi-Fi. The blue USB 3.1 port stays with the V4L.
  - Install it with apt (airspyhf 1.6.8-4build1 arm64). It runs natively in the SDR++ noble aarch64 nightly, SatDump and SDRangel; build SoapyAirspyHF from source.
  - Put it inside a shielded compartment bonded to the USB shield, because its case is plastic. Feed it from a clean 5 V rail with ferrites on a short USB lead.
  
  Antenna kit (no loops):
  - **Primary: a wire on a winder** (Tecsun AN-05 7 m reel, about $14.50, or 10-15 m of thin wire on a winder) with a Nooelec Balun One Nine v2 9:1 ($26.95) at the feed point.
    - Add a 3-5 m counterpoise wire on the ground.
    - Run 3-5 m of thin coax to the handheld, with clip-on ferrites at the receiver end as a general common-mode choke (not a loop accessory).
  - **For LF/VLF and camp use: a Bonito Boni-Whip** (14-17 cm, bias tee included, about $124-159).
    - Feed it 12 V from the 4S pack through a low-noise linear regulator and a polyfuse.
    - Mount it at least 2 m up and away from the device, with a ground stake or counterpoise.
    - A PA0RDT-type miniwhip clone (about €26) is the cheap substitute.
  - **The lab's 23 cm-1 m telescopic elements** serve only as a quick-look whip for strong stations, or as the Boni-Whip's radiator.
  - **Optional:** an AM broadcast band-stop (500 kHz-1.7 MHz, >50 dB, about €23) near strong MW transmitters. It matters mainly for the 8-bit V4L.
  
  Budget path: use the V4L's built-in upconverter (0.5-28.8 MHz) with the same wire and 9:1. A second V4L ($37.95, on a black USB 2.0 port) is needed if HF must run while the first V4L tracks satellites. This path has no LF/VLF.
  
  Do not buy the LimeFEA HF Micro ($199, ships Dec 15, 2026) until LimeSuiteNG support for its HF path is proven. Use the SDRplay RSPdx-R2 only as a bench or home upgrade: it is too big at 315 g, and its closed API needs restarts on ARM.
- **Requirements or findings:**
  - The V4L has an HF mode, and it is an upconverter, not direct sampling. The datasheet lists 'HF Implementation: Upconverter with 28.8 MHz LO', 500 kHz-1.766 GHz, a diplexer front end and no notch. RTL-SDR Blog says there is 'no need to activate direct sampling', and that activating direct sampling on a V4 'will yield no results'. Its two-tone results are identical to the V3, and 'very strong reception may still require front end attenuation/filtering'. There are spur families from 28.8 MHz. It has no LF/VLF.
  - The LimeSDR Micro M.2 covers only '30 MHz - 3.8 GHz'. Below 30 MHz you need the LimeFEA HF Micro: a separate 0-30 MHz direct-sampling third RX path into the LA9310 baseband inputs over FPC, $199, shipping Dec 15, 2026. Its HF-path software support is not documented. The Lime is also a 1T2R transceiver, so the menu must never expose TX.
  - USB budget: three black USB 2.0 ports share one FE1.1s hub with Wi-Fi, and the single blue USB 3.1 port is taken by the V4L (narrowband_sdr.json). An HF receiver must therefore be a USB 2.0 device with low throughput. The HF+ needs about 3.1 MB/s, a second V4L about 4.8 MB/s and the RSP1B up to 10 MS/s. USB-3-only HF SDRs (RX-888 MkII, Fobos) are ruled out.
  - Overload criteria for small antennas: the HF+ Discovery has 110 dB blocking dynamic range on HF (WRTH estimate about 116 dB at 10 MHz), IIP3 +15 dBm, max input +10 dBm and four HF preselector banks. The RSP1B and RSPdx-R2 have 11-12 band filters plus MW/FM/DAB notches, and the RSPdx-R2 adds HDR mode on LF/MW. The 8-bit V4L is the most overload-prone. A small whip delivers less signal than a wire, so overload matters mainly with long wires near MW/SW broadcast sites.
  - arm64 software (verified):
  - Ubuntu noble universe ships airspyhf, libairspyhf1 and libairspyhf-dev 1.6.8-4build1 for arm64.
  - SDR++'s ubuntu_noble aarch64 build installs libairspyhf-dev and the SDRplay API 3.15.2, copying the arm64 library, and enables OPT_BUILD_SDRPLAY_SOURCE.
  - SoapyAirspyHF and SoapySDRPlay3 are not packaged in noble; SoapySDRPlay3 needs API 3.15 or later.
  - SDRangel (v7.27.2) has airspyhf, sdrplayv3, rtlsdr and soapysdrinput plugins; no arm64 binary was confirmed.
  - SDRplay supports Linux only on Ubuntu LTS up to 24.04.
  - How small active E-field antennas work (PA3FWM): the receiver sees the potential difference between the plate or whip and its ground or coax shield. Signal is proportional to height. Grounding only through the coax picks up 'much noise', and a fully isolated system receives 'nothing'. A common-mode choke helps only when there is a ground. For a battery handheld, this means a ground stake or counterpoise wire at the mast or feed, with the antenna mounted at least 2 m up and away from the electronics.
  - Noise from the handheld: switching bucks, the 2000-nit backlight driver, HDMI, USB and the Q6A all radiate most strongly at HF. A portable HF+ build with a Pi and 7-inch touch LCD needed work on Pi USB-bus noise, and a commenter says the HF+ picks up host EMI.
  Mitigations (engineering recommendations):
  - Keep the antenna feed point 5-10 m away on thin coax lying on the ground, with ferrites at the receiver end.
  - Run on battery only, with no charger attached.
  - Shield the HF+ and bond it to the USB shield.
  - Use an 'HF quiet' menu profile that dims or blanks the display, turns Wi-Fi off and parks the Lime.
  - Do A/B noise-floor sweeps (terminated input, display on and off) at about 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10 and 20 MHz.
  - Expected antenna performance (engineering estimates, not measured):
  - A 7-15 m wire with a 9:1 transformer, raised 2-5 m and away from the device, should be limited by external noise across most of 3-30 MHz on the HF+.
  - A miniwhip or Boni-Whip at 2 m or more with a ground is the best compact option for LF/MF and lower HF.
  - A 1 m telescopic whip directly on 50 ohms loses roughly 50/30/20 dB at 1/10/30 MHz compared with a high-impedance buffer (C about 10 pF), so it suits only strong signals.
  - LF/VLF: the HF+ starts at 0.5 kHz, the Boni-Whip at 9-20 kHz, PA0RDT-type miniwhips at 10 kHz, the RSPdx-R2 at 1 kHz (with HDR) and the V4L at 500 kHz. Suitable receive-only targets include LF time signals (60/77.5 kHz), NDBs and NAVTEX (490/518 kHz). For SID space-weather monitoring, log only the carrier amplitude of VLF stations and never demodulate them. Performance below about 10 kHz (sferics, whistlers) with these antennas is unverified.
  - Receive-only HF functions suitable for the menu:
  - AM, SSB and CW listening in SDR++.
  - FT8 and WSPR decode-only, with no PTT or CAT configured.
  - NAVTEX/SITOR-B and HF WEFAX reception.
  - Time signals.
  - An HF band-scan and survey mode for the NPU classifier.
  The HF+'s 660 kHz windows mean the classifier must sweep; the V4L or RSP give wider windows.
  - Power: no maker publishes current draw for the HF+ Discovery, RSP1B or RSPdx-R2 (RigPix also leaves the HF+ field blank). Bench-measure each one. The V4L draws 250-270 mA, and the SpyVerter R2 under 100 mA from the bias tee. Active-antenna bias (9-15 V) must come from the 4S pack through a regulator, never from the USB 5 V rail.
- **Rejected:**
  1.
    - **Name:** Any loop antenna (YouLoop, MLA-30+, Wellbrook, etc.), loop amplifiers (including the LZ1AQ loop/dipole amplifier), loop frames and loop-specific chokes
    - **Why:** The user explicitly removed the loop and everything for it.
  2.
    - **Name:** HackRF One (and HackRF-class transceivers) as the HF receiver
    - **Why:** Starts at 1 MHz, 8-bit, no HF preselection, and is damaged above -5 dBm input. It is a half-duplex transceiver, which conflicts with the receive-only lab.
  3.
    - **Name:** RX-888 MkII
    - **Why:** Needs USB 3: ka9q-radio docs cite over 2 Gb/s at 129.6 MS/s. The only USB 3.1 port is used by the V4L. Users report thermal problems, powered hubs failing and Pi 4 enumeration trouble.
  4.
    - **Name:** RigExpert Fobos SDR
    - **Why:** A USB 3.0 device at £375-430 (Moonraker). Retailers give conflicting HF coverage (100 kHz versus 25 MHz floor). It duplicates the Lime's VHF/UHF coverage.
  5.
    - **Name:** Nooelec Ham It Up Plus v2 ($79.95, 300 Hz-65 MHz, 125 MHz TCXO) / Ham It Up Nano ($49.95 at launch)
    - **Why:** Redundant with the V4L's built-in upconverter. Behind the Lime, the 125-155 MHz IF falls below the Lime's matched LNAL range (from 300 MHz per narrowband_sdr.json). It needs its own USB 5 V power and adds a box with no gain over the HF+.
  6.
    - **Name:** RTL-SDR V3 or clone direct-sampling mode for HF
    - **Why:** Nyquist folding around 14.4 MHz and an HF MDS of about -115 to -120 dBm, versus about -135 dBm on the V4L upconverter (datasheet chart via narrowband_sdr.json).
  7.
    - **Name:** Standalone RTL-SDR Blog HF upconverter
    - **Why:** None was found in the sources checked. RTL-SDR Blog's HF path is the upconverter built into the V4/V4L (not exhaustively verified).
  8.
    - **Name:** Passive telescopic whip directly on 50 ohms as the main HF antenna
    - **Why:** Roughly -50 dB at 1 MHz and -30 dB at 10 MHz versus a buffered whip (estimate), and it sits right next to the device's noise. Kept only for quick looks, or as an active-whip radiator.
  9.
    - **Name:** KiwiSDR / WebSDR remote receivers
    - **Why:** They need a network, so they do not fit a standalone, no-phone handheld. At most, offer them as an optional online extra.
  10.
    - **Name:** Mounting the miniwhip or active whip directly on the handheld
    - **Why:** Per PA3FWM the coax shield or ground is half the antenna, so the device's own noise would be received. Place it at least 2 m up and away, with a ground.
- **Notes:** Unverified items:
  - Current draw of the HF+ Discovery, RSP1B, RSPdx-R2 and Boni-Whip.
  - The HF+ USB connector type and weight (iTead's 105.6 g may include packaging).
  - The Boni-Whip supply range (9-15 V comes from a search snippet of the WIMO Spanish page).
  - Price of the Passion Radio 10 kHz-30 MHz miniwhip (only the related €25.90 0-50 MHz unit was captured).
  - Whether the Airspy Mini's bias tee can power a SpyVerter R2.
  - An SDRangel arm64 binary.
  - LimeSuiteNG support for the LimeFEA HF path.
  - Whether the Boni-Whip thread fits the M5 dipole-kit elements.
  
  Engineering estimates, not measurements:
  - The 10 pF/m whip loss figures.
  - Expected wire and whip performance.
  - The 3.1 MB/s HF+ USB load (768 ksps x 2 x 16-bit).
  
  The AM band-stop price (€23 incl. VAT) is from the Passion Radio related-products listing.
  
  Prices are list prices, mostly in USD, GBP or EUR; shipping to the user's country is not verified.
  
  For the menu designer:
  - Keep HF decoders decode-only, with no PTT/CAT and no TX.
  - I did not add HFDL/ACARS message decoders, because their message text can carry private operational content.
  - Treat VLF stations only as amplitude beacons for SID logging.
  
  Web budget: 10 WebSearch calls used.

## labui:existing_software (run `wf_fceb75d0-87e`)

- **Area:** Lab UI software for a receive-only, menu-driven field lab on the Radxa Dragon Q6A (Ubuntu 24.04 noble arm64, 7 in 1920x1080 touch). Covers all-in-one SDR apps (SDRangel, OpenWebRX+, SDR++, SatDump, CyberEther, Gqrx), SDR distributions with menus, and touch or kiosk shells (cage, labwc, Phosh, GNOME, on-screen keyboards, Qt Quick launcher, local web app in a kiosk). Includes the HF receiver's software side. The loop antenna and everything for it were removed at the user's request, so no loop items appear anywhere below.
- **Options:**
  1.
    - **Name:** SDRangel 7.27.2, receive-only source build (core engine)
    - **What it is:** An all-in-one Qt5/OpenGL SDR receiver and analyzer built from plugins. It is the single existing program that covers the most lab functions. Version 7.27.2 was released 19 Aug 2026; master was at 137c608 on 17 Oct 2026.
    - **Key specs:** - Receive channel plugins (master): WDSP RX (HF communications receiver), SSB, AM, NFM, WFM, BFM, NAVTEX (518/490/4209.5 kHz), DSC, WEFAX, RTTY, PSK31, FT8 (receive), DRM, DAB, radio clock (MSF, DCF77, TDF, WWVB, JJY), ADS-B, AIS, VOR, ILS, packet/APRS, radiosonde (RS41), Inmarsat C (EGC/SafetyNET, 1537-1541 MHz), APT, heat map, noise figure (Y-factor), radio astronomy (spectrometer, radiometer, Tsys/Jy calibration), channel power, channel analyzer, frequency scanner, frequency tracker, SigMF/file sink, remote TCP sink and UDP sink.
  - Feature plugins: Map (2D/3D; shows ADS-B, AIS, APRS, satellites, radiosondes, heat maps), Satellite Tracker (on AOS it loads presets, starts or stops acquisition and corrects Doppler), Star Tracker, Sky Map, SID, AIS, APRS, Radiosonde, Frequency Display (large readout), Jogdial Controller, Remote Control (VISA, Home Assistant, Kasa), rigctl server, GS-232 rotator.
  - On master there is also an MCP server plugin (HTTP, port 8092). Whether it is in a tagged release is not verified.
  - Devices: native RTL-SDR, Airspy HF+, SDRplay (V3 API plugin 'sdrplayv3'), SoapySDR input, and LimeSDR (legacy LimeSuite only).
  - Configurations save the whole setup (workspaces, device sets, features, window geometry) in named groups. The REST API (Swagger) loads one with PATCH /sdrangel/configuration and also serves /deviceset/{i}/spectrum/data.
  - Touch: tap-and-hold acts as right-click (CRightClickEnabler), pinch zoom works on the spectrum and maps (PRs #1539/#1540), and there is an optional tabbed sub-window layout (the default on Android).
  - Build switches allow a receive-only build: ENABLE_CHANNELTX, ENABLE_FEATURE_SIMPLEPTT, ENABLE_CHANNELMIMO_BEAMSTEERINGCWMOD, ENABLE_CHANNELRX_DEMODDSD, ..._DEMODPAGER and others.
    - **Linux arm64 support:** - No upstream Linux arm64 binary. The 7.27.2 assets are amd64 .debs for Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, an amd64 snap, an x86_64 flatpak, Windows and macOS.
  - The Flathub flatpak is marked end-of-life.
  - Debian forky/sid ship 7.27.2+dfsg-1+b1 for arm64. Ubuntu has it only in the development series ('stonking'); noble does not.
  - Upstream's build guide targets Ubuntu 24.04 with Qt 5.15, the same base as Radxa OS r2. Build from source, or backport the Debian sid source package (not tested on Q6A).
  - On aarch64, use -DENABLE_LIBUNWIND=OFF if the link step fails (issue #2741).
    - **Price:** $0 (GPL-3.0)
    - **Pros:** - Covers in one process almost every receive function the lab plans: HF utility and maritime safety, ADS-B, AIS, APRS, radiosondes, SafetyNET, satellite tracking with Doppler, radio astronomy, noise figure and GPS heat maps, all with a shared map.
  - Can run several SDRs at once as separate device sets (V4L, LimeSDR Micro via Soapy, HF receiver).
  - Saved Configurations plus the REST API make it scriptable from a touch launcher.
  - Has real touch handling (long-press, pinch).
  - Build flags strip transmit.
    - **Cons:** - Dense desktop-style UI: many small widgets and digit wheels. At 315 PPI it needs about 2x scaling, which leaves roughly 960x540 logical pixels and is cramped.
  - Jogdial control works only while the plugin has focus.
  - No Meteor LRPT/HRPT imagery decoder, no SSTV, no CubeSat telemetry framework.
  - The native LimeSDR plugin uses legacy LimeSuite, so the LimeSDR Micro must go through SoapySDR (LimeSuiteNG registers driver 'limesuiteng').
  - The 3D map (Cesium; needs your own API key since 2025) and Sky Map (WWT, ESASky, Aladin) need internet. Field use needs a local or offline tile source for the 2D map.
  - The Heat Map wants NMEA from a serial GPS at 4800 baud.
  - Sample-sink (TX device) plugins are always built and must be deleted after install.
  - No published Q6A or A78 CPU benchmarks.
    - **Community reports:** - GitHub #2741 (closed 22 Jul 2026): aarch64 link error with libunwind on a Pi 5 running Trixie. -DENABLE_LIBUNWIND=OFF builds; upstream CMake fix in e83a546.
  - GitHub #2246: 3D map blank on Pi 5 under Raspberry Pi OS but fine on Ubuntu 24.04. A Cesium quota problem was found; the fix is your own key (#2446).
  - GitHub #2526: the ARM flatpak stopped starting after 7.22.9.
  - I could not reach groups.io (HTTP 402) for touchscreen reports.
    - **Size weight power:** Software only. The amd64 .deb is about 75 MB. CPU, RAM and power on the Q6A have not been measured.
    - **Sources:**
      - https://github.com/f4exb/sdrangel/releases/tag/v7.27.2
      - https://github.com/f4exb/sdrangel/releases/expanded_assets/v7.27.2

  2.
    - **Name:** OpenWebRX+ 1.2.126 (luarvique PPA, noble arm64), shown in a local kiosk view
    - **What it is:** A browser-based receiver server with built-in and background (scheduled) decoders. It is the most touch-friendly existing HF/VHF receiver UI and is designed to run headless on small ARM boards.
    - **Key specs:** - PPA lists noble packages for amd64, arm64 and armhf. Current: openwebrx 1.2.126, csdr 0.18.41, dump1090-fa 8.2, sonde-decoders 1.8.1, rtl-433 25.12, dream 2.2, csdr-skimmer 1.12, soapysdr-module-sdrplay3 0.8.11.
  - Decoders include FT8/FT4/WSPR and other WSJT modes, CW and RTTY skimmers, SSTV, FAX, NAVTEX, SITOR-B, DSC, AIS, ADS-B, APRS (direwolf), radiosondes, DRM, RDS, and SatDump-based weather-satellite background decoding (not real-time).
  - Scheduler runs background decoding. Map and a scanner are built in.
  - Touch: waterfall panning and zooming; a long press acts as right-click.
  - Devices: RTL-SDR v3/v4, Airspy HF+, SDRplay via SoapySDRPlay3, HackRF, Hermes Lite 2 (as a receiver), and SoapySDR devices.
  - Each mode appears only if its decoder binary is installed (owrx/feature.py). That makes policy filtering a matter of which packages you install.
  - Docker images exist for ARM64.
    - **Linux arm64 support:** - Native noble arm64 packages in the PPA.
  - LimeSDR support hard-codes Soapy driver 'lime' (owrx/source/lime_sdr.py), while LimeSuiteNG registers 'limesuiteng'. The LimeSDR Micro will not appear without a small source-module patch.
  - RTL-SDR and the planned HF receivers are supported.
    - **Price:** $0 (AGPL)
    - **Pros:** - Best touch UX of the existing receivers.
  - Background decoders keep logging while nobody watches: FT8/WSPR propagation, NAVTEX, FAX, ISS SSTV, APRS, radiosondes.
  - One web UI can be embedded in the launcher (QtWebEngine) or a Chromium kiosk.
  - Strong HF coverage for the new HF receiver.
  - Receive-only by design.
    - **Cons:** - A web server plus a browser costs CPU and RAM.
  - Its many optional decoders include ones that must not be installed under the lab rules: digital voice (digiham/codecserver), POCSAG/FLEX pagers, TETRA (dxlaprs-tetra), aviation datalink (acarsdec, dumphfdl, dumpvdl2), LoRa/Meshtastic, and speech-to-text (whisper).
  - The maps use online tiles.
  - Weather-satellite support is backup decoding only.
  - The author says SDRplay is unreliable.
  - Needs the LimeSDR Micro driver-name patch.
    - **Community reports:** - The author's documentation calls SDRplay operation unreliable and suggests a powered hub.
  - The original OpenWebRX wiki says it runs on a Pi 2 and up, and that digital voice needs a Pi 3B+ or better.
  - I found no published report of OpenWebRX+ as a local touchscreen kiosk on a portable (one search).
    - **Size weight power:** Software only. No Q6A load data.
    - **Sources:**

      - https://luarvique.github.io/ppa/noble/Packages
      - https://fms.komkon.org/OWRX/
      - https://github.com/luarvique/openwebrx/blob/master/owrx/feature.py
